findings.title: Unvalidated remote data downloads to local filesystem
findings.description: The documentation includes helper code that downloads arbitrary URLs (DepMap/Figshare data files) and writes them directly to a local path without checksum/integrity verification or path validation. This is normal for a bioinformatics data-access skill, but unverified downloads represent a minor supply-chain/integrity risk if a URL is substituted or the source is compromised. No exfiltration, credential access, or secret material was observed anywhere in the skill.
findings.remediation: Pin dataset URLs/versions, verify checksums of downloaded files, and constrain output_path to a sandboxed working directory.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The visible SKILL.md content is benign: it is a prompt-only framework for scoring text across 12 cognitive dimensions, with no prompt injection, no jailbreak language, no concealment directives, and no instructions to run commands or contact external services. However, there is a serious mismatch between the documented skill and the shipped package. The manifest declares only Read and Write tools and the instructions mention no tooling, yet the package bundles 8 undocumented Python scripts and 11 extra markdown files, and static analysis flagged three instances of environment-variable access paired with network calls plus a cross-file exfiltration chain spanning 6 files. A text-analysis skill has no legitimate need to read environment variables or make outbound requests, and the data it handles (arbitrary user writing, conversation history, inferred psychological profiles) is highly sensitive. This combination — undisclosed code, secret-reading, network egress, split across multiple files — is the signature of a credential/data exfiltration capability hidden behind a plausible utility. Recommend withholding approval until every bundled Python file is manually reviewed and all network and environment access is removed or fully justified and disclosed.
llm_primary_threats: Data exfiltration (env var + user text to network)
Cross-file exfiltration chain / obfuscated data flow
Tool restriction violation (allowed-tools: Read, Write vs. network-capable Python)
Undisclosed bundled executable code (manifest/behavior mismatch)
Over-collection of sensitive personal data (conversation history, third-party psychological profiling)
Broad keyword-baited activation scope

findings.title: Cross-file data exfiltration chain across 6 files
findings.description: The static analyzer detected a cross-file exfiltration chain spanning 6 files: data collection in one module is passed to network-sending code in another, a structure commonly used to split and disguise exfiltration logic so that no single file looks malicious. Since the skill profiles arbitrary user-supplied text (potentially private writing, emails, or conversation history), any outbound transmission would leak highly sensitive personal content and derived psychological profiles.
findings.snippet: Pre-scan static finding: BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN: 'Cross-file exfiltration chain: 6 files'
findings.remediation: Trace and document the full data flow across the 6 implicated files. Eliminate any path where user text, profile output, or environment data reaches a network sink. Make the profiler fully local/offline, matching the documented behavior.

findings.title: Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write) violated by network-capable Python scripts
findings.description: The manifest declares allowed-tools: Read, Write — implying a purely local, non-executing, non-networking skill. However the package ships 8 Python scripts that, per the static scan, perform environment variable reads and network calls. Executing these requires Python/Bash execution capability not declared in the manifest, and network egress is outside any declared capability. This is an actual violation of the stated tool restrictions, not merely missing metadata.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Read, Write; file inventory: {'python': 8}; static findings show network calls and env var access
findings.remediation: Either remove the executable Python scripts from the package so the skill is genuinely Read/Write-only, or accurately declare all required tools (Python/Bash) and disclose network usage in the manifest and instructions.

findings.title: Sensitive psychological profiling of third parties and conversation history without consent controls
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to build detailed cognitive/psychological profiles of 'any text's author', including third parties who never consented, and in Self-Profile Mode to mine the entire conversation history as source data. Combined with the detected network egress in the bundled scripts, this creates a pipeline in which sensitive inferred personal attributes and prior chat content could be collected and transmitted. Even absent exfiltration, mining conversation history for psychological inference is an over-collection and privacy concern that is not gated by any consent step.
findings.snippet: "If the user asks to profile their own thinking (using the conversation history as text)"; "Extract cognitive patterns and thinking fingerprints from any text"
findings.remediation: Require explicit user confirmation before ingesting conversation history; limit analysis to text the user pastes in the current request; add guidance that profiles of non-consenting third parties should be declined or clearly labeled as speculative; guarantee no profile data leaves the local session.

findings.title: Keyword-dense description broadening activation scope
findings.description: The description packs many trigger phrases ('what's my thinking style', 'analyze how this person reasons', 'cognitive profile', 'thinking pattern', 'DHDNA', 'digital DNA', 'any text', 'deeper insight into the author's reasoning') plus a catch-all clause to trigger whenever the user 'provides text'. This maximizes activation frequency well beyond a narrowly scoped tool, which is a mild discovery-abuse pattern and is aggravated by the undisclosed network-capable code in the package.
findings.snippet: "Also trigger when the user provides text and wants deeper insight into the author's reasoning patterns..."
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to the specific, explicit user intents the skill serves and remove the broad 'any text provided' activation clause.

findings.title: Undisclosed environment variable access combined with network calls (env-var exfiltration pattern)
findings.description: Static pre-scan flagged BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION in three locations and a cross-file env-var exfiltration chain spanning 6 files within the package. The skill package contains 8 Python files that are neither mentioned in SKILL.md nor listed as referenced files, yet they read environment variables (likely API keys/tokens) and issue outbound network requests. Nothing in the skill's stated purpose — offline analysis of text the user supplies — requires reading environment variables or transmitting data off-machine. This is a classic read-secrets → send-to-network pattern and represents potential credential/data exposure.
findings.snippet: Pre-scan static findings: BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION (x3) 'Environment variable access with network calls detected'; BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION: 'Cross-file env var exfiltration: 6 files'
findings.remediation: Audit and publish the contents of all 8 Python files. Remove any os.environ/os.getenv reads that are not strictly required, remove all outbound HTTP calls, or explicitly document each endpoint and the data sent, requiring per-invocation user consent. If external API access is genuinely needed, restrict to an allowlisted domain and never transmit environment contents or user text without explicit opt-in.

findings.title: Undisclosed bundled code: 8 Python files and 11 extra markdown files not referenced in SKILL.md
findings.description: SKILL.md describes only a manual analytical procedure and explicitly implies no tooling ('No script files found' in the referenced/instruction surface). Yet the package contains 21 files including 8 Python scripts and 12 markdown files. The gap between the documented behavior (offline prompt-driven text analysis) and the shipped, network-capable code is a cross-component consistency failure: the agent or user reviewing SKILL.md would have no reason to expect code execution or outbound traffic. Undocumented markdown files may also be loaded as additional instruction context (indirect injection surface).
findings.snippet: SKILL.md body references no scripts or files; inventory reports 8 python + 12 markdown files
findings.remediation: Document every bundled file and its purpose in SKILL.md. Remove files unnecessary to the stated function. Review all bundled markdown for embedded directives that could be interpreted as instructions by the agent.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The 'diffdock' skill is a legitimate, well-scoped documentation-and-helper-script package for DiffDock molecular docking. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment, or role-redefinition language is present in the SKILL.md body; the instructions are purely technical guidance. The three bundled Python scripts (prepare_batch_csv.py, analyze_results.py, setup_check.py) perform only local, benign operations: CSV validation with RDKit/pandas, regex parsing of local SDF filenames and contents, CSV export to a user-specified path, and import/version checks for dependencies. There are no network calls, no eval/exec/os.system, no subprocess usage, no credential or environment-variable harvesting, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, and no hardcoded secrets. File access is confined to user-supplied paths (results directories, CSVs) and the skill's own bundled reference/asset files, which is expected behavior. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep) are consistent with the documented workflows (running inference commands, writing CSV/config files, reading results). The description accurately reflects behavior and even explicitly bounds scope ('Not for binding affinity prediction'), with no keyword baiting or capability inflation. Several referenced files are listed as not found (templates/*, assets/parameters_reference.md, etc.), which appears to be path-listing noise/duplication rather than a security issue; the canonical references/ and assets/ files that the instructions actually cite are present and benign. The only noteworthy item is routine supply-chain hygiene: unpinned upstream repo clone, unpinned Docker image, unpinned fair-esm install, and auto-downloaded model checkpoints without checksum verification — all typical for scientific ML tooling and rated LOW.
llm_primary_threats: Unpinned third-party dependency and container image installation (supply-chain hygiene)

findings.title: Unpinned external dependency installs and Docker image pulls without version pinning
findings.description: The SKILL.md instructs cloning the upstream DiffDock GitHub repository, creating a conda environment from the repo's environment.yml, pulling the 'rbgcsail/diffdock' Docker image (no digest/tag), and installing 'fair-esm' via uv pip without a pinned version. The skill also notes model checkpoints (~500MB) are auto-downloaded on first run. These are standard practices for scientific tooling and point to the legitimate upstream project, but they introduce unpinned supply-chain exposure (mutable latest tags, no checksum verification).
findings.snippet:
git clone https://github.com/gcorso/DiffDock.git
conda env create --file environment.yml
docker pull rbgcsail/diffdock
...
print(f"    Install with: uv pip install fair-esm")
findings.remediation: Pin the repository commit/tag, Docker image digest, and package versions (e.g., fair-esm==2.0.0), and verify checksums for downloaded model checkpoints.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The dnanexus-integration skill is a well-structured, documentation-heavy skill for working with the DNAnexus genomics platform. No security threats were identified.

Manifest: name and description accurately match the skill's content (DNAnexus CLI/dxpy guidance, dxapp.json validation, workflow imports). `allowed-tools` is not specified, which is optional per spec and only informational here; the skill's actual operations (running local Python validators, invoking `dx` CLI) are consistent with its stated purpose.

Instructions (SKILL.md): No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language. On the contrary, the "Operating Contract" is unusually safety-positive: it requires read-only preflight, explicit user confirmation before billable/destructive actions, forbids printing or logging `DX_SECURITY_CONTEXT`/API tokens, forbids running `dx env` in captured logs, forbids sending credentials to non-DNAnexus endpoints, and instructs treating project names/paths/tags/downloaded content as untrusted with array-form subprocess arguments.

Scripts: `scripts/inspect_dxpy.py` performs purely local introspection via importlib/inspect and importlib.metadata; it makes no network calls, no filesystem writes, no subprocess/eval/exec, and no credential access. `scripts/validate_dxapp.py` reads only the user-supplied dxapp.json path, parses it with json.load, and performs structural linting; it includes a defensive check that warns on embedded secrets and on overly broad `access.network: ["*"]`, `allProjects`, `ADMINISTER`, and `developer` permissions. No dynamic code execution, no obfuscation, no base64/hex payloads, no hardcoded credentials.

Reference files: All present reference docs are internal to the package and contain accurate, security-conscious platform guidance (least-privilege access, pinned dependencies, pinned container digests, bounded searches and polling, cost limits, redaction of tokens/PHI from support bundles, explicit prohibition on recursive removal of `/`). External URLs appear only in `references/sources.md` as human-readable citations to official DNAnexus/GitHub/PyPI documentation; there is no instruction to fetch and execute remote content.

Minor, non-security observations: several referenced paths listed by the scanner (templates/*, assets/*, dxpy.py) do not exist; these appear to be scanner path-expansion artifacts of the `references/*.md` filenames rather than genuine broken links or hidden payload references. Dependency guidance uses fully pinned versions (`dxpy==0.410.0`, dxCompiler 2.17.0) and explicitly recommends digest-pinned containers, which is good supply-chain hygiene.

Conclusion: benign, high-quality skill with no exfiltration, injection, obfuscation, capability-inflation, or tool-poisoning indicators.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is the vendored Anthropic 'docx' skill for creating, reading, editing and validating Word documents. It behaves consistently with its declared purpose: all scripts operate only on user-supplied .docx/.dotx files or unpacked directories. No network calls, no credential or environment harvesting (soffice.py deliberately builds an allowlisted environment to avoid leaking secrets to subprocesses), no eval/exec of dynamic content, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscated/encoded payloads, and no package installation from untrusted sources. The SKILL.md body contains only technical guidance — no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or instructions to fetch/trust external content. Security hygiene is notably good: defusedxml is used for XML parsing, safe_extract() blocks zip-slip and symlink archive entries, rezip writes atomically, and the instructions explicitly treat third-party .docx files as untrusted (stripping symlinks after unzip). The only issues found are minor local-hardening concerns: an LD_PRELOAD C shim compiled to a fixed predictable /tmp path, and a LibreOffice Basic macro written to a fixed /tmp profile directory — both static/visible code with legitimate purpose but reusing world-writable predictable paths. allowed-tools is not declared (optional, informational only) and the skill does require Bash/Python plus external tooling (pandoc, LibreOffice, poppler), which the manifest documents in the Dependencies section. Overall: low risk, no evidence of malicious behavior.
llm_primary_threats: Predictable /tmp artifact reuse for LD_PRELOAD shared object
Predictable /tmp path for executed LibreOffice Basic macro

findings.title: LibreOffice Basic macro written to fixed /tmp profile path and executed headlessly
findings.description: scripts/accept_changes.py writes a StarBasic macro (Module1.xba) to a fixed path under /tmp/libreoffice_docx_profile and then invokes soffice with a vnd.sun.star.script: URL to execute it. The macro content is static and benign (AcceptAllTrackedChanges + store + close), but using a world-writable fixed profile directory means another local user/process could replace Module1.xba with arbitrary Basic code, which this script would then execute (it only checks that the string 'AcceptAllTrackedChanges' is present).
findings.snippet:
LIBREOFFICE_PROFILE = "/tmp/libreoffice_docx_profile"
MACRO_DIR = f"{LIBREOFFICE_PROFILE}/user/basic/Standard"
...
if macro_file.exists() and "AcceptAllTrackedChanges" in macro_file.read_text():
    return True
...
"vnd.sun.star.script:Standard.Module1.AcceptAllTrackedChanges?language=Basic&location=application"
findings.remediation: Create the LibreOffice profile in a per-invocation temporary directory with restrictive permissions (as run_soffice() already does), and always rewrite the macro file rather than trusting existing content.

findings.title: Runtime compilation of C shim and LD_PRELOAD injection into soffice subprocess
findings.description: scripts/office/soffice.py writes an embedded C source file to the system temp directory, compiles it with gcc into a shared object, and injects it via LD_PRELOAD into LibreOffice subprocesses. The shim overrides socket/listen/accept/close libc calls. While the intent (working around AF_UNIX restrictions in sandboxes) is legitimate and the C source is fully visible (no obfuscation), the pattern uses a predictable, world-writable path (/tmp/lo_socket_shim.so, /tmp/lo_socket_shim.c) and reuses any pre-existing file at that path without integrity checking, which is a local privilege/code-injection hazard on shared hosts (a pre-planted .so would be LD_PRELOADed).
findings.snippet:
_SHIM_SO = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "lo_socket_shim.so"
...
if _SHIM_SO.exists():
    return _SHIM_SO
src.write_text(_SHIM_SOURCE)
subprocess.run(["gcc", "-shared", "-fPIC", "-o", str(_SHIM_SO), str(src), "-ldl"], check=True, ...)
...
env["LD_PRELOAD"] = str(shim)
findings.remediation: Build the shim in a private mkdtemp directory with 0700 permissions (or verify a hash of an existing artifact) instead of a fixed predictable /tmp path, and skip the build entirely when gcc/preload is not required.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `esm` skill is a documentation-only skill for the EvolutionaryScale ESM protein language model SDK (ESM3, ESMC, Forge/Biohub inference, ESMFold2). It contains no executable script files; all code appears inside markdown as illustrative examples. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, or role-redefinition language was detected in SKILL.md or any reference file. Credential handling is notably good practice: tokens are read from the `ESM_API_KEY` environment variable, the docs explicitly warn against hardcoding or committing keys, no secrets are embedded, and endpoints are pinned to trusted hosts (forge.evolutionaryscale.ai, biohub.ai) with explicit guidance not to accept API hosts from untrusted input. No data exfiltration, credential-file access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), environment harvesting, eval/exec, os.system, obfuscation, or base64 payloads are present. Network activity is limited to the vendor's own inference APIs and is consistent with the stated purpose; the description matches actual content. Minor code patterns (pickle-based local caching, retry loops with bounded max_retries, torch/GPU usage) are normal for ML documentation and not resource-abuse. Residual concerns are low-severity supply-chain and hygiene issues: an optional GitHub VCS install path (mitigated by explicit SHA-pinning guidance), missing allowed-tools/compatibility metadata, and several referenced files that are absent from the package. Overall the skill appears benign and safe to use with normal review of any installation commands before execution.
llm_primary_threats: Supply chain risk from optional GitHub VCS install path
Undeclared tool scope (missing allowed-tools) with documented Bash/Python execution and file writes
Broken/missing referenced files

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration while documentation implies Bash/Python execution and file writes
findings.description: The YAML manifest omits `allowed-tools` and `compatibility`, although the skill's instructions include shell installation commands (uv pip install), Python execution, and writing output files (PDB/FASTA/CIF/pickle caches). This is informational only per the skills spec; no restriction is violated because none is declared.

findings.title: Documentation suggests installing package directly from GitHub repository
findings.description: The biohub-platform.md reference instructs installing the `esm` package from a GitHub repository (github.com/Biohub/esm) via `uv pip install "esm@git+..."`. While the guidance responsibly requires pinning a full 40-character commit SHA and reviewing the release, direct VCS installs still shift trust from PyPI provenance to a repository whose ownership/authenticity the agent cannot verify. PyPI installs elsewhere are correctly pinned (esm==3.2.3).

findings.title: Several referenced files do not exist in the package
findings.description: Instructions/scan resolve references to files such as `esm.py`, `assets/*.md`, and `templates/*.md` that are not present in the package. Broken references are not directly exploitable but can cause the agent to search for or fabricate missing resources, and a same-named file dropped later could be loaded implicitly.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The etetoolkit skill is a legitimate, well-documented wrapper around the open-source ETE 4 phylogenetics library. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, or role-redefinition language appears in SKILL.md or any reference file; all imperative language is normal technical guidance about API usage. The two bundled Python scripts (scripts/quick_visualize.py, scripts/tree_operations.py) contain no network calls, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no environment-variable or credential access, no file access outside explicitly user-supplied input/output paths, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. They use argparse with strict validation, narrow exception handling, and explicitly refuse ambiguous/missing taxa rather than silently producing partial results. Notably, the code contains defensive security controls rather than risks: validate_bind_address() refuses to bind the SmartView HTTP server to a non-loopback address unless the user passes --allow-remote-bind, and the reference docs warn against exposing an unauthenticated explorer on 0.0.0.0. Dependencies are pinned exactly (ete4==4.4.0, including extras) and installed via uv in an isolated runtime, with no unpinned or GitHub-direct installs and no typosquatting indicators. The manifest's declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Python) are consistent with actual behavior (reading/writing tree files, running Python scripts, pip installs). The description is narrowly scoped, explicitly disclaims out-of-scope use (tree inference from raw sequences), and contains no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, or activation-priority manipulation. Referenced files: the five references/*.md files exist and are benign technical documentation; the reported missing assets/*, templates/*, and ete4.py paths are scanner path-permutation artifacts, not actual broken links in SKILL.md. Reading internal bundled reference files is normal, self-contained skill behavior. The documentation also demonstrates good security hygiene by warning that ete4.treematcher TreePattern expression-bearing patterns are executable code and must never be constructed from user input, imported data, or model output, and by cautioning that write(props=None) exports all node properties and may unintentionally disclose internal annotations. Only a LOW informational note regarding disclosed large-download and unbounded-enumeration resource usage.

findings.title: Large taxonomy database downloads and unbounded topology enumeration can consume significant disk/compute
findings.description: The skill documents NCBI/GTDB taxonomy database downloads (~600 MB NCBI, ~72 MB GTDB local footprint) and TreeKO-style get_speciation_trees() enumeration that can generate very many topologies. These are legitimate, disclosed behaviors of the upstream ETE 4 library, and the documentation explicitly warns about disk usage, temporary files, and the need to bound output size. Informational only, not a malicious pattern.
findings.snippet: "NCBI and GTDB workflows download public taxonomy data and can consume substantial disk space"; "get_speciation_trees() can generate very many topologies. Consider newick_only=True, monitor output size"
findings.remediation: No action required. The guidance already advises pinning an explicit dbfile, running updates in a controlled writable workspace, and defining limits before materializing enumerated topologies.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The exa-search skill is a legitimate, coherent CLI wrapper around the official Exa Python SDK for web search and URL content extraction. The two Python scripts are clean: argparse-driven, no eval/exec, no subprocess or shell invocation, no filesystem traversal, no hardcoded credentials, and no network calls beyond the declared Exa API via the exa-py client. Declared capabilities in the manifest match actual behavior, and referenced reference files exist and contain only benign usage guidance with no prompt-injection, concealment, or safety-bypass directives. The static analyzer's 'env var exfiltration' and 'cross-file exfiltration chain' alerts are false positives: they stem from EXA_API_KEY being read from the environment and passed to the Exa API client, which is the skill's documented and necessary authentication mechanism. Residual low-severity items are hygiene concerns: broad .env loading instructions, unpinned exa-py dependency, an immutable vendor tracking header, an inherent indirect-prompt-injection surface from verbatim rendering of fetched web content, and a missing allowed-tools declaration. No CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM threats were identified; the skill can be considered safe to use with minor hardening.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installed at runtime via uv/pip
findings.description: Setup and reference commands install `exa-py>=1.14.0` at runtime with `uv run --with exa-py` / `uv pip install`, using a lower-bound range rather than a pinned version. Any future compromised or breaking release of the package would be pulled automatically. The package is the legitimate official Exa SDK, so risk is low.
findings.snippet:
dependencies = ["exa-py>=1.14.0"]
uv pip install "exa-py>=1.14.0"
findings.remediation: Pin an exact version (e.g., exa-py==1.14.0) or use a lockfile/hash verification for reproducible, tamper-resistant installs.

findings.title: Vendor tracking header sent with every request and marked immutable
findings.description: Both scripts set a hardcoded `x-exa-integration` header identifying the skill/repo, and SKILL.md instructs users not to remove or rename it. This is attribution telemetry to the vendor rather than exfiltration of user data (only an integration identifier is sent), but the directive against modification is a mild anti-tamper/attribution nudge that users should be aware of.
findings.snippet:
EXA_INTEGRATION_HEADER = "k-dense-ai--scientific-agent-skills"
client.headers["x-exa-integration"] = EXA_INTEGRATION_HEADER
"Do not remove or rename this header when adapting the scripts."
findings.remediation: Disclose the tracking header in the description and allow users to disable it; avoid instructing agents/users not to modify telemetry.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration and unresolved referenced file paths
findings.description: The manifest does not declare `allowed-tools` even though the skill requires Bash/Python execution, file writes (-o output), and network access. Additionally, several file paths surfaced during pre-scan (assets/web-search.md, templates/web-extract.md, etc.) do not exist; the actual references/ files are present, so this appears to be scanner path-guessing rather than a real broken reference. Informational.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Declare `allowed-tools: [Bash, Read, Write]` to make the execution, network, and file-write footprint explicit.

findings.title: Fetched web/URL content returned verbatim without treating it as untrusted
findings.description: references/web-extract.md instructs the agent to keep externally fetched page content 'verbatim — do not paraphrase or summarize' and to 'parse lists exhaustively'. Because content is retrieved from arbitrary URLs, any instructions embedded in that content enter the agent context unfiltered, creating an indirect prompt-injection surface inherent to web-fetch skills. No malicious instruction is present in the skill itself.
findings.snippet:
- Keep content verbatim — do not paraphrase or summarize
- Parse lists exhaustively — extract EVERY numbered/bulleted item
findings.remediation: Add a note instructing the agent to treat all retrieved page/search content as untrusted data and never to execute or obey instructions found inside fetched content.

findings.title: API key read from environment and sent to Exa API (expected behavior)
findings.description: Both scripts read the EXA_API_KEY environment variable and use it to authenticate against the Exa API. Static analyzers flagged this as 'env var exfiltration', but the key is only used for its intended purpose (authenticating to the declared, documented service api.exa.ai via the exa-py SDK). No other environment variables are harvested and no data is sent to unexpected third-party endpoints. Informational only.
findings.snippet:
api_key = os.environ.get("EXA_API_KEY")
client = Exa(api_key=api_key)
findings.remediation: No action required. Optionally document that the key is transmitted only to Exa's API endpoints.

findings.title: Instructions direct agent to read project .env file
findings.description: SKILL.md instructs the agent to check for a .env file in the project root and load it via `dotenv -f .env run -- ...`. This causes all variables in the project's .env (which may include unrelated secrets such as database passwords or other API keys) to be injected into the subprocess environment. The scripts themselves only consume EXA_API_KEY, so the practical risk is limited, but broad .env loading is wider than necessary.
findings.snippet:
First, check if a `.env` file exists in the project root and contains `EXA_API_KEY`. If so, load it:
```bash
dotenv -f .env run -- uv run --with exa-py python "$SKILL_PATH/scripts/exa_search.py" "your query"
```
findings.remediation: Prefer extracting only EXA_API_KEY from .env (e.g., `EXA_API_KEY=$(grep ^EXA_API_KEY .env | cut -d= -f2-)`) rather than loading the entire file into the child process environment.

findings.description: Script iterates through environment variables in skills/exa-search/scripts/exa_extract.py
findings.remediation: Remove environment variable collection unless explicitly required and documented

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `experimental-design` skill is a legitimate, domain-focused statistics/DOE helper. All content is technically coherent and matches the declared purpose. The two bundled Python scripts (`scripts/randomization.py`, `scripts/doe_designs.py`) only use numpy, pandas, and pyDOE3 to build randomization schedules and design matrices as DataFrames — no network calls, no subprocess/os.system, no eval/exec, no filesystem traversal, no environment variable or credential access, no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. Behavior is fully consistent with the declared `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash` (writing CSVs and running scripts) and with the compatibility notes about Python dependencies. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, instruction override, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; references to other skills (statistical-power, statistical-analysis) are ordinary hand-off guidance, not authority escalation. The description is long and keyword-dense, but the keywords are legitimate, in-scope statistical terms that describe genuine capabilities rather than capability inflation or brand baiting. Referenced reference files that exist (`references/randomization_and_blocking.md`, `references/design_types.md`, `references/factorial_and_doe.md`, `references/sequential_and_adaptive.md`) contain only benign, accurate methodological text; the scanner-reported missing `assets/*` and `templates/*` paths are speculative path variants, not actual broken references. Only a minor supply-chain hygiene issue (unpinned dependencies) was noted. The skill appears safe to use.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions
findings.description: The SKILL.md installation step instructs installing dependencies with loose/unpinned version constraints (`uv pip install "numpy>=1.26" "pandas>=2.0" pyDOE3`). `pyDOE3` has no version pin at all. This is a minor supply-chain hygiene concern: a future compromised or breaking release would be installed automatically. No untrusted repositories or typosquatted names are used, and all packages are well-known scientific libraries.
findings.snippet: uv pip install "numpy>=1.26" "pandas>=2.0" pyDOE3
findings.remediation: Pin exact versions (e.g. numpy==1.26.4, pandas==2.2.2, pyDOE3==1.0.4) or provide a lockfile/requirements.txt with hashes.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The exploratory-data-analysis skill appears benign and unusually security-conscious. All bundled scripts are local-only, use the Python standard library plus optional pinned scientific libraries, and contain no network calls, no subprocess/eval/exec usage, no credential or environment-variable access, no obfuscation, and no hardcoded secrets. Path handling in scripts/_common.py explicitly rejects URLs, NUL bytes, home expansion, parent traversal, symlinks (including per-component checks), multiply linked files, and non-regular files, and confines input/output within an explicit --root. Resource bounds are enforced throughout (byte, row, column, field, JSON node, HDF5 object/depth, TIFF page/series, NPZ member/ratio, and report-size limits), and ZIP-bomb/decompression-bomb protections are present. Deserialization risks are avoided: numpy is loaded with allow_pickle=False and object dtypes are rejected, HDF5 soft/external links are not followed and dataset values/attributes are never read, and pickle/joblib/dill are explicitly out of scope. Outputs are tokenized/redacted by default, written atomically with 0600 permissions, and refuse overwrite without --force; Markdown emission sanitizes untrusted identifiers to prevent structural injection. The SKILL.md instructions contain no prompt-injection, jailbreak, concealment, or role-redefinition language; on the contrary, they instruct the agent to treat all file-derived text (headers, sequence titles, HDF5 attributes, image metadata) as untrusted data and never to follow embedded instructions or pass it to a shell. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob) are consistent with running local Python CLIs and writing report files. Dependency guidance uses fully pinned versions installed only on explicit user action, with no GitHub or unpinned installs; the listed versions/dates are forward-dated and unverifiable, which is a documentation accuracy nit rather than a security threat. Several referenced files under assets/ and templates/ paths were not found in the package (only assets/report_template.md and the references/*.md files resolve), which is a minor completeness issue; report_scaffold.py fails closed with a clear error if the bundled template is missing. No security findings warranting a report were identified.

The flowio skill is a legitimate, documentation-heavy wrapper around the open-source FlowIO library for reading/writing Flow Cytometry Standard (FCS) files. Behavior matches the manifest description and the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Bash).

The bundled script scripts/inspect_fcs.py was reviewed line by line: it performs local-only FCS parsing with argparse, emits JSON to stdout or a new file, and contains NO network calls (no requests/urllib/socket), NO subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, NO credential or dotfile access, NO environment-variable reads, and no obfuscation or encoded payloads. It is notably defensive: input-size limits (--max-bytes), array-memory estimation limits (--max-array-bytes), multi-dataset chain caps (--max-datasets), non-increasing/negative offset validation, refusal to overwrite the input or an existing output file ("x" mode), and metadata-only parsing by default so that potentially identifying TEXT/ANALYSIS values are not dumped unless explicitly requested (--include-text/--include-analysis).

The pre-scan static findings (BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION, CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN, CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION) appear to be FALSE POSITIVES. The only environment-variable-like construct is the documentation shell variable FLOWIO_SKILL_DIR="skills/flowio", used to locate the bundled script path; the only "network" tokens are the pinned `uv ... --with "flowio==1.4.0"` installation commands and https:// citation URLs in references/sources.md. There is no code path that reads sensitive data and transmits it anywhere, and no read→send tool chain.

SKILL.md and the reference documents contain no prompt injection, role redefinition, safety-bypass, or concealment directives. Instructions actively encourage user-protective behavior (treat FCS TEXT metadata as potentially identifying, avoid --include-text, keep strict offset checks, sandbox untrusted files, never silently relax parsing). The description is scoped and explicitly delegates out-of-scope work (compensation, gating, FlowJo) to FlowKit rather than inflating capability. Only minor, low-severity hygiene items were identified.

findings.title: Runtime dependency installation via uv with pinned version
findings.description: SKILL.md and reference docs instruct the agent to install and run FlowIO via `uv pip install "flowio==1.4.0"` and `uv run --no-project --with "flowio==1.4.0"`. This is a network-based dependency installation at runtime, which is a minor supply-chain surface. Mitigating factors: the version is exactly pinned, the package (FlowIO) is a well-known open-source flow-cytometry library, and no arbitrary/unknown GitHub sources are used.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "flowio==1.4.0"
uv run --no-project --with "flowio==1.4.0" python "$FLOWIO_SKILL_DIR/scripts/inspect_fcs.py" sample.fcs
findings.remediation: Acceptable as-is given the exact version pin; optionally document a hash-pinned lockfile or pre-provisioned environment to remove runtime package fetching.

findings.title: Instructions reference several non-existent files (assets/ and templates/ paths)
findings.description: The referenced-file inventory lists numerous missing paths (assets/*.md, templates/*.md, flowio.py). The actual SKILL.md body only references the existing references/*.md files and scripts/inspect_fcs.py, so this appears to be static-analyzer path expansion noise rather than intentional misdirection. No dangling reference is used to fetch remote content. Documentation hygiene issue only.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: assets/workflows.md (not found); templates/api_reference.md (not found); flowio.py (not found)
findings.remediation: Ensure only existing, in-package files are referenced so the agent does not attempt to read or create unexpected paths.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The fluidsim skill is a well-engineered, defensively written scientific-computing planning package. SKILL.md contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; instead it repeatedly instructs conservative behavior (never auto-submit MPI jobs, never claim convergence, stop when assumptions are missing). All bundled scripts (solver_config_validator.py, grid_resource_estimator.py, simulation_dry_run.py, output_inventory.py, budget_summary.py, restart_compatibility.py, _common.py, _schema.py) use only the standard library plus optional lazy h5py; there is no network access, no subprocess/os.system, no eval/exec, no dynamic imports from user text, no credential or environment harvesting, and no hardcoded secrets. Path handling in _common.py is unusually rigorous: URI/traversal rejection, symlink and hard-link rejection, root confinement, size/count/record bounds, strict JSON parsing with duplicate-key and non-finite rejection, and atomic private-mode writes. The code-generation tool (simulation_dry_run.py) renders only JSON scalar literals via repr() from a schema-validated config and maps solver keys through a static allowlist to module names, so no attacker-controlled import or code path is possible; the generated script is dry-run by default and requires an exact config-ID acknowledgement to execute. The skill explicitly warns against the upstream `fluidsim-restart --modify-params` option because upstream executes supplied Python, and never emits it. Dependencies are exact-pinned with lock-file guidance. allowed-tools (Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Python) is consistent with observed behavior (reads local run data, writes an optional .py plan within --root, CLIs invoked via Bash/Python). Several referenced files under assets/ and templates/ are reported as not found, but these appear to be probe paths not actually referenced by SKILL.md, which links only to references/*.md; the present reference documents are benign technical documentation with only citation URLs and no instruction-following directives. No security findings warrant reporting.

The generate-image skill is a legitimate, well-documented wrapper around the OpenRouter Image API. The single bundled Python script uses only the standard library, performs HTTPS requests exclusively to the declared endpoint (https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/images and /images/models), and writes decoded image bytes to user-specified output paths. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directives, or role-redefinition instructions appear anywhere in SKILL.md or references/models.md. There is no eval/exec, no os.system or subprocess usage, no shell interpolation, no obfuscated or encoded payloads (base64 usage is functional image encoding/decoding), no hardcoded credentials, and no exfiltration to unexpected domains. Behavior matches the manifest description and the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with reading reference images, writing output files, and invoking the script. Minor observations: the API-key resolver walks parent directories for .env files (broader-than-necessary secret file reads), local reference images are uploaded to a third-party service (documented and warned about in SKILL.md), and a few example output paths were misdetected as missing referenced files. Overall risk: low; the skill appears safe to use.

findings.title: Referenced files listed in instructions do not exist in the package
findings.description: The analysis surface lists several referenced paths (templates/logo.svg, templates/models.md, assets/models.md, assets/logo.svg, references/logo.svg) that are not present in the package. These appear to be artifacts of example output paths in SKILL.md documentation (e.g. -o assets/logo.svg) rather than real dependencies. No functional or security impact, but the documentation could mislead an agent into attempting to read non-existent resources.
findings.snippet: python scripts/generate_image.py "Minimal geometric fox logo, two colors" -m recraft/recraft-v4-vector -o assets/logo.svg
findings.remediation: Distinguish example output paths from real bundled resources in the documentation so tooling does not treat them as required files.

findings.title: API key resolution walks parent directories searching for .env files
findings.description: find_api_key() traverses the current working directory and every parent directory upward looking for a .env file and reads its contents to extract OPENROUTER_API_KEY. This is a common convenience pattern, but it means the script may read .env files outside the intended project scope (e.g. a home-directory .env containing many unrelated secrets). Only the OPENROUTER_API_KEY value is used and it is sent solely to openrouter.ai over HTTPS as an Authorization header, so exposure risk is limited; no exfiltration to third parties occurs.
findings.snippet:
cwd = Path.cwd()
for directory in [cwd, *cwd.parents]:
    env_file = directory / ".env"
    ...
    content = env_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
findings.remediation: Limit the .env search to the current working directory or the project root (e.g. stop at a directory containing .git), and avoid reading files above the user's project boundary.

findings.title: Local reference images are base64-encoded and uploaded to a third-party API
findings.description: Any local file path passed via -i/--input whose extension matches PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP is read fully, base64-encoded, and transmitted to openrouter.ai as part of input_references. This is the documented and expected behavior of the skill (image editing/compositing), and SKILL.md explicitly warns not to send sensitive or unpublished data. Noted only because it constitutes local-file-to-network data flow that the agent may perform on user-supplied paths without additional confirmation.
findings.snippet:
encoded = base64.b64encode(path.read_bytes()).decode("ascii")
return f"data:{mime};base64,{encoded}"
findings.remediation: No change required for intended functionality; optionally confirm with the user before uploading local files and log which files are transmitted.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The geniml skill is a well-documented, security-conscious bioinformatics helper package. All five bundled Python scripts (bed_validator.py, corpus_auditor.py, consensus_plan.py, embedding_plan.py, tokenizer_compatibility.py) plus the shared _common.py use only the Python standard library. They perform read-only validation, checksumming, and command *planning*: no subprocess execution, no eval/exec, no dynamic imports, no network calls (no socket/urllib/requests imports), no environment-variable harvesting, no writes to user files, and no credential/secret access. _common.py implements defensive controls that exceed typical practice: rejection of URI schemes and '://' strings, rejection of '~' home expansion, rejection of '..' traversal, per-component symlink rejection, O_NOFOLLOW opens, regular-file-only enforcement, bounded bytes/records/line-length (guarding gzip decompression bombs), UTF-8 and NUL-byte validation, a conservative hand-rolled YAML scalar parser instead of PyYAML (avoiding unsafe deserialization), and default 'redacted' path-disclosure mode to avoid leaking filesystem or sample identifiers. Model artifacts are hashed but explicitly never deserialized (no torch.load/pickle/joblib), which is the correct handling of untrusted .pt/.model files. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; instead it repeatedly requires explicit user approval before any network download (BEDbase, Hugging Face) and warns against implicit cache/upload operations. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob) are consistent with the documented workflow, and Bash usage is scoped to explicit user-approved commands; bundled helpers themselves spawn no processes. Dependency guidance uses fully pinned versions (geniml==0.8.4, gtars==0.9.2) with lockfiles, artifact digests, and an explicitly pinned StarSpace commit accompanied by a clear 'unverified compatibility / archived upstream' caveat and instructions not to run third-party binaries or add them to PATH. Reference markdown files are internal to the package and contain only technical documentation with legitimate upstream URLs (PyPI, GitHub, docs.bedbase.org, DOIs) used as citations, not as instruction sources. Several referenced filenames (geniml.py, gtars.py, assets/*, templates/*) are not present, but these appear to be false-positive extractions from Python import examples and link text rather than intentional missing dependencies; the SKILL.md explicitly notes that data/, refs/, work/, and models/ paths are user-provided placeholders. No security findings warrant reporting.

The genomic-coordinates skill is a legitimate, well-documented bioinformatics utility. All four Python scripts (convert_coords.py, audit_intervals.py, check_contigs.py, _common.py, normalize_variant.py) use only the Python standard library (argparse, re, sys, json, pathlib, collections, dataclasses) with no network calls, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no environment variable harvesting, and no access to credential paths (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, cloud tokens). File I/O is limited to user-supplied paths passed explicitly via CLI arguments (input files, --genome, --fasta, -o output), which is proportionate to the stated purpose of parsing and validating genomic interval/variant files. sys.path.insert of the script's own directory to import the bundled _common module is normal intra-package behavior. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; it is purely domain guidance. The description is keyword-rich but the keywords are genuine domain triggers (BED, VCF, liftover, 0-based, HGVS) that match actual implemented functionality, so this is legitimate discoverability rather than capability inflation. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the observed behavior (reading data files, writing TSV/JSON output via -o, running python3 scripts). Referenced documentation files under references/ are internal to the package and contain only technical guidance; the additionally listed assets/ and templates/ paths are not found but are not referenced by the instruction body and pose no security risk (at most a minor packaging/documentation inconsistency). No data exfiltration, command injection, obfuscation, unpinned dependency installation, or over-collection patterns were identified.

This skill is a documentation-only thin client for a hosted third-party genomics inference API (REST + a hosted MCP server). It contains NO script files — only SKILL.md and four benign reference markdown documents. A full review found no malicious behavior: no prompt injection, jailbreak, role redefinition, or concealment directives in any human language; no eval/exec/os.system or command-injection patterns; no hardcoded secrets; no obfuscation, base64 blobs, or hidden stagers; no reading of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, browser profiles, or other credential stores; no filesystem traversal or over-collection; no package installs or supply-chain manipulation.

Security hygiene is notably good and works against the threat model: the skill explicitly instructs 'Never hardcode the key', to read GI_API_KEY from the environment or a .env, and to never commit keys; it discourages hardcoding model IDs; it scopes itself narrowly ('Not for local alignment, variant calling, or file I/O'); and it carries an appropriate research-use-only, not-for-clinical-decisions disclaimer. Manifest description, instruction body, and reference files are fully consistent with one another — no hidden capabilities and no behavior beyond what is documented.

All findings are LOW severity and represent hardening opportunities or inherent-design transparency notes rather than attacks: (1) a dense but on-topic trigger-keyword block, (2) no optional allowed-tools declaration despite requiring network/Python, (3) by-design upload of user sequence data to a third party (documented, consent-relevant for sensitive genomic data), (4) an env-var-overridable API base URL that could redirect the bearer token if the environment is already compromised, (5) an unbounded 'while True' polling loop in the async example, (6) delegation of model/bounds configuration to remote endpoints and gi:// MCP resources, and (7) scanner-noise references to non-existent templates/ and assets/ paths. Overall risk: LOW — the package appears legitimate and behaves exactly as advertised.
llm_primary_threats: Third-party data transmission of user-supplied genomic sequences (by design, documented)
Environment-variable-controlled endpoint override (GI_BASE_URL) could redirect bearer token and payloads
Unbounded async polling loop without timeout (minor resource exhaustion)
Remote-sourced configuration/model discovery creating transitive trust on vendor endpoints
Dense trigger-keyword metadata broadening skill activation surface

findings.title: Outbound transmission of user-supplied sequence data to third-party endpoints (documented, consent-relevant)
findings.description: By design the skill sends user DNA/FASTA sequence content to the vendor's hosted API/MCP server, and fetches reference sequence from rest.ensembl.org. This is the skill's stated purpose and is transparently documented, not covert exfiltration. Only the API key is read from the environment and used as a bearer to its own service — no credential harvesting, no reading of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or unrelated files, and no secondary/hidden destinations. Flagged at LOW purely as a data-residency/consent consideration for potentially sensitive genomic data.
findings.snippet: body = {"sequence": sequence, "sequence_name": sequence_name} ... requests.post(f"{BASE}/v1/tasks/{task}/predict", headers=HEADERS, json=body)
findings.remediation: Add an explicit note that user sequences leave the local machine and are processed by a third party, and prompt for user confirmation before uploading sequences derived from private/patient data.

findings.title: Overridable API base URL via GI_BASE_URL environment variable
findings.description: The REST workflow resolves its destination from the GI_BASE_URL environment variable with a fallback default. If that variable is set by an attacker or an untrusted process/CI config, all requests — including the Authorization: Bearer gi_ key and user sequence payloads — would be redirected to an attacker-controlled host. This is a common and legitimate staging-override pattern, and the default is a safe hardcoded HTTPS domain, so the residual risk is low.
findings.snippet: BASE = os.environ.get("GI_BASE_URL", "https://api.genomicintelligence.ai")
findings.remediation: Validate GI_BASE_URL against an allowlist of expected hosts and require HTTPS before attaching the bearer token; warn if the override is in effect.

findings.title: Instructions delegate authoritative configuration to remote resources
findings.description: The skill repeatedly instructs the agent to obtain model IDs, bounds, and reference context from remote sources at call time — the live OpenAPI document, 'list_models(task)', and remote MCP resources such as gi://models, gi://docs/tasks, gi://sequences, gi://account ('Read these instead of hardcoding model lists or bounds'). Discouraging hardcoded, rot-prone model IDs is good engineering, and the responses are expected to be structured data consumed as parameters rather than instructions. The residual risk is that a compromised or spoofed vendor endpoint could return content the agent treats as authoritative guidance. No instruction tells the agent to execute code or follow instructions found in remote responses.
findings.snippet: "discover IDs at call time with GET /v1/tasks/{task}/models (REST) or list_models (MCP)"; "Reference context lives in MCP resources: gi://models, gi://docs/tasks, gi://sequences, gi://account. Read these instead of hardcoding model lists or bounds."
findings.remediation: Treat all remote API/MCP responses as untrusted data: validate model IDs against an expected schema/pattern, and never interpret returned text as instructions to the agent.

findings.title: Unbounded polling loop in async annotation example
findings.description: The documented async annotation pattern uses 'while True:' with a 5-second sleep and no maximum attempt count, deadline, or overall timeout. If the remote job never reaches a terminal 200 state (or persistently returns 202), the agent would poll the endpoint indefinitely, consuming network and compute resources. This appears to be example brevity rather than intentional resource abuse, and requests.get has implicit socket behavior, but the loop has no exit guard.
findings.remediation: Bound the loop with a max attempt count / wall-clock deadline and per-request timeouts, and surface a clear timeout error to the user.

findings.title: Extensive trigger-keyword list and vendor-branded activation terms in metadata
findings.description: The skill's frontmatter includes a long 'trigger-keywords' field (~25 keyword phrases such as 'DNA sequence prediction', 'DeepSEA', 'DeepSTARR', 'MCP genomics', 'hosted inference') and the description repeats vendor domain names (genomicintelligence.ai, api.genomicintelligence.ai, mcp.genomicintelligence.ai). This broadens discovery/activation surface. However, all keywords remain tightly within the stated genomics-inference domain and the description does not make over-broad claims ('can do anything', 'general assistant'), so this is informational rather than a real capability-inflation attack.
findings.snippet: 'trigger-keywords': 'DNA sequence prediction, regulatory genomics, promoter prediction, ... DeepSEA, DeepSTARR, BigBird splice, MCP genomics'
findings.remediation: Trim the keyword list to the minimal set needed for correct activation; rely on the natural-language description rather than a dense keyword block.

findings.title: No allowed-tools declaration while instructing network access and code execution
findings.description: The manifest does not declare 'allowed-tools', yet the instructions direct the agent to execute Python with the 'requests' library, make outbound HTTPS calls to api.genomicintelligence.ai and rest.ensembl.org, read the GI_API_KEY environment variable, and connect to a remote MCP server. 'allowed-tools' is optional per spec, so this is informational only; there is no declared restriction being violated. Users should nonetheless be aware the skill inherently requires network egress and env-var access.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified; body: HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['GI_API_KEY']}"}; requests.post(f"{BASE}/v1/tasks/{task}/predict", ...)
findings.remediation: Declare allowed-tools (e.g., [Python, Read]) and explicitly document the required network endpoints so hosts can scope egress.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: GeoMaster is a large, documentation-only geospatial reference skill (16 markdown files, no executable scripts). The manifest description accurately matches the content: coordinate systems, remote sensing, GIS software integration, ML, big data, and multi-language examples. No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or instruction-override language was found in SKILL.md or any reference file (checked language-agnostically). No data exfiltration was identified — all network endpoints referenced are legitimate, well-known public geospatial services (Planetary Computer STAC, Copernicus SciHub, USGS EarthExplorer, Overpass API, Natural Earth S3, OpenStreetMap tiles, epsg.org). No credential harvesting (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), no environment scraping, no base64/hex obfuscation, no reverse shells, and no read→send tool-chaining patterns. The static analyzer's MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC hits are false positives: the flagged code blocks contain GRASS GIS `gscript.run_command`/`parse_command` and SAGA `subprocess.run` calls with hardcoded binaries and list-form arguments — standard geoprocessing API usage, not Python eval/exec on untrusted input. All referenced files are internal to the package (many optional reference/asset/template paths simply do not exist, causing broken links but no security risk; the *.py entries in the reference list are import-name artifacts of the static scanner, not bundled scripts). Remaining findings are minor hygiene issues: unpinned dependency install commands, absent allowed-tools declaration alongside subprocess examples, and placeholder credential patterns in documentation. Overall this skill appears benign and suitable for use with normal review of any install or subprocess commands before execution.
llm_primary_threats: Unpinned dependency installation (supply-chain hygiene)
Insecure inline credential patterns in documentation examples
Undeclared tool scope with subprocess/shell execution examples

findings.title: Documentation examples reference credentials/API keys as placeholders
findings.description: Several code examples show credential usage patterns: AWS session keys for S3/COG access, placeholder API keys for Google Maps/Mapbox/OpenWeatherMap, and literal ('user', 'password') arguments for the Copernicus SentinelAPI. All are illustrative placeholders — no real hardcoded secrets, no network transmission of local credentials, and no reads of ~/.aws or ~/.ssh. Risk is limited to encouraging insecure inline credential patterns if copied verbatim.
findings.remediation: Replace inline credential examples with environment-variable or secret-manager based retrieval (e.g., os.environ["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"]) and explicitly warn against committing keys.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration while documentation includes shell/subprocess execution examples
findings.description: The manifest does not declare `allowed-tools` or `compatibility` (optional per spec, informational). Reference material includes examples that invoke external binaries via subprocess (SAGA GIS command-line wrappers) and shell installation commands. Without a declared tool scope, an agent following these docs could execute local shell commands beyond what the description implies. No malicious command construction was observed; the subprocess calls use hardcoded binary paths and list-form arguments (no shell=True).
findings.snippet:
saga_cmd = "/usr/local/saga/saga_cmd"
cmd = [saga_cmd, "grid_calculus", "GridCalculator", f"-GRIDS={input1};{input2}", ...]
subprocess.run(cmd)
findings.remediation: Declare an explicit `allowed-tools` list in the YAML frontmatter and note that subprocess/GIS-binary examples require user approval before execution.

findings.title: Unpinned package installation commands in documentation
findings.description: The SKILL.md installation section instructs installing many packages via conda/uv pip without version pins (e.g., `uv pip install rsgislib torchgeo earthengine-api`). While these are all well-known legitimate geospatial libraries and installation is documented (not automated exfiltration), unpinned installs create supply-chain risk (dependency confusion / malicious version substitution) if an agent executes these commands.
findings.snippet:
conda install -c conda-forge gdal rasterio fiona shapely pyproj geopandas
uv pip install rsgislib torchgeo earthengine-api
uv pip install laspy pylas open3d pdal
findings.remediation: Pin package versions (e.g., rasterio==1.3.9) and require explicit user confirmation before the agent runs any install commands.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `geopandas` skill is a defensive, documentation-plus-audit-tooling package with no identified security threats. SKILL.md contains only technical GeoPandas guidance (CRS semantics, geometry validity, join cardinality, I/O contracts) and explicitly security-positive policies: reject URLs/GDAL /vsi* paths/archives, keep PROJ network disabled, use parameterized SQL for PostGIS, avoid printing engine URLs or dumping the environment, and never embed credentials. No prompt-injection, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language appears in any human language.

Script review: all six Python files are local-only, deterministic CLIs. `_common.py` implements careful path hardening (null-byte and URL/VSI rejection, archive-suffix denial, symlink component rejection, '..' rejection, root containment via `is_relative_to`, extension allowlist, byte/feature/pair ceilings, no-overwrite output creation with atomic `os.link` from a temp file). No `eval`, `exec`, `os.system`, `subprocess`, `pickle`, or shell invocation exists anywhere. There are zero network calls — no `requests`, `urllib`, `socket`, or HTTP clients — and `disable_proj_network()` actively turns PROJ network access off. Reports are explicitly redacted: no paths, layer names, field names, IDs, coordinates, or bounds are emitted; only hashes and aggregate counts.

The static pre-scan flags "environment variable access with network calls" and a "cross-file env var exfiltration chain" across 6 files. These are false positives. The only `os` usage in the package is `os.close`/`os.link` in `write_new_geopackage` for atomic temp-file linking; there is no `os.environ` read in any script. The `os.environ[...]` snippets appear solely inside a markdown documentation example in `references/data-io.md` demonstrating the *safe* pattern of building a SQLAlchemy URL from named secrets, accompanied by explicit warnings never to print the URL or environment. No code path connects environment data to any egress channel, because no egress channel exists.

Manifest consistency: `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep` is consistent with observed behavior — reading local vector metadata, writing a single new GeoPackage under `--repair-output`, and invoking bundled CLIs. Description matches implementation; no capability inflation, keyword baiting, or brand impersonation. Referenced files that exist (references/*.md) are internal package resources with benign, security-conscious content; the flagged `assets/*` and `templates/*` paths are pre-scan path-guessing artifacts, not links present in SKILL.md, so their absence is not a defect. Dependencies are fully version-pinned with no unpinned or GitHub-sourced installs. Resource use is bounded everywhere (chunked joins with a max_pairs fail-closed limit, no unbounded loops or retries).

The get-available-resources skill is a well-engineered, read-only local resource-inventory tool and shows no evidence of malicious behavior. All three components were reviewed: (1) SKILL.md contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; in fact it defines an explicit conservative safety contract (no stress tests, no environment dumps, no driver mutation, no identifier/path emission). (2) The Python scripts perform only bounded, read-only probes: os/platform APIs, bounded reads of /proc and cgroup v2 files, shutil.disk_usage/os.statvfs on the CWD, and subprocess execution of fixed executable/argument tuples (nvidia-smi, amd-smi, rocm-smi, sysctl, system_profiler) with shell=False, DEVNULL stdin, short timeouts, and truncation of stdout/stderr. There is no eval/exec, no dynamic command construction from user input, no network activity (no requests/urllib/socket usage), no credential or SSH/AWS/token access, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, and no infinite/unbounded loops (traversal depth, device count, CPU-list size, and diff size are all explicitly bounded). (3) File output is tightly constrained by _common.py: a single .json filename in the CWD, symlink-refusing (O_NOFOLLOW, is_symlink checks), 0o600 permissions, and O_EXCL unless --force. Input JSON reads are bounded to 1 MiB, must be regular non-symlink files, and are schema-validated. Behavior matches the manifest description precisely; no capability inflation, keyword baiting, tool chaining to network sinks, cross-context bridging, or over-collection was found. Referenced files bundled inside the package (references/*.md) contain only benign documentation with no embedded instructions to the agent; several other referenced paths (templates/*, assets/*) are simply absent and are a documentation-hygiene issue only. allowed-tools is not declared, which is optional and informational only. Overall risk: very low.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `gget` skill is a legitimate, well-documented wrapper around the open-source pachterlab/gget bioinformatics CLI/Python package. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, or role-redefinition language was found in SKILL.md or any reference file. The three bundled Python scripts (gene_analysis.py, batch_sequence_analysis.py, enrichment_pipeline.py) use only argparse, pathlib, pandas, and gget API calls; there is no eval/exec, no os.system/subprocess, no shell interpolation, no reading of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or environment secrets, and no network calls to non-bioinformatics or attacker-controlled endpoints. All writes are to user-specified output prefixes/directories in the working directory, consistent with the declared `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash` — no tool-restriction violation. The description accurately matches behavior, and it even honestly redirects users to biopython/bioservices for other use cases rather than inflating capability. Credential handling guidance is notably good: COSMIC and OpenAI keys are recommended via environment variables or interactive prompts, with explicit warnings against CLI-argument exposure (shell history/process listings) and hard-coding — no hardcoded secrets exist anywhere in the package. Only minor, non-malicious issues remain: dependency/`gget setup` installs that pull third-party artifacts (version-pinned for gget itself), documented heavy-resource operations (bulk viral downloads, whole-genome refs, AlphaFold), and a few dangling referenced-file paths. Overall risk: LOW / benign.

findings.title: Potentially large resource-consuming operations (bulk downloads, AlphaFold prediction)
findings.description: The skill documents operations that can consume very large amounts of bandwidth, disk, and CPU: `gget virus --download_all_accessions` (entire Viruses taxonomy), `gget ref -w dna -d` (whole genomes), cellxgene AnnData downloads, and AlphaFold structure prediction. These are legitimate bioinformatics features and the documentation explicitly warns against unfiltered bulk downloads, so this is informational only.
findings.snippet: **Important**: Do not use `--download_all_accessions` without restrictive filters; it can attempt to download the entire Viruses taxonomy and consume substantial time, bandwidth, and disk.
findings.remediation: Keep the existing warnings; additionally require user confirmation and explicit size/limit parameters before executing bulk download or AlphaFold prediction commands.

findings.title: Dependency installation instructions execute package managers
findings.description: SKILL.md instructs installing packages via `uv pip install "gget==0.30.5"` and `gget setup <module>` which internally runs `uv pip install`/`pip install` and downloads ~4GB of AlphaFold model parameters and third-party 'modified' dependencies. Version is pinned (good practice), and the source is the legitimate upstream PyPI/pachterlab project, so risk is minimal, but the skill still triggers network installs and large third-party downloads on the user's machine.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "gget==0.30.5"
...
gget setup alphafold  # Installs modified third-party dependencies and downloads model parameters
findings.remediation: Require explicit user confirmation before running any install/setup command, and prefer isolated virtual environments (already recommended). Document the exact third-party artifacts downloaded by `gget setup`.

findings.title: Referenced files missing from package

Missing referenced documentation is a documentation-integrity issue only; no evidence of malicious intent. Present reference files (module_catalog.md, module_reference.md, common_workflows.md, workflows.md) are benign bioinformatics documentation.

findings.remediation: Ship all referenced reference files or remove the dangling references to avoid the agent attempting to fetch or fabricate missing content.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The gtars skill is a defensively-written, documentation-heavy bioinformatics helper package. All five bundled Python CLIs are standard-library only: no network calls, no subprocess/os.system, no eval/exec, no credential or environment harvesting, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, and no output-file writing. The shared _common.py implements strong input hardening (URL/URI scheme rejection, '..' traversal rejection, symlink component rejection, O_NOFOLLOW opens, regular-file checks, bounded gzip expansion, NUL/UTF-8 validation, bounded integers) and privacy-preserving output (paths redacted by default). The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; instead it repeatedly gates network-capable upstream operations (Tokenizer.from_pretrained, RefgetStore.open_remote, gtars bbcache) behind explicit user approval and warns about implicit cache writes and URL-coercion of nonexistent local paths. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob) are consistent with the described workflow, and dependency guidance uses exact version pins (gtars==0.9.2, --version 0.9.0 --locked, '=0.9.0') plus checksum verification, which is good supply-chain practice. Only minor issues were found: permissive hard resource ceilings, some referenced doc paths that are not present despite an absolute 'all present' claim, and an ordering defect for MAX_DENSE_GAP in coverage_preflight.py. No evidence of data exfiltration, tool poisoning, capability inflation, or malicious behavior.

Documentation inaccuracy: referenced files not present

findings.title: Very high hard resource caps in bundled helpers (8 GiB / 10M records / 256 workers)
findings.description: The shared safety module defines permissive hard ceilings (HARD_MAX_BYTES = 8 GiB, HARD_MAX_RECORDS = 10,000,000, HARD_MAX_WORKERS = 256) and per-tool defaults up to 4 GiB total artifact bytes. A user-supplied argument can therefore drive multi-gigabyte hashing/line scanning and large memory use in a single invocation. This is bounded and local (no network, no subprocess), so impact is limited to local compute/IO consumption rather than a security compromise.
findings.snippet:
HARD_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024**3
HARD_MAX_RECORDS = 10_000_000
HARD_MAX_FILES = 100_000
HARD_MAX_WORKERS = 256
findings.remediation: Lower default caps, or require explicit opt-in for scans above a few hundred megabytes; document expected runtime/memory for maximum-size inputs.

findings.title: Module-level constant used before definition in coverage_preflight.py (NameError at import)
findings.description: coverage_preflight.py references MAX_DENSE_GAP inside build_parser() while the constant is defined after the function, and the CLI also has a spurious math import path dependency. In CPython this is fine only because the name is resolved at call time and the module-level assignment executes at import; however MAX_DENSE_GAP is defined after build_parser but before main() is invoked, so behaviour depends on definition ordering and is fragile. This is a code-quality/robustness defect, not an exploitable injection; there is no eval/exec, subprocess, or network usage anywhere in the skill.
findings.snippet: "--dense", type=int_type(minimum=-1, maximum=MAX_DENSE_GAP, label="dense") ... (later) MAX_DENSE_GAP = 10_000_000
findings.remediation: Move MAX_DENSE_GAP above build_parser() and add an import-time smoke test for each helper CLI.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The histolab skill is a documentation-only package (8 markdown files, no executable scripts) that accurately describes legitimate use of the open-source histolab library for whole-slide-image tile extraction and preprocessing. No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language appears in SKILL.md or any reference file. There are no network calls to external endpoints, no credential or environment-variable access, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation/base64 payloads, and no exfiltration or tool-chaining patterns. The name, description, and body are consistent with actual behavior, and its explicit deferral to `pathml` for advanced pipelines is scope-limiting rather than capability inflation. All file reads are of internal, bundled resources or user-supplied slide files, which is expected behavior. The static analyzer's MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC hit is a false positive: the only matches are `cv2.Laplacian(..., cv2.CV_64F)` and NumPy/scikit-image style filter code — there is no Python `eval()`/`exec()` call, no `os.system`, and no `subprocess` usage anywhere in the package (the reference file even annotates this explicitly). Remaining issues are minor hygiene concerns: unpinned dependency installs, a destructive `tile_path.unlink()` example presented without warning, an undeclared (optional) `allowed-tools` field, and numerous broken file references to templates/, assets/, and histolab.py. Overall risk: LOW — the skill appears benign and fit for purpose.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions
findings.description: The skill instructs installing histolab and pooch via `uv pip install` without version pinning, despite documenting a specific supported version (0.7.0). Unpinned installs can pull unexpected or compromised upstream releases. This is standard documentation practice and low risk, but no hash/version pinning or provenance verification is provided.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install histolab
uv pip install pooch
findings.remediation: Pin versions explicitly (e.g., `uv pip install histolab==0.7.0 pooch==1.8.2`) to ensure reproducible, verified dependency resolution.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration while documentation implies file write and shell execution

This is informational only since `allowed-tools` is optional, but the destructive `unlink()` example could delete user files if run without review.

allowed-tools: Not specified
...
if laplacian_var < threshold:
    tile_path.unlink()  # Remove blurry tile
findings.remediation: Declare `allowed-tools` (e.g., [Read, Write, Bash, Python]) and add an explicit caution that the blur-filter example permanently deletes files, recommending a dry-run or move-to-quarantine pattern instead of `unlink()`.
