scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The hugging-science skill appears to be a legitimate discovery/documentation helper for Hugging Face scientific resources. The bundled script (scripts/fetch_catalog.py) is stdlib-only, read-only, and does exactly what it claims: HTTP GETs three fixed endpoints on huggingscience.co, parses markdown into structured entries, and prints them. There is no eval/exec, no subprocess, no filesystem writes, no credential reading, no obfuscation, no hardcoded secrets, and no exfiltration channel. Description and behavior are consistent, and the markdown body contains no prompt injection, concealment, or safety-bypass language. The residual risks are inherent to the skill's design rather than malicious: (1) it treats remote markdown from a third-party domain as authoritative input for choosing code/repos to run, an indirect prompt-injection and unvetted-pointer surface; (2) it documents trust_remote_code=True (arbitrary remote code execution) and HF_TOKEN loading from .env with onward transmission to Spaces. Notably, the skill itself explicitly flags both of these, states that catalog inclusion is not a vetting signal, and mandates user confirmation before enabling trust_remote_code or uploading files/tokens to non-org Spaces — unusually good security hygiene for a skill. Remaining nits: unpinned dependency installs, missing manifest metadata, and several referenced files that do not exist. Overall: LOW-to-MEDIUM risk, no evidence of malicious intent; safe to use with the documented confirmation gates enforced.
llm_primary_threats: Indirect prompt injection via network-fetched catalog markdown treated as authoritative
Arbitrary code execution pathway via trust_remote_code=True on catalog-sourced model repos
Credential/data exposure via .env HF_TOKEN loading and gradio_client uploads to third-party Spaces
Unpinned dependency installation (supply-chain)
Broad keyword-dense activation description
Missing manifest metadata and dangling referenced files

findings.title: Guidance to enable trust_remote_code=True (arbitrary code execution from remote model repos)
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent on using `trust_remote_code=True` with model repository names that may originate from the remotely fetched catalog. This flag causes arbitrary Python from a third-party HF repo to execute on the user's machine with their filesystem and credentials in scope. The skill does include a clear human-in-the-loop control ('ask the user before you set it, naming the repo, and wait for an answer'), which substantially mitigates the risk, but the code-execution pathway remains an inherent risk worth noting.
findings.snippet: model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("arcinstitute/evo2_7b", trust_remote_code=True)  — "the flag executes arbitrary Python from the model repo on the user's machine — so ask the user before you set it"
findings.remediation: Keep and strengthen the confirmation requirement: require the user to explicitly name/approve the exact repo and revision, prefer pinned `revision=` commits, and never enable trust_remote_code for repo names sourced from network-fetched catalog data without independent verification.

findings.title: Instructs loading HF_TOKEN from .env, with token forwarded to third-party Spaces
findings.description: The skill directs the agent to auto-load secrets from any `.env` in cwd or parent directories via python-dotenv, and notes that once loaded, gradio_client will send HF_TOKEN to whichever Space is called and `file(...)` uploads local files to that Space's operator. This creates a credential/data exposure path if a Space identifier comes from the untrusted remote catalog. Mitigations are documented (never hard-code or echo tokens, add .env to .gitignore, name the Space and files to the user and get approval before calling non-org Spaces), so this is informational rather than malicious.
findings.snippet: load_dotenv()    # picks up HF_TOKEN from .env in cwd or any parent dir  /  "once HF_TOKEN is loaded, gradio_client sends it to whatever Space you call, and file(...) uploads local data to that Space's operator."
findings.remediation: Scope token loading to the project directory only (avoid parent-directory traversal), prefer per-call explicit token passing over global env loading, and require explicit user confirmation naming the destination Space and the exact files before any upload or authenticated call.

findings.title: Very broad, keyword-dense activation description
findings.description: The frontmatter description enumerates a long list of trigger domains (biology, chemistry, physics, astronomy, climate, genomics, materials, medicine, ecology, energy, engineering, math, drug discovery, protein design, weather modeling, theorem proving, single-cell, PDE solving), which increases activation breadth. This is plausibly legitimate for a multi-domain catalog skill and the body includes an explicit negative scope ('If the task is generic ML ... this skill is not the right tool'), so impact is minimal.
findings.snippet: description: Use when the user is doing AI/ML work in a scientific domain such as biology, chemistry, physics, astronomy, climate, genomics, materials, medicine, ecology, energy, engineering, math, drug discovery, protein design, weather modeling, theorem proving, single-cell, or PDE solving.
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to the skill's actual function (discovering resources in the Hugging Science catalog) and rely on the body for domain enumeration.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation guidance

- allowed-tools: Not specified

findings.title: Skill fetches and consumes remote markdown from huggingscience.co as authoritative guidance
findings.description: The skill's core workflow instructs the agent to fetch markdown files from an external domain (https://huggingscience.co/llms.txt, llms-full.txt, topics/<slug>.md) and use the content to decide which datasets/models/Spaces to load and run. The fetched content is untrusted network data that is rendered directly into the agent's context, creating an indirect prompt injection surface: whoever controls (or spoofs/compromises) huggingscience.co can insert instructions, malicious repo names, or Space names that the agent may act upon. The skill partially mitigates this by explicitly stating the catalog is 'not a vetting signal' and requiring user confirmation before `trust_remote_code=True` or uploading files/tokens to non-org Spaces, which lowers severity. No sanitization of fetched content is performed in fetch_catalog.py (it is parsed and printed verbatim).
findings.snippet: BASE = "https://huggingscience.co" ... with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as resp: return resp.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")  # content printed to agent context; SKILL.md: "These are markdown files designed to be fetched and read."
findings.remediation: Treat all fetched catalog content as untrusted data, not instructions. Strip/neutralize imperative content and code blocks before presenting to the agent, validate that URLs resolve to huggingface.co/<org>/<name> patterns, pin TLS/host expectations, and require explicit user approval before acting on any repo/Space identifier obtained from the remote catalog.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `hypogenic` skill is a defensive planning/auditing wrapper for the ChicagoHAI HypoGeniC hypothesis-generation package. All five bundled Python scripts are local-only, standard-library based (optional pinned PyYAML for YAML parsing), and perform strictly bounded read-only file operations: JSON/YAML schema validation, SHA-256 checksum verification, dataset split-leakage auditing, arithmetic cost estimation, and model-free classification metrics. No network calls, subprocess execution, eval/exec, dynamic imports, pickle deserialization, or credential reads are present. Security controls are unusually strong and deliberate: path traversal and symlink rejection (`_reject_symlink_components`, `_within_root`), rejection of URLs and any `.env` path component, duplicate-JSON-key rejection, non-finite number rejection, node/depth/size/row caps preventing resource exhaustion, YAML restricted to SafeLoader with anchors/aliases/tags forbidden and an exact PyYAML version pin, and an explicit secret-detection regex that rejects configs containing API-key-like values or secret-bearing field names. Credential handling is limited to `os.getenv()` presence checks on an allowlisted, provider-specific variable name (`OPENAI_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) with the value never printed. Reports redact raw dataset text, hypotheses, IDs, labels, and predictions using hash fingerprints. The SKILL.md instructions contain no prompt injection, jailbreak, concealment, or role-redefinition language; instead they repeatedly instruct the agent to treat dataset/prompt/hypothesis text as untrusted data and never follow embedded instructions — a defensive posture, not an injection. Declared `allowed-tools` (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep) are consistent with running local read-only Python CLIs. Manifest description matches actual behavior; installation guidance uses a fully pinned version (`hypogenic==0.3.5`) with wheel/sdist SHA-256 hashes and PyPI trusted-publisher provenance, plus explicit warnings against installing unpinned branch tips — strong supply-chain hygiene. Referenced documentation files that are present (configuration.md, upstream.md, datasets.md, evaluation.md, security.md, sources.md) contain only benign technical guidance; several other paths listed as "referenced" (templates/*, assets/*.md, references/*.example.json) are missing, which is at most a minor documentation-completeness issue and not a security threat since no script depends on them and all file access is boundary-checked at runtime. No security findings warranting a report were identified.

This skill is a documentation- and validation-oriented research-planning package. All seven bundled Python CLIs are pure standard-library, deterministic, and strictly local: they contain no network calls, no subprocess/exec/eval, no environment-variable or credential access, no dynamic imports, and no base64/obfuscated payloads. The shared helper module (`_common.py`) implements notably strong defensive input handling — rejection of URL-like paths and symlinks, suffix allow-listing, 2 MiB input caps, row/cell/list/text bounds, NUL-byte and non-UTF-8 rejection, duplicate JSON key detection, exact CSV header matching, safe relative-path checks with `..` rejection, no implicit overwrite without `--force`, and atomic writes with 0600 permissions. The Markdown scaffold generator escapes interpolated text to keep output inert. The SKILL.md instruction body contains no prompt injection, no instruction override, no concealment directives, and no safety-bypass language; instead it repeatedly asserts human accountability and ethics/biosafety/dual-use stop gates, and explicitly refuses to provide harmful operational detail for pathogens, toxins, or weapons. The description matches actual behavior, with no capability inflation or keyword baiting. Only two minor, non-exploitable issues were identified: the optional `allowed-tools` field is absent, and a set of documented asset paths (mostly under a `templates/` prefix) do not exist in the package. Neither enables data access, exfiltration, or code execution. Overall: SAFE.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration in manifest
findings.description: The YAML frontmatter does not declare an `allowed-tools` field. This is an optional field per the Agent Skills specification, so this is informational only. The compatibility field and instruction body do constrain behavior to local, standard-library-only Python CLIs with no network, credential, or subprocess use, and the bundled scripts are consistent with that claim.
findings.snippet: - allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Optionally declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash, Python]` (or a narrower set) to make the execution surface explicit.

findings.title: Several documented/referenced file paths are absent from the package
findings.description: The instruction body and references point to bundled assets, but a number of referenced paths (mostly under a non-existent `templates/` prefix, plus `assets/search_boundary_template.json` variants under `references/`) are not present in the package. No script performs network fallback or substitute retrieval when a file is missing — the shared loader rejects URL-like paths and non-existent files with a validation error — so the practical impact is documentation drift, not remote data ingestion. Note that the bundled `references/security_validation.md` pre-emptively characterizes such findings as "analyzer false positive"; that self-assessment should not substitute for independent verification.
findings.snippet: Referenced but not found: templates/evidence_ledger_template.csv, templates/hypothesis_record_template.json, references/search_boundary_template.json, assets/tool_reference.md, ... ; _common.safe_input_path raises ValidationError(f"input file does not exist: {path}")
findings.remediation: Reconcile the documented asset paths with the files actually shipped, and remove references to non-existent `templates/` paths.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This appears to be a legitimate, well-documented research skill from the NCI Imaging Data Commons team (ImagingDataCommons/idc-claude-skill) for querying and downloading public cancer imaging data via the idc-index package. No prompt injection, instruction-override, concealment directives, credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), environment-variable harvesting, hardcoded secrets, obfuscated/encoded payloads, eval/exec, or exfiltration of local data to attacker-controlled endpoints was found. All network destinations are official/public and consistent with the declared purpose (portal.imaging.datacommons.cancer.gov, proxy.imaging.datacommons.cancer.gov, storage.googleapis.com/idc-index-data-artifacts, bigquery-public-data, idc-open-data S3/GCS buckets), and data flow is inbound (download) rather than outbound exfiltration. No script files ship with the package; all code is illustrative inside markdown. The description matches actual documented behavior, and licensing/attribution guidance is responsible. Residual concerns are hygiene issues: an autonomous pip install using --break-system-packages executed as the first step, unpinned `pip install --upgrade` recommendations, f-string SQL construction in one example, missing allowed-tools declaration for a skill that needs Bash/Python/network/disk-write, and the potential for very large (multi-TB) downloads. Several referenced files under templates/ and assets/ (and idc_index.py) were not found, which is a documentation-resolution issue rather than a security threat, though missing referenced files should be verified so the agent does not fetch substitutes from untrusted locations.
llm_primary_threats: Autonomous package installation with --break-system-packages and unpinned upgrades (supply-chain hygiene)
SQL string interpolation pattern in example code
Undeclared broad tool scope (Bash/Python execution, network access, filesystem writes)
Potential resource exhaustion from unbounded dataset downloads

findings.title: SQL built via f-string interpolation in example code (injection-prone pattern)
findings.description: Example workflow code constructs SQL queries by interpolating values directly into the query string with f-strings. Although the values originate from IDC metadata (manufacturer/model names) rather than direct user input, the pattern is unsafe if an agent adapts it to user-supplied filters, allowing SQL string breakage or injection into the local DuckDB query engine. Impact is limited because the target is a read-only local metadata database.
findings.snippet:
query = f"""
    SELECT SeriesInstanceUID
    FROM index
    WHERE Manufacturer = '{mfr}'
      AND ManufacturerModelName = '{model}'
    ...
"""
findings.remediation: Demonstrate parameterized queries (DuckDB supports parameter binding) or explicit escaping/allow-listing of values instead of f-string interpolation, so the agent does not learn an injection-prone pattern.

findings.title: Potentially large unbounded data downloads to local disk
findings.description: The skill's core workflow downloads DICOM datasets, and examples include downloading entire collections (e.g., `client.download_from_selection(collection_id="tcga_luad")`) where IDC collections can be terabytes in size. This can exhaust local disk/bandwidth if executed without size estimation. The skill does include a mitigating best practice ('Estimate size first') and LIMIT-based guidance, so risk is low and expected for the stated purpose.
findings.snippet:
client.download_from_selection(
    collection_id="tcga_luad",
    downloadDir="./data",
    dirTemplate="%collection_id/%PatientID/%Modality"
)
findings.remediation: Require an explicit size-estimation query and user confirmation before any collection-level download; enforce batching and a maximum default download size.

findings.title: No allowed-tools declaration despite instructions requiring Bash/Python execution, network and filesystem writes
findings.description: The manifest omits the optional allowed-tools and compatibility fields, while the instructions direct the agent to execute Python and shell commands, install packages, perform network requests to external endpoints (GCS/S3 buckets, DICOMweb proxy, BigQuery), open a web browser, and write files/downloads to local directories. This is informational: the behaviors are consistent with the stated purpose of the skill, but the absence of declared tool scope means no restriction is asserted for these fairly broad capabilities.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified; compatibility: Not specified — while body instructs pip install, subprocess.run, webbrowser.open, and large downloads to local disk
findings.remediation: Declare allowed-tools explicitly (e.g., [Read, Write, Bash, Python]) and note network/disk requirements plus expected download sizes so the user can evaluate scope before activation.

findings.title: Automatic package installation with --break-system-packages during skill startup
findings.description: The SKILL.md instructs the agent to run a version check block FIRST that automatically invokes pip3 install with the --break-system-packages flag via subprocess.run, without asking the user for confirmation. While the version is pinned (idc-index==0.11.14), which mitigates supply-chain drift, the --break-system-packages flag intentionally overrides the environment's protection against modifying system-managed Python packages, and this occurs autonomously as part of a discovery/setup step. Other locations in the same file additionally recommend unpinned installs (`pip install --upgrade idc-index`, `pip install pandas numpy pydicom`), which can pull arbitrary newer versions.
findings.snippet:
subprocess.run(
    ["pip3", "install", "--break-system-packages", f"idc-index=={REQUIRED_VERSION}"],
    check=True,
)
findings.remediation: Do not auto-install packages without explicit user consent. Remove --break-system-packages or prefer a virtual environment / --user install, and surface the intended command to the user for approval. Pin versions for all recommended installs (e.g., pandas==x.y.z) rather than using --upgrade.

findings.title: Python code block executes shell commands
findings.description: Code block in SKILL.md at line 27 contains potentially dangerous Python code.
findings.snippet: subprocess.run(
findings.remediation: Review the code block for security implications.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `infographics` skill is a coherent, well-documented image-generation wrapper and appears benign. Two Python scripts implement exactly what SKILL.md and the reference files describe: build a prompt from type/style/palette presets, call OpenRouter (Gemini image model for generation, Perplexity Sonar for optional research, Gemini for scored quality review), save versioned PNGs plus a JSON review log, and stop early when the quality threshold is met.

No malicious behavior was identified. Specifically: no eval/exec/os.system, no shell=True, no reverse shells, no base64-encoded executable payloads (base64 use is strictly image encode/decode), no reads of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, browser stores, or SSH/cloud credentials, no home-directory or filesystem traversal, no unpinned package installs or GitHub installs, and no writes outside the user-specified output directory. The only network destination is https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, which the manifest, docs, and env-var metadata all disclose. The subprocess invocation uses a list-form argv (no shell), and notably passes an allow-listed minimal environment instead of the full parent environment — a security-positive design choice.

The pre-scan 'env var exfiltration' and 'cross-file exfiltration chain' signals are false positives from the read-env-then-network heuristic: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is the API credential for the declared provider, used as an Authorization Bearer header, not harvested data sent to an attacker. Manifest consistency is good: declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) match observed behavior (reads context images, writes images/JSON logs, invoked via Bash/Python), the description matches implementation, and there is no keyword baiting or activation-priority manipulation. SKILL.md and all reference markdown contain no prompt injection, concealment directives, role redefinition, or safety-bypass language; referenced files are internal to the package (several listed under templates/ and assets/ are simply absent, a documentation-path inconsistency rather than a security issue).

Minor residual observations, both LOW: (1) optional python-dotenv loading reads .env from the current working directory, so running the skill in an untrusted directory could pick up credentials from that directory, and review/research logs persist prompts and model output to disk; (2) web-derived research text and model critique text are concatenated into subsequent prompts without sanitization, a limited indirect-prompt-injection surface whose only consumer is an image model — no tool, shell, or filesystem action is driven by it. Overall: low risk, safe to use with a valid OpenRouter key, noting that user prompts and researched content are transmitted to third-party model providers.

findings.title: Cross-file env var exfiltration: 2 files
findings.description: Environment variable access with network calls in scripts/generate_infographic.py, scripts/generate_infographic_ai.py
findings.remediation: Review data flow across files: scripts/generate_infographic_ai.py, scripts/generate_infographic.py

findings.title: Cross-file exfiltration chain: 2 files
findings.description: Multi-file exfiltration chain detected: scripts/generate_infographic.py, scripts/generate_infographic_ai.py collect data → scripts/generate_infographic_ai.py → scripts/generate_infographic_ai.py transmit to network
findings.remediation: Review data flow across files: scripts/generate_infographic_ai.py, scripts/generate_infographic.py

findings.title: API key read from environment and sent to OpenRouter (expected, benign)
findings.description: Static analyzers flagged an 'env var exfiltration' chain across scripts/generate_infographic.py and scripts/generate_infographic_ai.py. Review shows this is the documented, legitimate pattern: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from the environment (or --api-key) and used as a Bearer token in HTTPS requests to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions, the declared provider. The parent script explicitly builds a minimal allow-listed environment for the subprocess rather than passing the whole parent environment, which reduces secret leakage to the child. No secrets are hardcoded, no third-party/unknown endpoints are contacted, and no local credential files (~/.aws, ~/.ssh) are read. Residual note: optional .env loading via python-dotenv reads .env from CWD and the script directory, so a .env in an untrusted working directory could supply credentials, and the JSON review log persists the user prompt and research output to disk.
findings.remediation: No action required for core behavior. Optionally restrict .env discovery to the skill directory only (or require an explicit path), and document that review logs (*_review_log.json, *_research.json) contain prompts and model output so users avoid including sensitive content.

findings.title: External model/search output is embedded into subsequent prompts without sanitization
findings.description: When --research is used, content returned by Perplexity Sonar (which performs live web search) is concatenated verbatim into the image-generation prompt via _enhance_prompt_with_research, and the review model's free-text critique is concatenated into the next generation prompt via improve_prompt. This is a mild indirect-prompt-injection surface: text retrieved from the web could contain instructions that alter the generation prompt. Impact is limited because the downstream consumer is an image-generation model and no tool execution, file writes outside the output directory, or shell commands are driven by that text. Model-supplied text is never passed to eval/exec or a shell.
findings.remediation: Wrap externally retrieved research and critique text in clearly delimited, explicitly untrusted blocks and instruct the downstream model to treat it as data only; optionally strip imperative/meta-instruction patterns and cap injected length.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
This is a benign, unusually well-scoped documentation/validation skill for ISO management-system and laboratory-accreditation readiness evidence. No malicious behavior was identified.

Manifest vs. behavior: The declared description matches the implementation. allowed-tools (Read, Write, Bash, Glob) is consistent with observed behavior — the scripts read local JSON/Markdown, write a report only when --output is passed, and are invoked via python3 from Bash. No Python tool declaration is needed since execution occurs through Bash; no restriction violation was found.

Instruction body: No prompt injection, jailbreak, role redefinition, concealment directive, or safety-bypass language. The opposite pattern is present: extensive negative-capability boundaries, mandatory human-approval gating, fail-closed defaults, and explicit prohibitions on making compliance/certification claims. Copyright guidance instructs the agent NOT to retrieve or reproduce ISO clause text, which reduces rather than increases risk.

Scripts: All seven Python files use only the standard library (argparse, json, hashlib, pathlib, re, datetime, dataclasses, collections). There is no network access, no subprocess/os.system, no eval/exec/compile, no pickle or other executable deserialization, no environment-variable harvesting, no credential-path access, and no hardcoded secrets. The pre-scan flag MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC is a false positive: the only matching tokens are the docstring/help strings asserting 'no dynamic evaluation' and the argparse-adjacent word 'executable' — there is no eval() or exec() call anywhere in the package.

Input handling is defensively strong and worth noting positively: symlink refusal on input, output, and evidence paths; suffix allowlisting; size caps (2 MB); JSON depth (30), item (5,000), and string-length (20,000) bounds; duplicate-JSON-key rejection via object_pairs_hook; non-finite number rejection via parse_constant; path-traversal defense in _safe_evidence_file using is_absolute/'..' checks plus resolve(strict=True) and relative_to() containment against the resolved base; refusal to overwrite existing output without --force; and allow_nan=False on serialization. Recursion during JSON parse is caught. The depth/size walker is iterative, so no unbounded recursion or loop was identified.

File reads are limited to user-supplied controlled-export paths that are explicitly constrained relative to a user-provided --base-dir, and evidence content is never interpreted as instructions — load_markdown returns raw text and does not execute or follow embedded content, and SKILL.md explicitly states that local_path/evidence.location values refer to the user's own export and that unresolved placeholders must never be opened. This is the correct posture against indirect prompt injection.

Data flow: purely local read → validate → stdout or local file. No collection beyond the explicitly enumerated manifest entries, no directory walking, no cross-context bridging, no autonomy escalation, and no tool chaining toward any network sink. The SHA-256 comparison is correctly documented as a local-mismatch check only, not a provenance claim.

Supply chain: no pip/npm installs, no external downloads, no third-party dependencies. All URLs in templates and references are documentation citations to official publishers (iso.org, fda.gov, ecfr.gov, eur-lex, cms.gov, ilac.org, mdsap.global); none is fetched by code. Template placeholder URLs use https://example.invalid deliberately so they fail closed.

Referenced files: many entries in the referenced-file list are static-analyzer path permutations (assets/*, templates/* variants of the same references/* files) and are 'not found' as expected; the real bundled paths (references/*.md, assets/templates/*) all resolve and are internal to the package, which is normal and expected behavior.

Discovery: the description is long but precisely scoped with explicit negative scope ('Not for legal applicability, compliance, certification, or accreditation decisions; contains no clause text'). This is legitimate disambiguation for a narrow regulated domain rather than keyword baiting or capability inflation. Provenance metadata (version, author, license, supersedes, last-reviewed) is present.

Only one low-severity, non-security observation is recorded: hardcoded future-dated regulatory constants that will require maintenance to avoid emitting incorrect blocking findings. The skill is safe to install and run.

findings.title: Hardcoded future-dated regulatory "facts" may mislead if stale
findings.description: SKILL.md and reference files assert dated regulatory baselines (e.g., FDA QMSR effective 2026-02-02, GLOBAC replacing ILAC/IAF on 2026-01-01, ISO 15189 transition closed December 2025) and check_qmsr_transition.py hard-codes an expected basis date of '2026-07-23' and effective date '2026-02-02', emitting a blocker finding if a user's data differs. If these baselines drift or are inaccurate, the deterministic checks will produce incorrect blocking findings on compliance-adjacent work. This is a content-accuracy/maintenance concern, not a security exploit; the skill repeatedly and prominently disclaims compliance, certification, and legal determinations, and the source ledger explicitly flags unverified entries with [confirm on iso.org].
findings.snippet:
if effective != "2026-02-02":
    review.add("EFFECTIVE_DATE", ..., "current QMSR effective date must be recorded as 2026-02-02", "blocker")
findings.remediation: Move dated regulatory constants into a single versioned data file with an explicit review date, and surface a warning (not a blocker) when the skill's baseline date is older than a defined staleness threshold.

metadata.aisubtech_name: Safety Harms and Toxicity: Scams and Deception

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill appears benign and is unusually security-conscious. All three bundled scripts use only the Python standard library, perform no network I/O, spawn no subprocesses, and contain no eval/exec, base64-decoded payloads, or obfuscation. Credential handling is defensive: only five explicitly named LABARCHIVES_* environment variables are read, .env files are never loaded, secrets are never printed (only truncated SHA-256 fingerprints of the signature and Access Key ID are emitted), and getpass is used for interactive secret entry. setup_config.py enforces an HTTPS-only allowlist of five vendor API hosts and rejects embedded credentials, custom ports, queries, and fragments. entry_operations.py validates ELN method names and Inventory routes with strict regexes and rejects traversal/placeholder/encoded segments. notebook_operations.py is a hardened ZIP inspector: it bounds member count, total uncompressed size, and compression ratio (zip-bomb defense), rejects absolute/traversing/backslash/NUL member paths, rejects symlink and encrypted members, blocks DOCTYPE/ENTITY (XXE/billion-laughs defense) before ElementTree parsing, never extracts, and writes output only via O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW with mode 0600 while refusing to overwrite the input. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, concealment, role-redefinition, or safety-bypass language; on the contrary it explicitly instructs the agent to treat returned notebook XML/JSON, attachment names, captions, and comments as untrusted data and to never execute instructions found in them, to require explicit approval before remote writes, to keep TLS verification enabled, and to avoid logging query strings or auth headers. The description matches actual behavior with no capability inflation or keyword baiting, and dependency guidance explicitly discourages an unmaintained community repo and requires exact version pinning if one is approved. Findings are limited to informational items: a publicly documented dummy test vector, an undeclared allowed-tools field, and stale template/asset reference paths.

findings.title: allowed-tools not declared in manifest
findings.description: The YAML frontmatter does not declare allowed-tools. The skill instructs the agent to execute local Python via `uv run`, so Bash/Python capability is implied but not scoped. This is informational only, as allowed-tools is optional per the skill spec, and observed script behavior (stdlib-only, no network) is consistent with the description.
findings.snippet: - allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Bash]` (or the minimal needed set) to make the execution surface explicit.

findings.title: Reference file naming inconsistency / missing template and asset paths
findings.description: The reference-file resolution list includes templates/*.md and assets/*.md paths that do not exist in the package. The SKILL.md body itself only links to references/*.md, all of which are present. Missing files would only cause failed reads, not a security compromise, but they create documentation drift and could later be shadowed by attacker-supplied files of the same name in the working directory.
findings.snippet: **Referenced File: templates/api_reference.md** (not found); **Referenced File: assets/sources.md** (not found)
findings.remediation: Ensure all referenced documentation resolves to existing files inside the skill package and remove stale template/asset path references.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a documentation-only Agent Skill for LaminDB (biological data lakehouse). No script files are bundled; all content is markdown guidance with illustrative Python/Bash snippets. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, role redefinition, or system-prompt extraction attempts were found in any language. There is no data exfiltration: no network POSTs of local data, no reading of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or credential files, no hardcoded secrets (all credentials are placeholders such as '<redacted>' and '<set-in-secret-manager>'), and no obfuscation, base64/hex blobs, eval/exec, or hidden stagers. The name and description match the actual content, and the description is appropriately scoped rather than keyword-baited or over-broad. Notably, the skill includes an explicit 'Safety and Security Defaults' section instructing the agent never to display, log, or transmit API keys, cloud credentials, or connection strings, to prefer IAM roles/secret managers, to check only for the presence of named environment variables, to validate/sanitize external REST/DB/user-provided content with a schema or curator before saving, and to pin package versions — all positive security posture. Dependency guidance uses pinned versions (lamindb==2.5.1, bionty==2.4.0) and recommends lock files, with no unpinned GitHub installs or typosquat-like package names. Referenced external URLs are legitimate official LaminDB/GitHub documentation links and are not used as instruction sources. Several referenced files (templates/*, assets/*, and Python module names like lamindb.py, bionty.py, wandb.py, joblib.py) are reported as not found; the latter are almost certainly false-positive extractions of Python import statements from code examples rather than real missing dependencies, and the missing templates/assets duplicates are cosmetic. Only minor, low-severity issues remain: absent optional metadata and vendor-typical documentation examples that include privileged/destructive shell commands and one f-string SQL interpolation. Overall the skill appears benign and safe to use.

findings.title: Documentation examples include privileged/destructive shell commands and f-string SQL interpolation
findings.description: Reference documentation includes example commands that require elevated privileges or are destructive if run without confirmation (`sudo mkdir/nano/chmod/chown` on shared cache paths, `shutil.rmtree(ln.settings.cache_dir)`, `lamin delete --force`, `artifact.delete(permanent=True)`), and a DuckDB example that interpolates a filesystem path directly into a SQL string. These are conventional vendor-doc patterns rather than malicious payloads, but an agent could execute them verbatim on a user's machine.
findings.snippet:
sudo chown -R shared-user:shared-group /shared/cache/lamindb
shutil.rmtree(ln.settings.cache_dir)
lamin delete --force instance-name
result = duckdb.query(f"""SELECT ... FROM read_parquet('{path}')""")
findings.remediation: Add explicit guidance that destructive or privileged commands require user confirmation before execution, and use parameterized/escaped values instead of f-string interpolation in query examples.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools and compatibility metadata
findings.description: The YAML frontmatter does not declare `allowed-tools` or `compatibility`. This is optional per the skill spec, but the skill's documentation contains many shell commands (uv pip install, lamin init, pg_dump, sudo chmod/chown) and Python snippets that an agent may execute, so declaring tool scope would improve safety. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The latchbio-integration skill is a documentation-heavy reference package for the LatchBio Python SDK/CLI. The single executable script (scripts/inspect_latch_sdk.py) performs purely local introspection: it imports latch modules, inspects signatures via importlib/inspect, normalizes memory addresses out of reprs, and prints text or JSON. It contains no network calls, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no file writes, no credential or environment-variable reads, and no obfuscation. The reference markdown files provide idiomatic, security-conscious guidance: they explicitly instruct never to read/print ~/.latch/token, never to log secrets or signed URLs, to call get_secret() only inside tasks, to avoid passing untrusted strings through shells (prefer subprocess.run with argument lists and check=True), to pin SDK versions, and to require user confirmation before paid compute or destructive operations (rmr, Registry deletion). No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language is present anywhere in SKILL.md or the references. All URLs are official LatchBio/PyPI/GitHub documentation links used as citations, not as instruction sources the agent is told to obey. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the documented workflows (creating workflow files, running latch CLI and uv commands); the compatibility field honestly discloses required network access, Docker, and a Latch account. The pre-scan behavioral flags (ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION, CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN) appear to be false positives triggered by legitimate documentation patterns — mentions of get_secret(), OAuth/token handling guidance, and code examples that upload workflow outputs to the user's own Latch workspace (LPath.upload_from, latch cp/sync). No sink sends local data to an attacker-controlled or third-party endpoint. Dependency guidance is version-pinned (latch==2.76.8), which is a positive supply-chain practice; the noted alpha pin (2.62.1a2) is accompanied by explicit warnings to isolate the environment. Only a minor hygiene issue was identified: numerous referenced file paths (templates/*, assets/*, latch.py) do not exist in the package, likely artifacts of path extraction from prose.", "primary_threats": []

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The latex-posters skill is a legitimate, documentation-heavy LaTeX poster authoring skill. Its markdown body contains no prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, or role-redefinition attempts — the emphatic "MANDATORY"/"CRITICAL"/"DO NOT PROCEED" language is entirely about poster design quality gates (font sizes, element counts, white space, overflow checks), not about bypassing agent safety controls. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with observed behavior: writing LaTeX/figures, running pdflatex, and invoking helper scripts.

The scripts were reviewed line by line. review_poster.sh only inspects a user-supplied PDF with pdfinfo/pdffonts/pdfimages and prints checklists; the filename is properly quoted and no eval/os.system/dynamic execution is present anywhere. generate_schematic.py invokes a sibling script via subprocess with an argument list (no shell=True) and, notably, builds a minimal allow-listed environment specifically to avoid leaking unrelated secrets to the child process — a defensive control, not an exfiltration primitive. generate_schematic_ai.py sends the prompt and image data to the officially documented OpenRouter API using the OPENROUTER_API_KEY the manifest openly declares; there are no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation/base64 payload execution (base64 is used only for legitimate image encoding/decoding), no credential-store or filesystem harvesting (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, os.walk of home), and no undisclosed third-party endpoints. Iterations are hard-capped at 2 with a 120s request timeout, so there is no unbounded-loop or resource-exhaustion risk.

The static analyzer's ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION and cross-file exfiltration-chain hits are false positives arising from the ordinary pattern of reading an API key from the environment and passing it to that API's own endpoint. Only minor, low-severity hygiene issues remain: implicit .env loading from the current working directory, unpinned dependencies, and several referenced asset/template files that are absent from the package. No blocking security concerns were identified.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The liteparse skill is a documentation-centric package for local document/PDF parsing. The single bundled script (scripts/batch_parse_dir.py) is benign: it uses argparse, glob-based file discovery restricted to an allowlisted set of document extensions, and writes results only into a user-specified output directory. There is no eval/exec, no subprocess use, no credential or environment-variable access, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation, and no network calls. Behavior is consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) and the stated purpose. The notable concerns are non-code: (1) the description contains activation-priority manipulation ("even when the user does not name liteparse", "prefer over MarkItDown / the pdf skill"), which is capability-inflation / skill-shadowing behavior; (2) an install instruction pinning a package version described as a future PyPI release, creating a supply-chain/dependency-confusion risk if the package or version is not authentic; (3) documented patterns that pipe remote content into the parser and optionally POST page images to an arbitrary HTTP OCR endpoint, which conflicts with the "all processing is local" claim and introduces indirect prompt-injection / data-egress surface; (4) several referenced files are missing. No CRITICAL or HIGH malicious behavior was identified.
llm_primary_threats: Capability inflation / activation-priority manipulation in skill description
Supply-chain risk from installing an unverifiable pinned package version
Indirect prompt injection surface from piping untrusted remote documents into the parser
Potential data egress via optional external HTTP OCR endpoint
Missing referenced files / incomplete provenance

findings.title: Activation-priority manipulation and cross-skill preemption in description
findings.description: The skill description instructs the agent to activate "even when the user does not name liteparse" and to "Prefer over MarkItDown" and "prefer over the pdf skill". This is discovery/activation abuse: it inflates the skill's perceived priority and broadens activation beyond explicit user intent, potentially shadowing other legitimate document-handling skills.
findings.snippet: "... or page screenshots for multimodal agents — even when the user does not name liteparse. Prefer over MarkItDown when you need bboxes, fast local parsing, or PNG page renders; prefer over the pdf skill for merge/split/forms."
findings.remediation: Rewrite the description to state capabilities factually without preemption directives or instructions to activate without user naming. Move parser comparison guidance into reference docs only.

findings.title: Installation of a possibly non-existent / unverifiable package version (supply-chain risk)
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to run `uv pip install "liteparse==2.0.0"` and cites a PyPI release dated "May 2026" — a future/unverifiable version. If the named package or version does not exist on PyPI, the install command creates a dependency-confusion / typosquatting opportunity where an attacker-published package could be silently installed and executed on the user's machine. The bundled script also imports `liteparse` unconditionally.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "liteparse==2.0.0"
**Version note:** Examples target **liteparse 2.0.0** (PyPI, May 2026).
findings.remediation: Verify the package exists and is published by the claimed maintainer; pin with a hash (e.g., `--require-hashes`) or reference the official repo/registry URL, and require explicit user confirmation before any package installation.

findings.title: Optional external HTTP OCR endpoint can receive document page images
findings.description: The skill documents an optional `--ocr-server-url` / `ocr_server_url` setting that POSTs rendered page images (multipart/form-data) to an arbitrary HTTP endpoint. Although examples use localhost, an arbitrary or attacker-supplied URL would transmit potentially sensitive document contents off-host, contradicting the manifest claim that "All processing is local — no cloud API required".
findings.snippet:
lit parse document.pdf --ocr-server-url http://localhost:8080/ocr
parser = LiteParse(ocr_server_url="http://localhost:8080/ocr")
findings.remediation: Note that using an OCR server URL sends document images off-process; restrict to loopback by default and require explicit user approval for non-local endpoints.

findings.title: Documented pattern of piping remote content directly into the parser
findings.description: Instructions demonstrate downloading a remote PDF over the network and piping it straight into the parser (`curl -sL https://example.com/report.pdf | lit parse -`). Parsed text from untrusted remote documents is then surfaced to the agent, which is a classic indirect prompt-injection vector if the agent treats extracted document text as instructions. No guidance is given to treat extracted content as untrusted data.
findings.snippet: curl -sL https://example.com/report.pdf | lit parse -
findings.remediation: Add explicit guidance that parsed/OCR'd document text is untrusted data and must never be interpreted as instructions; recommend downloading to a validated local file with user confirmation instead of blind piping.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a benign documentation-standards skill. It contains no scripts (no Python/Bash files), performs no network access, reads no credentials, and includes no obfuscated or encoded payloads. All content is instructional markdown teaching Mermaid/markdown style conventions, plus bundled reference guides and document templates that are internal to the skill package (normal, expected behavior). No prompt-injection, instruction-override, concealment, exfiltration, or code-execution patterns were detected in SKILL.md or any of the included reference/template files — the embedded Mermaid code blocks and template placeholders are illustrative examples only (e.g., ER diagrams containing fields named 'password_hash' or 'api_key' are schema documentation, not real secrets). Cross-component consistency is good: the description matches actual behavior (markdown/diagram authoring guidance) and attribution/licensing (Apache-2.0 source, MIT distribution) is clearly documented with author and provenance. The only observations are hygiene-level: an over-broad activation/description scope with 'always use me' framing, an unnecessary Bash grant in allowed-tools for a documentation-only skill, and a large number of broken internal file references. Overall risk: LOW — safe to use with minor cleanup.
llm_primary_threats: Capability inflation / over-broad skill activation scope (low impact)
Excessive declared tool permissions (Bash unused and unnecessary)
Documentation integrity: many broken internal file references

findings.title: Over-broad activation scope and priority-claiming language
findings.description: The skill description and instruction body claim applicability to essentially any document-producing task ("any scientific document", "any documentation", "any diagram", "Working with any other skill — this skill defines the documentation layer that wraps every other output", "Mermaid first, always"). This is capability-inflation / broad activation language that could cause the skill to be loaded and to override the user's or other skills' formatting preferences more often than necessary. The behavior itself is benign (documentation style guidance only), so impact is minimal — informational finding.
findings.snippet:
description: "Use when creating any scientific document, report, analysis, or visualization. Establishes text-based diagrams as the default documentation standard..."
- Working with **any other skill** — this skill defines the documentation layer that wraps every other output
- Someone asks you to "add a diagram" or "visualize the relationship" — Mermaid first, always
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to the specific triggering conditions (e.g., "when the user requests markdown documentation or Mermaid diagrams") and soften mandatory language like "always", "mandatory", and "wraps every other output" so it does not preempt user or sibling-skill preferences.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The market-research-reports skill appears benign and unusually well-hardened. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; instead it enforces evidence discipline, privacy minimization, and explicit prohibitions on deceptive collection, PII disclosure, paywall/authentication circumvention, brand impersonation, and investment/legal advice. All six bundled Python CLIs plus a shared helper module are standard-library only, purely local, and deterministic: they validate CSV/JSON ledgers, compute TAM/SAM/SOM and forecast scenarios, and generate a Markdown report scaffold. Security controls are explicitly implemented — bounded file size (5 MB) and row/cell limits, symlink-input rejection, suffix allow-lists, no-implicit-overwrite output handling with atomic temp-file replacement, relative-path-only archive fields rejecting `..` traversal, rejection of URLs containing embedded credentials, and numeric bounds preventing runaway computation. There is no network access, no subprocess/shell execution, no eval/exec/pickle/dynamic import, no credential or environment-variable harvesting, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, and no dependency installation (no pip/npm, so no supply-chain surface). Referenced files are all internal to the package (some under alternate `templates/`/`references/` paths are simply absent, a documentation/packaging hygiene issue rather than a security threat), and their contents are consistent with the stated purpose. Documentation-only external URLs point to legitimate official sources (SEC, Census, BLS, BEA, FRED, World Bank, IMF, OECD, Eurostat, AAPOR, ICO) and are not auto-fetched by any script. The manifest description matches actual behavior; `allowed-tools` is unspecified (optional per spec) and the skill's actual footprint — local file read/write plus Python execution — is disclosed in the compatibility field. The pre-scan environment-variable-exfiltration and cross-file-chain signals are false positives traceable to `os.sys.stderr`/`os.replace` usage and URL-string validation. No remediation is required beyond optional cosmetic changes and restoring the missing referenced asset paths.

findings.title: Static analyzer flagged env-var/network pattern is a false positive
findings.description: Pre-scan heuristics reported 'environment variable access with network calls' and a cross-file exfiltration chain. Manual review of all bundled scripts shows only `os.sys.stderr` usage in `_common.py::error_exit` and `os.replace` for atomic file writes; there are no imports of urllib/requests/socket/subprocess, no os.environ reads, no eval/exec/pickle, and no outbound network calls anywhere in the package. The 'network' signal appears to derive from documentation strings and HTTP(S) URLs used only for URL-format validation in the source ledger validator (`urlsplit` parsing, no fetching). No exfiltration capability exists.
findings.snippet:
print(f"ERROR: {exc}", file=os.sys.stderr)  # only os usage besides os.replace
parsed = urlsplit(text)  # URL is validated, never requested
findings.remediation: No action required. Optionally import `sys` directly instead of `os.sys` to reduce false-positive matches in automated scanners.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The "markitdown" skill is a well-structured, security-conscious documentation and tooling package for Microsoft MarkItDown 0.1.6. No malicious behavior was identified.

Manifest: name/description accurately reflect functionality (document-to-Markdown conversion). `allowed-tools` is not specified, which is optional per spec and only informational here; the skill's actual behavior (Python/Bash for local conversion) matches the stated scope. Compatibility notes honestly disclose that URL, YouTube, audio transcription, LLM, Azure, and MCP paths may use network/external services.

Instructions (SKILL.md): No prompt injection, jailbreak, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language. On the contrary, the skill explicitly instructs the agent to treat converted document text as untrusted data and to never execute instructions found inside converted content — a defensive, anti-injection posture. It also requires user approval before transmitting private/regulated data to external services, keeps plugins opt-in, and recommends the narrowest conversion API.

Scripts: 
- `scripts/inspect_installation.py` only reads installed package metadata via importlib.metadata and `shutil.which`; no network, no subprocess execution, no credential access. Plugin entry points are enumerated but explicitly not loaded.
- `scripts/batch_convert.py` and `scripts/convert_literature.py` operate on user-specified input directories only, use `convert_local()`, resolve paths and verify they remain under the input root (path-traversal check), skip symlinks, enforce a maximum byte size, write atomically via NamedTemporaryFile in the destination directory, keep plugins disabled unless an explicit `--plugins` flag is passed (with a stderr warning), and gate audio formats that could trigger external Google Web Speech transcription behind `--allow-external-services`. No eval/exec, no os.system/subprocess with variables, no network calls, no environment harvesting, no hardcoded secrets.

Supply chain: All installation commands use exact pinned versions (markitdown==0.1.6, markitdown-ocr==0.1.0, markitdown-mcp==0.0.1a4, openai==2.41.1) and reference official Microsoft repositories/PyPI. Reference docs include an explicit typosquatting/plugin trust checklist.

Data flow: No read→exfiltrate chains. Outputs are written to a user-specified local directory. The manifest/catalog records only paths, hashes, versions, and status — no document contents or secrets. Guidance explicitly forbids logging API keys, document contents, or base64 payloads and forbids combining credentials with user-controlled endpoints.

Referenced files: Present reference docs (`references/*.md`) are internal to the package and contain accurate, security-hardening guidance (SSRF controls, archive-bomb limits, MCP binding restrictions, prompt-injection handling). Several enumerated paths (`assets/*.md`, `templates/*.md`, `markitdown.py`) are not found, but these appear to be scanner-generated path permutations of the same `references/` filenames rather than genuine broken references in SKILL.md; SKILL.md itself only references the `references/` files, all of which resolve. No external URL is fetched and treated as instructions — external links are only cited as authoritative documentation sources.

Conclusion: No security findings. This skill demonstrates above-average defensive design and can be considered safe.

The matchms skill is a legitimate, well-scoped scientific computing skill for tandem mass-spectra processing. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; its instructions are technical guidance for matchms 0.33.1 API usage. Reference docs also repeatedly warn against untrusted pickle deserialization and against overstating identification confidence. No data exfiltration, credential access, obfuscation, hardcoded secrets, capability inflation, or tool-poisoning patterns were found. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The molecular-dynamics skill is a documentation-only reference for running OpenMM simulations and analyzing trajectories with MDAnalysis. No executable script files ship with the package. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language, and the description accurately matches the content. All code examples are standard, well-known scientific computing patterns: PDB loading, force-field setup, energy minimization, NVT/NPT integration, DCD/checkpoint reporters, RMSD/RMSF/contact analysis, PDBFixer cleanup, and OpenFF ligand parameterization. File operations are limited to writing local simulation outputs (minimized.pdb, *_traj.dcd, *_log.txt, rmsd.png) in the working directory; there is no home-directory traversal or over-collection. All URLs are documentation links to legitimate project sites (openmm.org, mdanalysis.org, charmm-gui.org, ambermd.org) and no code fetches or executes remote content. The pre-scan's BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION and cross-file exfiltration-chain signals are not corroborated by any content in the provided material: there are no network calls (no requests/urllib/curl/socket), no os.environ or credential-file access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, tokens), no hardcoded secrets, and no eval/exec/os.system or subprocess usage. The only environment-related code is `Platform.getPlatformByName('CUDA')` with a `DeviceIndex` property, a benign GPU platform selection pattern that heuristics commonly misclassify as environment harvesting. These pre-scan findings are assessed as false positives. Residual risks are minor and inherent to the domain: unpinned dependency install commands, and computationally expensive long-running GPU/CPU simulations launched without an explicit confirmation guardrail. Overall the skill appears benign and appropriate for its stated structural-biology and biophysics purpose.

No prompt injection, jailbreak, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language appears anywhere in SKILL.md or the reference documents (checked language-agnostically).
