There is no network activity (no requests/urllib/socket), no subprocess or shell invocation, no eval/exec/compile, no os.system, no environment-variable harvesting, no access to ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or other credential stores, and no hardcoded secrets. Reports deliberately redact filesystem paths (path_redacted: true) and emit only aggregate statistics rather than row values, and real-data commands require an explicit --deidentified acknowledgement. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob) are consistent with actual behavior: local CSV/JSON reads and bounded local CSV/JSON writes invoked via Bash. Dependency handling is a strength rather than a risk: NeuroKit2 is pinned to ==0.2.13, the pinned version is verified at runtime, and the skill explicitly declines to install the upstream floating 'full' extra in an automated workflow, recommending a reviewed uv.lock instead. The only observations are informational: a security note asserting eval/exec scanner hits are false positives (accurate for this code), and several referenced markdown files that are not shipped. The description accurately matches behavior and contains no keyword baiting or over-broad capability claims. Overall risk: very low.

findings.title: SKILL.md pre-emptively instructs the agent to treat eval/exec scanner hits as false positives
findings.description: The 'Security note' section in SKILL.md tells the agent that no helper uses eval()/exec() and that static-scanner eval/exec findings should be recorded as false positives. In this package the claim is factually accurate (no dynamic execution is present in any of the reviewed scripts), so it is documentation rather than an active evasion attempt. It is nonetheless a pattern that could bias automated review if the bundled scripts were later modified, and is noted for awareness only.
findings.snippet: "No example or helper uses Python `eval()` or `exec()`. ... record it as a scanner false positive only after confirming no dynamic execution exists."
findings.remediation: No action strictly required. If retained, keep the guidance conditional (as written, requiring confirmation) and re-verify scripts on every version bump so the statement cannot become stale cover for future dynamic-execution code.

findings.title: Instructions reference numerous documentation files that do not exist in the package
findings.description: SKILL.md lists 12 reference documents, and the referenced-file scan additionally probed templates/ and assets/ paths. Several referenced markdown files are absent from the package (e.g., references/eeg.md-adjacent templates/*, assets/*, and reference entries not shipped). Missing files cause the agent to fail reads or potentially search outside the skill directory for substitutes. No malicious content was found in the files that do exist; all present references are internal, benign, technical documentation.
findings.snippet: Referenced files reported as not found include templates/hrv.md, assets/eog.md, templates/bio_module.md, assets/eeg.md, assets/signal_processing.md, and others.
findings.remediation: Ship every referenced markdown file or remove references to files not bundled, and instruct the agent to only read paths under the skill's own references/ directory.

metadata.aisubtech_name: Safety Harms and Toxicity: Scams and Deception

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate, well-documented scientific computing skill for Neuropixels electrophysiology analysis built on the real SpikeInterface API. The name, description, instructions, and bundled scripts are fully consistent: every script performs domain-appropriate operations (loading SpikeGLX/OpenEphys/NWB recordings, filtering, drift/motion correction, spike sorting, quality metrics, curation, and export to Phy/NWB/CSV). No prompt injection, jailbreak language, role redefinition, or concealment directives were found in SKILL.md or any reference file. Scripts contain no eval/exec/os.system calls, no subprocess shell invocations, no network exfiltration, no credential or environment harvesting, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, and no hidden file traversal — all paths are explicit CLI arguments and all writes go to user-specified output directories. Notably, the skill demonstrates good security hygiene: it repeatedly and explicitly instructs users to read API keys from environment variables and never hardcode credentials, and it warns that `.skops` ML models loaded with `trust_model=True` must come from trusted sources. Optional ANTHROPIC_API_KEY usage is declared in metadata and is read via os.environ only in illustrative documentation examples, with the key used solely for the user's own vision-model calls (no third-party endpoints). Several referenced files under templates/ and assets/ are missing, which is a documentation hygiene issue rather than a security threat. Only two low-severity, informational findings were identified: unpinned dependency install commands (typical of scientific documentation) and absent optional allowed-tools/compatibility metadata. Overall risk: LOW / benign.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools and compatibility declarations
findings.description: The YAML frontmatter does not declare `allowed-tools` or `compatibility`, although the skill ships Python scripts intended to be executed via Bash/Python and writes files to disk (output folders, CSV/JSON/PNG artifacts). This is informational only: `allowed-tools` is optional in the spec and no restriction is violated because none is declared. All file writes are to user-specified output directories consistent with the documented purpose.
findings.snippet:
- allowed-tools: Not specified
- compatibility: Not specified
findings.remediation: Optionally declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash, Python]` and `compatibility` so users can see that the skill executes code and writes analysis output files.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions including remote model downloads
findings.description: The SKILL.md Installation section instructs installing multiple packages (spikeinterface[full], kilosort, spykingcircus, mountainsort5, huggingface_hub, skops, anthropic, ibl-neuropixel, ibllib, bombcell) without version pins in the primary commands (pins are only suggested as a footnote). Reference docs additionally recommend `git clone` + `pip install -e .` from GitHub repos and downloading `.skops` ML models from Hugging Face with `trust_model=True`, which deserializes remote artifacts. These are legitimate, widely-used scientific tools and the docs explicitly warn to only load models from trusted sources, so the risk is minor/informational rather than malicious.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "spikeinterface[full]" probeinterface neo
uv pip install kilosort
...
sc.model_based_label_units(repo_id="SpikeInterface/UnitRefine_noise_neural_classifier", trust_model=True)
findings.remediation: Pin exact versions in the primary install commands, prefer PyPI over direct git installs, and keep the existing guidance that `.skops`/pickle models must be treated as executable artifacts loaded only from verified sources.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a documentation-only Agent Skill for Nextflow/nf-core. It contains SKILL.md plus six bundled reference markdown files; no executable Python or Bash scripts are included in the package for review, and all file reads are internal to the skill directory. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directives, role redefinition, obfuscation, hardcoded secrets, credential-harvesting code, or data-exfiltration code was found. The static pre-scan signals (env var access + network calls, cross-file exfiltration chain) are explained by legitimate documentation content: Nextflow environment variables (NXF_*, TOWER_ACCESS_TOKEN) and first-party observability/cloud features (-with-tower, -with-weblog, S3/GCS workDir, Wave/Fusion) described in prose and config snippets — not by any active code path that reads secrets and sends them to a third party. Residual concerns are minor and typical of upstream-documented tooling: curl-pipe-to-bash installers with a sudo move, unpinned pip/conda installs, and a somewhat broad activation clause telling the agent to engage even when the user does not mention Nextflow. Overall the skill appears benign and consistent with its stated purpose; recommended hardening is limited to pinning installs, avoiding pipe-to-shell, and narrowing the activation description.
llm_primary_threats: Broad/over-eager skill activation scope (capability inflation, low severity)
Supply-chain risk from unpinned installs and curl-pipe-to-bash setup commands
Documented (not executed) credential env vars and external telemetry endpoints

findings.title: Documented credential environment variables and telemetry endpoints (legitimate, low risk)
findings.description: Reference files document TOWER_ACCESS_TOKEN / secrets.TOWER_ACCESS_TOKEN for Seqera Platform and options that transmit run data off-host (`-with-tower`, `-with-weblog <url>`, cloud workDir on S3/GCS/Azure). Static pre-scan flags of "env var exfiltration" and "cross-file exfiltration chain" correspond to these documented, first-party Nextflow features described in prose/config examples rather than to any executable code. No script in the package reads credentials or performs network transmission; the skill contains no Python/Bash payloads despite the pre-scan file inventory listing python files (none were provided or referenced). No hardcoded secrets were found.
findings.snippet:
tower.accessToken = secrets.TOWER_ACCESS_TOKEN   # some Wave features use Seqera creds
| `TOWER_ACCESS_TOKEN` | Seqera Platform token (with `-with-tower`) |
| `-with-weblog <url>` | POST run events to an HTTP endpoint |
findings.remediation: No action strictly required; optionally note that `-with-tower`/`-with-weblog` transmit run metadata to external endpoints and should only be enabled with user consent and secrets supplied via a secret manager rather than plain environment variables.

findings.title: Broad activation language in description encourages use beyond explicit user intent
findings.description: The skill description instructs the agent to activate "for any reproducible scientific/bioinformatics workflow work even if the user does not say the word 'Nextflow'". This is mild activation-broadening/keyword-dense phrasing typical of legitimate domain skills, but it does widen activation scope beyond explicit user requests. No deceptive naming or hidden capability was found; the instructions and reference files are consistent with a Nextflow/nf-core documentation skill.
findings.snippet: Make sure to use this skill for any reproducible scientific/bioinformatics workflow work even if the user does not say the word "Nextflow"
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to concrete triggers (Nextflow, nf-core, .nf files, DSL2) and remove the directive to activate when the user has not indicated the domain.

findings.title: Unpinned installation commands piping remote scripts to shell
findings.description: Setup instructions include `curl -s https://get.nextflow.io | bash`, `curl -fsSL https://get.nf-test.com | bash`, `sudo mv nextflow /usr/local/bin/`, and unpinned `pip install nf-core` / `conda install nf-core`. These are the officially documented installation methods for Nextflow/nf-test, so risk is low and expected, but curl-to-bash execution plus a sudo move grants remote code execution and privileged file placement if the upstream endpoint or DNS is compromised, and unpinned package installs provide no supply-chain provenance guarantees.
findings.snippet:
curl -s https://get.nextflow.io | bash      # creates ./nextflow
sudo mv nextflow /usr/local/bin/
pip install nf-core
curl -fsSL https://get.nf-test.com | bash
findings.remediation: Prefer versioned/pinned installs (e.g. `pip install nf-core==<version>`, conda with pinned version), download-then-verify-checksum instead of piping to bash, and avoid `sudo` by installing to a user-local bin directory.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The omero-integration skill is a well-engineered, security-conscious package for interacting with OMERO microscopy servers. No malicious behavior, prompt injection, data exfiltration, or obfuscation was found.

Manifest/description consistency: The declared purpose (scoped OMERO inventory, metadata export, transfer planning) matches the bundled code exactly. No keyword baiting, brand impersonation, or over-broad capability claims.

SKILL.md instructions: The markdown body contains no instruction overrides, jailbreak language, concealment directives ("do not tell the user"), role redefinition, or system-prompt extraction. On the contrary, it defines a restrictive operating contract requiring dry runs, explicit user-selected scope, secure transport defaults, and mandatory resource cleanup. Instructions to "not print names" are data-minimization controls, not concealment from the user.

Script review:
- omero_common.py: Reads only an explicit allowlist of six OMERO_* environment variables (no os.environ dumps, no .env crawling, no ~/.aws or ~/.ssh access). Credentials are held in a frozen dataclass that is never serialized; config_summary() emits only host/port/boolean presence flags with "credential_values_included": false. scrubbed_error() deliberately suppresses exception text to avoid credential leakage. atomic_write_json() enforces .json suffix, refuses symlinks, requires an existing parent directory, refuses overwrite without an explicit flag, and sets mode 0600 via mkstemp + fchmod + os.replace — a strong safe-write implementation. json_safe() bounds recursion depth, string length, and collection length, and omits raw bytes.
- inventory.py / export_image_metadata.py: Read-only, dry-run by default, require an explicit --execute flag, use an allowlisted object-type set (no user-controlled type strings), enforce numeric bounds on every limit, refuse cross-group (-1) scope, and redact names/values/owner names/file names/ROI labels by default. Connections are opened via a contextmanager that always closes in finally.
- plan_transfer.py: Purely local; never imports omero. Uses strict regex full-match validation on target and image selectors, builds command arrays (list form, no shell string interpolation), never emits -w/--password/-k credential flags, and never executes the proposed commands.
- validate_config.py: Local validation only; optional DNS resolution is bounded to 10 unique addresses and does not open an OMERO connection.

No eval/exec/os.system/subprocess with shell=True, no network POSTs to third-party endpoints, no hardcoded secrets, no base64/hex-obfuscated payloads, no unbounded loops (all paging loops have monotonic progress and hard caps), and no infinite retry patterns.

Filesystem scope: os.walk in plan_transfer.py operates only on user-supplied explicit paths with followlinks=False, symlink skipping, a depth cap (1..20) and a file-count cap — no home-directory or repository-wide traversal.

Referenced files: All resolved reference documents (connection, data_access, metadata, image_processing, rois, tables, scripts, advanced, sources) are internal to the package and contain defensive guidance (avoid HQL/table-condition interpolation, avoid eval/exec, never derive local paths from untrusted remote filenames, treat deletion/ownership changes as separately approved writes). Numerous listed assets/*.md and templates/*.md paths were "not found", but these appear to be scanner path-permutation artifacts rather than genuine references from SKILL.md, which links only to references/*.md. No external URL is fetched or executed; documentation URLs are citations only.

Overall risk: LOW. The two findings are informational hardening suggestions.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration in manifest
findings.description: The skill manifest does not declare an `allowed-tools` field, although the skill instructs the agent to run Python scripts, execute bash commands (uv venv, omero CLI, pip install), and write JSON output files. This field is optional per the spec, so the finding is informational only; no evidence of capability inflation or behavior beyond the stated microscopy-data purpose was found.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Optionally declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash, Python]` to make the required capability surface explicit and auditable.

findings.title: Instructions direct installation of a locally supplied wheel file
findings.description: The setup instructions tell the operator to install a ZeroC IcePy 3.6.5 wheel from an arbitrary absolute local path obtained from an externally linked vendor (Glencoe) binary matrix. The omero-py dependency itself is pinned (omero-py==5.22.1), which is good practice, but the Ice wheel has no hash/provenance verification, so a substituted or tampered wheel would be silently installed. This is a normal, documented OMERO installation path and is mitigated by the explicit version pin and the instruction to use a 'reviewed matching wheel', so severity is low.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "/absolute/path/to/zeroc_ice-3.6.5-<matching-tags>.whl"
uv pip install "omero-py==5.22.1"
findings.remediation: Recommend verifying the wheel checksum/signature against the official OME-linked release artifact before installation, and document the expected hash for the pinned 3.6.5 wheel.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `onekgpd` skill is a well-documented, coherent genomics query wrapper and appears benign. Manifest, instructions, and code are consistent: the description and compatibility notes accurately state that variant/sample/kinship queries require outbound TLS to a single fixed endpoint (`db.dnaerys.org:443`) while metadata commands run fully offline against a bundled asset (`assets/kgpe.json`), and the code matches exactly that. No prompt injection, jailbreak, role redefinition, concealment directive, or instruction-override text was found in the SKILL.md body or in the reference markdown files (checked language-agnostically). No `eval`/`exec`/`os.system`/`subprocess` usage, no shell interpolation, no dynamic code loading, no base64/hex-encoded payloads, and no obfuscation. All inputs are parsed via `argparse` with typed/validated fields; user values are passed as structured keyword arguments to a typed client library rather than concatenated into commands or queries. There is no access to credentials, SSH/AWS directories, environment variables, browser data, or home-directory traversal, and no reading of external URLs or user-provided files. Data flow is one-directional and purpose-bound: query parameters out, dataset results in, results written to a local JSON file. Retries are bounded (3 attempts, exponential backoff), and default result caps exist. Declared `allowed-tools: Write, Bash` is consistent with observed behaviour (writing JSON output, invoking `uv run`). The findings below are all LOW-severity hygiene and robustness items: a range-pinned rather than exactly-pinned PyPI dependency provisioned at runtime by `uv`, disclosed outbound transmission of query parameters to a vendor endpoint, unbounded in-memory accumulation in the `--page-size` pagination path, and an unvalidated `--output` path that can overwrite existing files. Several documentation files referenced under `templates/` and `assets/` are absent, but each has an existing counterpart under `references/`, so this is a cosmetic path-listing artifact, not a security issue. Recommendation: approve for use.

findings.title: Arbitrary output path written without validation
findings.description: Both scripts accept an unvalidated `--output PATH` and write JSON to it with `open(path, "w")`, silently overwriting any existing file. Because the skill is invoked by an agent via Bash, a mistaken or injected path (e.g. a dotfile or config file) could clobber user data. The declared `allowed-tools: Write, Bash` does cover file writing, so this is consistent with the manifest and is a low-severity hygiene issue rather than a restriction violation.
findings.snippet:
if output_path:
    path = output_path
    with open(path, "w") as fh:
        json.dump(data, fh, indent=2)
findings.remediation: Validate that `--output` resolves inside an expected directory (e.g. the temp dir or CWD), refuse to overwrite existing files without an explicit `--force` flag, and reject paths containing traversal sequences.

findings.title: Unbounded result collection when --page-size is used
findings.description: In `_run_select_variants`, the `--page-size` branch walks every page of the result set and accumulates all variants in memory (`collected.extend(page.variants)`) with no overall cap, unlike the `--limit` branch which is bounded to 200 by default. A broad region (e.g. an entire chromosome) combined with `--page-size` could produce very large memory and disk usage. The SKILL.md mitigates this behaviourally by mandating a `count-*` call before any `select-*` call, and the retry logic is bounded (MAX_RETRIES=3 with exponential backoff), so this is a robustness concern rather than a deliberate DoS pattern.
findings.snippet:
collected = []
for page in pq:
    collected.extend(page.variants)
return collected, pq.metadata, False
findings.remediation: Add a hard maximum on total variants collected in the pagination path (or stream results incrementally to the output file) and warn the user when the cap is reached.

findings.title: Third-party dependency provisioned at runtime via uv inline metadata (range-pinned)
findings.description: scripts/onekgpd_api.py declares an inline PEP 723 dependency `dnaerys>=0.2.1,<0.3.0`, which `uv run` resolves and installs from PyPI at execution time. The version is range-pinned rather than exactly pinned, so any 0.2.x release (including a future compromised or hijacked release) will be pulled automatically without user review. This is a normal and low-risk pattern for scientific tooling, but represents a minor supply-chain exposure since the code executed is not fully determined by the skill package.
findings.snippet:
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.11"
# dependencies = ["dnaerys>=0.2.1,<0.3.0"]
# ///
findings.remediation: Pin the dependency to an exact version (e.g. `dnaerys==0.2.1`) and, if feasible, add a hash/lock file so the provisioned environment is reproducible and auditable.

findings.title: Outbound network transmission of user-supplied query parameters to a fixed third-party endpoint
findings.description: All variant/sample/kinship commands open a TLS connection to the hardcoded endpoint `db.dnaerys.org:443` and transmit the query parameters (genomic regions, sample IDs, filter criteria) supplied by the user. This is the skill's declared and documented purpose (the compatibility field explicitly discloses outbound network access, and no credentials, environment variables, or local files are read or sent). The residual consideration is only that query content — which in a research context could reflect a user's genomic region of interest — leaves the local machine to a single-vendor service. No credential harvesting, file reading, or exfiltration of unrelated local data occurs.
findings.snippet: DEFAULT_ENDPOINT = "db.dnaerys.org:443"   # public 1000 Genomes instance (fixed)
findings.remediation: No action strictly required; behaviour matches the manifest. Optionally document that query parameters are sent to a third-party service operated by the skill author, and consider allowing the endpoint to be overridden or self-hosted for privacy-sensitive deployments.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
This skill is a well-engineered, legitimate bioinformatics utility for resolving free-text scientific labels to ontology term IDs and validating CURIEs against the public EBI Ontology Lookup Service (OLS4). A full review of all three Python scripts and the reference documentation found no evidence of malicious behavior.

Key verification points:

1. Network activity is narrowly scoped and benign. All HTTP traffic goes through a single hardcoded constant, OLS_BASE = "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ols4/api", a public, well-known EMBL-EBI service that requires no API key. Requests are GET-only via urllib.request; there are no POST/PUT calls and therefore no outbound data transmission channel. The only data sent is the user-supplied query string or CURIE in the URL query parameters, which is inherent to the skill's stated purpose. The ancestor_curies() function follows a HATEOAS href returned by OLS itself, which stays within the same trusted API domain. This matches the compatibility declaration exactly.

2. No credential or secret access. No reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.netrc, browser stores, or keychains. No os.environ harvesting. No hardcoded API keys, tokens, or secrets anywhere in the package.

3. No command or code execution. There is no eval(), exec(), compile(), os.system(), subprocess, pickle, __import__, or shell invocation in any of the three scripts. The pre-scan flag "MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC" is a false positive: the only Python snippet in the markdown (references/curation-rules.md) is a three-line illustrative example that imports term_detail from the skill's own local module and reads a dictionary key. No dynamic evaluation occurs. Note that all 13 files were classified as markdown by the inventory, so the flag most plausibly derives from a substring heuristic (e.g. matching "exec" inside a word or matching the documented code fence) rather than real dynamic-execution behavior.

4. File I/O is proportionate and user-directed. Reads are limited to explicit --input paths (or stdin) supplied by the user on the command line; writes are limited to an explicit -o/--output path. There is no os.walk, no glob, no directory traversal, no home-directory enumeration, and no over-collection of files beyond what the user names.

5. Input handling is safe. CURIEs are validated against a strict anchored regex (CURIE_RE = ^([A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.]*):([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+)$) before use, and all URL parameters are properly encoded with urllib.parse.urlencode, preventing parameter injection. IRI templates are used only as read-only lookup fallbacks whose worst-case failure is an empty result set.

6. sys.path manipulation is benign. Both CLIs insert Path(__file__).resolve().parent - the script's own directory - to import the bundled sibling module ols_client.py. This is a standard self-contained-package pattern, not a path-hijacking vector, since it resolves to the skill's own directory rather than an attacker-controllable or relative location.

7. No prompt injection or instruction manipulation. The SKILL.md body and all reference documents contain only domain guidance on ontology curation. There is no instruction override, no role redefinition, no concealment directive ("do not tell the user"), no safety-bypass language, and no attempt to extract the system prompt - in English or any other language. Notably, the guidance pushes in the safety-positive direction: it repeatedly instructs the agent never to emit an ontology ID from memory, to surface "unresolved" as a legitimate output rather than guessing, and to escalate ambiguous partial matches to a human for decision. This reduces hallucination risk rather than creating it.

8. No autonomy or trust-delegation red flags. There is no unbounded retry loop (MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3 with bounded linear backoff and a 30-second timeout), no cross-session memory bridging, and no read-then-send tool chaining. The ancestor pagination loop is bounded by the API's finite _links.next chain. External content fetched from OLS is parsed strictly as structured JSON data fields and is never interpreted as instructions.

9. Supply chain is clean. dependencies = [] with a pinned requires-python = ">=3.11"; standard library only. No pip/npm installs, no GitHub clones, no typosquatting risk, no unpinned third-party packages. Provenance is declared (version 1.0, skill-author K-Dense Inc., MIT license).

10. Manifest consistency holds. allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash is consistent with observed behavior - reading input files, writing output files, and running python3 scripts. Network access is explicitly and accurately disclosed in the compatibility field rather than hidden.

Minor housekeeping observation (not a security issue): the referenced-files list includes templates/* and assets/* variants of the three reference documents that do not exist. The canonical references/ols4-api.md, references/ontology-registry.md, and references/curation-rules.md are all present and are the only paths actually cited in SKILL.md, so these appear to be scanner path-permutation artifacts rather than missing dependencies or attempts to load external content.

Conclusion: no CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM findings. The single LOW finding concerns keyword density in the description, which is a discoverability nuance rather than a genuine threat. This skill is assessed as safe to use.

findings.title: Keyword-heavy description broadens activation surface
findings.description: The skill description enumerates an extensive list of trigger keywords ("ontology term", "CURIE", "UBERON", "CL:", "MONDO", "HPO", "EFO", "ChEBI", "NCBITaxon", "GO term", "PATO", etc.). While these are all legitimately within the skill's stated scope of ontology term resolution/validation, the density of trigger terms slightly increases the likelihood of unwanted activation. No capability inflation beyond the actual implemented functionality was observed - the scripts do exactly what the description claims.
findings.snippet: Triggers include "ontology term", "ontology ID", "CURIE", "controlled vocabulary", "UBERON", "CL:", "MONDO", "HPO", "EFO", "ChEBI", "NCBITaxon", "GO term", "PATO", "annotate this tissue/cell type/disease"
findings.remediation: Optionally trim the trigger keyword list to the most representative examples. No functional change required; behavior matches declared purpose.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The open-notebook skill is a legitimate, well-documented integration wrapper for the open-source Open Notebook self-hosted research platform (github.com/lfnovo/open-notebook). All three Python scripts are straightforward REST client examples that talk exclusively to a user-configured, locally-defaulted endpoint (http://localhost:5055/api). No prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directives, obfuscation, eval/exec, shell command construction, credential-file access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), environment harvesting, or exfiltration to external/attacker-controlled domains was found. The static analyzer's 'env var exfiltration' and 'cross-file exfiltration chain' alerts are false positives: the only environment variable read is OPEN_NOTEBOOK_URL, which supplies the base URL of the user's own server, and the data sent is user-authored research content, not secrets or scraped local files. Behavior matches the manifest description; referenced api_reference.md is an internal, benign API doc (two alternate paths, assets/ and templates/, are simply absent). Residual issues are minor hygiene items: unvalidated base-URL configuration over plain HTTP, plaintext API-key examples, unpinned pip dependency and unverified remote docker-compose fetch, missing optional allowed-tools metadata, unconfirmed destructive DELETE calls in demo blocks, and the inherent indirect-prompt-injection surface of ingesting arbitrary web content. Overall risk: LOW — safe to use with standard configuration hygiene.
llm_primary_threats: False-positive env-var/network heuristic (configuration-only URL, no secret transmission)
Configuration-dependent endpoint redirection over plain HTTP
Plaintext API key handling in documentation examples
Unpinned dependency and unverified remote docker-compose download
Indirect prompt injection surface from ingesting arbitrary external URLs/documents
Unconfirmed destructive delete operations in demo scripts

findings.title: Unpinned dependency and remote docker-compose fetch in setup instructions
findings.description: Setup guidance instructs `pip install requests` without a version pin and downloads docker-compose.yml directly from a GitHub raw URL before running `docker-compose up -d`, executing remote-defined container configuration without integrity verification. The repository referenced is the legitimate upstream project (lfnovo/open-notebook), so risk is low, but supply-chain integrity is unverified.
findings.snippet:
curl -o docker-compose.yml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lfnovo/open-notebook/main/docker-compose.yml
docker-compose up -d
findings.remediation: Pin dependency versions (e.g., requests==2.32.x), reference a tagged release rather than main branch, and advise reviewing the downloaded compose file before launching.

findings.title: Environment variable read combined with HTTP requests (benign localhost configuration pattern)
findings.description: Static analyzers flagged an 'env var exfiltration' chain because the scripts read OPEN_NOTEBOOK_URL via os.getenv() and then issue requests.post/get calls. In context this is a standard configuration pattern: the env var only supplies the base URL of the user's own self-hosted Open Notebook server (defaulting to http://localhost:5055), and no credentials, secrets, or local file contents are transmitted to third-party endpoints. The only residual risk is that a maliciously-set OPEN_NOTEBOOK_URL could redirect API traffic (including any notebook content submitted) to an attacker-controlled host, and requests are made over plain HTTP without validation.
findings.snippet: BASE_URL = os.getenv("OPEN_NOTEBOOK_URL", "http://localhost:5055") + "/api"
findings.remediation: Optionally validate/allow-list the configured OPEN_NOTEBOOK_URL scheme and host (e.g., warn if it is not localhost or an HTTPS endpoint) before sending research content to it. No other change needed.

findings.title: Ingestion of arbitrary external URLs feeds untrusted content into AI context
findings.description: The skill ingests arbitrary web URLs, PDFs, and documents into notebooks and then includes that content as context for chat/transformation calls (include_sources: true). Retrieved third-party content is inherently untrusted and could contain embedded instructions that influence downstream AI output (indirect prompt injection). This is inherent to the documented purpose of a NotebookLM-style tool rather than a hidden capability, and no instruction in the skill tells the agent to obey content found in sources.
findings.snippet: add_url_source(notebook_id, "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRISPR_gene_editing") ... "context": {"include_sources": True}
findings.remediation: Document that ingested source content is untrusted data and should not be treated as instructions; consider sanitizing or delimiting retrieved content before passing it to models.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
This is a legitimate, well-documented scientific computing skill for Particle Image Velocimetry analysis using the OpenPIV library. All three Python scripts (runner.py, run_example.py, analyze.py) perform exactly what the manifest and instructions describe: reading local image pairs, cross-correlation, vector validation/replacement, scaling, saving vectors.txt/params.npz/PNG outputs, and computing vorticity, strain, and spatial statistics with numpy.

No prompt injection, jailbreak, role-redefinition, or concealment language appears anywhere in SKILL.md or the reference markdown. No network calls (no requests/urllib/curl/sockets), no credential or environment-variable access, no reads of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, or other sensitive paths, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec usage, no base64/hex obfuscation, and no hardcoded secrets. File writes are confined to a user-specified --output_dir, consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). Data access is proportionate: only the two user-supplied image files and the analyzer's own params.npz — no directory walking or over-collection.

The pre-scan hint "MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC: Python code block uses eval/exec" appears to be a false positive: no `eval(`, `exec(`, `compile(`, `pickle.loads`, or `__import__` calls exist in any code block or script. The likely trigger is benign substring matching (e.g., `np.savez`/`extended_search_area` or the word "executable"-like tokens); `np.load` is used only on a params.npz the skill itself wrote, and without `allow_pickle=True`, so no deserialization code-execution path exists.

Only minor hygiene issues were found: an unpinned install command (with a pinned alternative offered) and documentation references that resolve to non-existent paths. Overall risk: very low; the skill appears safe to use.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency install instruction (uv pip install openpiv)
findings.description: The SKILL.md Quick Start instructs installing the `openpiv` package without a version pin (`uv pip install openpiv`), though it does immediately offer a pinned alternative (`openpiv==0.25.4`) for reproducibility. This is a minor supply-chain hygiene concern only; the package is the legitimate, well-known OpenPIV library and no third-party/GitHub/unknown sources are used.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install openpiv

# Pin it when the analysis needs to be reproducible...
uv pip install "openpiv==0.25.4"
findings.remediation: Prefer the pinned form (`uv pip install "openpiv==0.25.4"`) as the primary instruction to ensure reproducible, verified dependency resolution.

findings.title: Documentation references files that are not present in the package
findings.description: The instruction body's file references resolve to several paths that do not exist in the package (assets/advanced_algorithms.md, templates/advanced_algorithms.md, openpiv.py, matplotlib.py, analyze.py as a bare path). These appear to be artifacts of static reference extraction (module import names and the real path is references/advanced_algorithms.md / scripts/analyze.py, both of which exist). No external URLs or untrusted remote sources are fetched. Impact is limited to potential agent confusion / failed reads.
findings.snippet: Referenced Files: assets/advanced_algorithms.md (not found), templates/advanced_algorithms.md (not found), openpiv.py (not found), matplotlib.py (not found), analyze.py (not found); references/advanced_algorithms.md and scripts/analyze.py exist
findings.remediation: Use consistent, explicit relative paths (e.g., `scripts/analyze.py`, `references/advanced_algorithms.md`) in the documentation so every referenced resource resolves inside the package.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The opentrons-integration skill is a legitimate, documentation-heavy engineering skill for authoring Opentrons Python Protocol API v2 protocols. All five bundled Python scripts are pure Opentrons protocol templates: they import only `opentrons.protocol_api`, define metadata/requirements, and call load_labware/load_instrument/transfer/module APIs. There is no network I/O, no subprocess/eval/exec, no filesystem traversal, no environment-variable or credential access, no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscation or encoded payloads. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; instead it repeatedly emphasizes conservative safety practices (simulate, App analysis, operator review, dry run, emergency stop). The description accurately matches behavior and even directs users to a different skill (pylabrobot) for multi-vendor workflows, which is the opposite of capability inflation. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the workflow of writing protocol files and running `opentrons_simulate`/`py_compile` via Bash. Referenced reference docs are internal to the package and contain only technical guidance; notably they explicitly advise against top-level network calls, downloading packages during runs, embedding credentials, and using `-D` on directories containing credentials — security-positive guidance. Residual risks are minor: pinned-but-network-dependent `uv run --with`/`uv pip install` dependency fetching, and a few unresolved referenced file paths (assets/*, templates/*, opentrons.py). Note that the skill drives physical laboratory hardware, so operational (not cyber) safety depends on the user following the documented validation ladder, which the skill adequately stresses.
llm_primary_threats: Third-party dependency installation from PyPI during simulation (pinned versions, low risk)
Unresolved referenced documentation file paths

findings.title: Some referenced files are unresolved/missing

This is largely a path-resolution artifact of the scan (the references/ versions exist), but missing files could later be supplied by an untrusted source and silently loaded as guidance. No malicious content was found in the resolved files.
findings.snippet: **Referenced File: assets/liquid_handling.md** (not found); **Referenced File: opentrons.py** (not found)
findings.remediation: Ensure all referenced documentation files are bundled inside the skill package with consistent relative paths, and avoid referencing files that do not exist.

findings.title: Package installation via uv from PyPI during simulation workflow
findings.description: The skill instructs running `uv run --with "opentrons==9.1.1"` and `uv pip install -r requirements-flex.txt`, which downloads and executes third-party packages from PyPI at simulation time. Versions are pinned (good practice), but the workflow still triggers automatic dependency resolution/installation on the user's machine without explicit confirmation. Referenced requirements files (requirements-flex.txt / requirements-ot2.txt) were not included in the analyzed package, so their pin contents cannot be verified.
findings.snippet:
uv run --with "opentrons==9.1.1" opentrons_simulate protocol.py
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r skills/opentrons-integration/requirements-flex.txt
findings.remediation: Include the referenced requirements-*.txt files in the package with fully pinned versions and hashes, and note that dependency installation requires network access and user consent.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate, well-structured technical documentation skill for GPU-accelerating Python with the NVIDIA RAPIDS/CUDA ecosystem. Despite the manifest listing 5 "python" files, no executable scripts were provided — the package consists of SKILL.md plus reference markdown files. Manual review of all supplied instruction and reference content found NO prompt injection, no instruction-override or concealment language, no jailbreak attempts, no obfuscation/encoding, no hardcoded secrets, no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or other credential stores, no outbound network calls to attacker-controlled endpoints, and no read-then-send tool-chaining. All code examples are standard, accurate, publicly documented API usage (CuPy, cuDF, cuML, cuGraph, Warp, KvikIO, cuVS, cuCIM, cuSpatial, cuxfilter, RAFT, Numba CUDA), and the skill's own guidance advises safe practices such as CPU fallbacks and numerical-correctness validation. All referenced files resolve to internal paths within the skill package (the assets/ and templates/ "not found" entries are path-guessing artifacts of the scanner, not external fetches); no external URLs are read as instructions — the only URLs present are documentation links and NVIDIA's official package index. The static pre-scan alerts for "env var exfiltration" and "cross-file exfiltration chain" are false positives arising from KvikIO documentation that merely explains AWS credential environment variables alongside read-only S3/HTTP ingest examples; there is no data egress path anywhere in the package. Residual concerns are minor hygiene issues: an aggressively keyword-baited description that self-activates "even if not explicitly requested," unpinned dependency install commands via an extra package index, and absent allowed-tools/license/compatibility metadata. Overall risk: LOW — this skill appears safe to use with the noted metadata and dependency-pinning improvements.
llm_primary_threats: Capability inflation / over-broad activation description (keyword baiting, self-activation without explicit user request)
Unpinned dependency installation guidance via an alternate package index (minor supply-chain surface)
Missing manifest metadata (no allowed-tools, license, or compatibility declarations)

findings.title: Documentation examples reference remote data reads (S3/HTTP) and AWS credential environment variables — no exfiltration path
findings.description: Static pre-scan flagged "env var exfiltration" chains. Manual review shows the matches come solely from the KvikIO reference documentation, which explains that AWS credentials are read from AWS_DEFAULT_REGION / AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and shows read-only examples for kvikio.RemoteFile.open_s3 / open_http. These are inbound reads to user-specified buckets/URLs, contain no attacker-controlled endpoints, and no code in the package reads credentials or transmits data anywhere. Assessed as a false positive; recorded at LOW severity for transparency only.
findings.snippet:
AWS credentials come from environment variables (`AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`) or can be passed as keyword arguments.
with kvikio.RemoteFile.open_http("https://example.com/data.bin") as f:
findings.remediation: No action strictly required. Optionally add a note that credentials should be sourced from the environment/instance role and never hardcoded or echoed into generated code, and that RemoteFile is read-only.

findings.title: Over-broad activation description encourages unsolicited skill invocation
findings.description: The skill description is extremely keyword-dense (12+ library names, ~15 workload domains) and explicitly instructs activation "even if not explicitly requested" when CPU-bound Python code is seen. This is capability/keyword inflation that increases unwanted activation, though the claimed capabilities are legitimately covered by the bundled reference material and the behavior is limited to code-rewriting advice.
findings.snippet: "Also use when you see CPU-bound Python code (loops, large arrays, ML pipelines, graph analytics, image processing) that would benefit from GPU acceleration, even if not explicitly requested."
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to explicit user intent (e.g., "use when the user asks to GPU-accelerate Python code") and remove the self-activation clause and redundant keyword lists.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation guidance from an alternate package index
findings.description: Reference files instruct the agent to always install packages with `uv add` without version pins, and several commands add `--extra-index-url=https://pypi.nvidia.com`. The index is NVIDIA's official RAPIDS index and the package names are legitimate, so risk is low, but unpinned installs plus an extra index broaden the supply-chain surface (dependency confusion / unexpected version drift) if the agent executes these commands.
findings.snippet:
uv add --extra-index-url=https://pypi.nvidia.com cugraph-cu12
uv add cupy-cuda12x
"Always use `uv add` (never `pip install` or `conda install`) in all install instructions..."
findings.remediation: Recommend pinned versions (e.g., cudf-cu12==26.6.*) and note that installation commands should be surfaced to the user for approval rather than executed automatically; document why the NVIDIA index is required.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools / license / compatibility metadata
findings.description: The manifest declares only name, description, version, and author. There is no `allowed-tools` restriction, no license, and no compatibility field. Since the skill's guidance implies package installation, profiling commands (nsys, nvprof), file IO, and dashboard servers (d.show() binds a local HTTP port), absent tool restrictions mean the agent may run Bash/Python without declared bounds. Informational only — the field is optional per spec.
findings.snippet:
- license: Not specified
- compatibility: Not specified
- allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Declare `allowed-tools` (e.g., [Read, Write, Grep, Glob]) and add license/compatibility metadata. If Bash is needed for installs, state it explicitly so the user can reason about the blast radius.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The pacsomatic skill is a legitimate, well-scoped operator wrapper for the nf-core/pacsomatic Nextflow pipeline. No prompt injection, concealment instructions, credential access, network exfiltration, hardcoded secrets, obfuscation, or environment harvesting was found. The static 'eval/exec + subprocess' flag is a false positive: the script uses subprocess.run with argv lists (no shell=True, no eval/exec), and the author explicitly documents avoiding a shell for LSF stdin submission. Behavior matches the manifest description: input validation, samplesheet/params generation, launch-script generation, and scheduler submission. Residual risks are inherent to an HPC launcher: free-form --extra-args and --module-load values become shell content in a generated executable script that may be run with --run, and --repo-url/--checkout-dir allow cloning and executing an unpinned (potentially caller-substituted) pipeline repository. These warrant input validation and version pinning but are not indicators of malicious intent. Overall risk: LOW-to-MEDIUM, safe to use with normal operator care and user confirmation before --run.
llm_primary_threats: Unvalidated caller-supplied text written into an executable launch script (--module-load / --extra-args) that is later executed
Unpinned git clone / conda environment creation (supply-chain trust in overridable --repo-url)
Missing allowed-tools declaration for a skill that writes executables and spawns subprocesses
Documentation drift: references to non-existent asset/template files

findings.title: Arbitrary Nextflow arguments injected into generated launch script via --extra-args
findings.description: The helper accepts a free-form --extra-args string that is split with shlex.split() and appended to the Nextflow command, then written verbatim (though shell-quoted) into an executable launch script that is later executed with bash/bsub/sbatch/qsub when --run is used. Similarly, --module-load is inserted into the generated script as a raw, unquoted shell line ('lines.append(args.module_load)'), allowing arbitrary shell commands to be embedded in the generated script and executed at launch time. This is expected operator behavior for an HPC launcher CLI, but it constitutes an unvalidated path from caller-supplied text to shell execution, which an agent processing untrusted user text could be steered into.
findings.remediation: Validate/allow-list --module-load content (e.g., restrict to 'module load <name>' pattern) and --extra-args tokens (reject tokens beginning with shell metacharacters or unexpected flags). Require explicit user confirmation before writing arbitrary shell lines into an executable script that will be run.

findings.title: Unpinned git clone of pipeline repository and unpinned conda environment creation
findings.description: When --checkout-dir is provided the script clones a repository (default https://github.com/nf-core/pacsomatic.git, but overridable via --repo-url) with no revision/tag pin and no integrity verification, then treats the cloned main.nf as the pipeline to execute. It can also create a conda/mamba environment from a YAML file (--conda-env-file, arbitrary path). Both are legitimate operator conveniences but represent supply-chain trust decisions: a caller-supplied --repo-url could point to an attacker-controlled repo whose Nextflow code is subsequently executed with --run.
findings.snippet:
parser.add_argument("--repo-url", default="https://github.com/nf-core/pacsomatic.git", ...)
cmd = ["git", "clone", args.repo_url, str(target)]
...
cmd = ["mamba", "env", "create", "-n", env_name, "-f", str(env_file)]
findings.remediation: Pin the cloned revision (git clone --branch <tag> / checkout a specific commit), warn or require confirmation when --repo-url differs from the trusted nf-core default, and pin package versions in the bundled environment YAML.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration despite command execution and file writes
findings.description: The manifest does not declare allowed-tools or compatibility, while the skill writes executable files (chmod 0o755), spawns subprocesses (git, conda/mamba, nextflow, bsub/sbatch/qsub/bash), and creates directories. This is informational only — the behavior matches the stated purpose — but the absence of tool restrictions removes a useful guardrail for an agent that may run this skill with broad permissions.
findings.snippet:
- allowed-tools: Not specified
- compatibility: Not specified
(script performs os.chmod(script_path, 0o755) and subprocess.run of scheduler/bash commands)
findings.remediation: Declare allowed-tools (e.g., [Read, Write, Bash, Python]) and compatibility in the frontmatter so the required privileges are explicit and auditable.

findings.title: Broken/missing referenced file paths in documentation
findings.description: Instructions and pre-scan inventory reference several files that do not exist in the package (assets/*.md, templates/*.md). Missing references can cause an agent to search elsewhere or fabricate content; they also indicate documentation drift. No malicious content was found in the three existing reference files, which contain only legitimate Nextflow/HPC usage guidance.
findings.snippet:
Referenced File: assets/config-and-output.md (not found)
Referenced File: templates/pacsomatic_guide.md (not found)
findings.remediation: Remove stale references or add the missing files so all documented paths resolve inside the skill package.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The paper-lookup skill is a documentation-only skill (no executable scripts) that maps user literature queries onto 10 well-known, legitimate public scholarly APIs (NCBI E-utilities, PMC, bioRxiv/medRxiv, arXiv, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, CORE, Unpaywall). All reviewed reference files contain accurate, benign API documentation — endpoints, parameter tables, response shapes and rate limits — with no hidden instructions, obfuscated payloads, base64 blobs, credential harvesting, or exfiltration endpoints. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Bash) are consistent with the described behavior: reading bundled reference files and issuing curl requests to the documented public API hosts. Notably, the skill contains several defensive, security-positive instructions: it treats all API responses as untrusted third-party data, forbids following instructions embedded in responses, forbids pasting raw response text into shell commands, forbids echoing API keys, mandates URL-encoding of user input, and imposes explicit bounds (~1,000 records / ~50 calls) with user confirmation to avoid resource abuse. Residual concerns are minor and inherent to the design: .env/environment API-key loading, Bash+curl usage with user-derived strings (explicitly mitigated in-text), a broad activation description, and a set of referenced-but-missing templates/assets paths. No prompt injection, tool poisoning, data exfiltration, or command-injection payloads were identified. Overall risk: LOW — the skill appears benign and reasonably well-hardened.

findings.title: Bash/curl usage with user-supplied query strings (mitigated by explicit guidance)
findings.description: The skill directs the agent to invoke curl via Bash to reach REST endpoints, including passing user search terms and identifiers into URLs. Shell interpolation of untrusted strings is a general command-injection risk, but the skill explicitly mitigates it: it mandates URL-encoding, recommends `--data-urlencode`, forbids interpolating unescaped user strings into URLs or shell commands, and forbids pasting raw API response text into shell commands. No scripts are bundled, so no unsafe concrete command exists in the package.
findings.snippet: "Never interpolate an unescaped user string into a URL or shell command." / "never paste raw response text into a shell command"
findings.remediation: Keep and reinforce the encoding guidance; consider adding an allow-list of permitted hosts (eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, api.openalex.org, api.crossref.org, api.semanticscholar.org, api.core.ac.uk, api.unpaywall.org, api.biorxiv.org, export.arxiv.org) so the agent never curls arbitrary URLs derived from response data.

findings.title: Instruction to read API keys from environment and .env files
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to load API keys from environment variables and a working-directory .env file (NCBI_API_KEY, CORE_API_KEY, S2_API_KEY, OPENALEX_API_KEY). This is legitimate and necessary for authenticated API access, and the skill explicitly instructs the agent to never echo API keys. Risk is limited to the general possibility of secret exposure when a .env is parsed by an agent; no exfiltration path to third-party endpoints is present (keys are only sent to the documented official API hosts).
findings.snippet: "**Loading keys:** Check the environment first (`$NCBI_API_KEY`, etc.), then a `.env` in the working directory." ... "never echo API keys"
findings.remediation: Restrict key loading to explicitly named environment variables only, or require the user to confirm before the agent parses a .env file; keep the existing prohibition on echoing key values.

findings.title: Broad trigger keyword list in description
findings.description: The description enumerates many trigger phrases and database names ("Triggers on mentions of any supported database or requests like 'find papers on X'...", "or any scholarly literature query"). This maximizes activation breadth, but it is proportionate to the skill's genuine scope (10 academic literature APIs) and does not impersonate other tools or claim unrelated capabilities. Informational only.
findings.snippet: "Use when searching for papers, citations, DOI/PMID/arXiv lookups, ... or any scholarly literature query. Triggers on mentions of any supported database or requests like \"find papers on X\"..."
findings.remediation: Optionally narrow the trigger phrasing to the specific scholarly-lookup use cases rather than "any scholarly literature query".

findings.title: Missing referenced files (templates/ and assets/ variants) could be substituted
findings.description: The reference-file detection lists templates/*.md and assets/*.md paths that do not exist in the package (only references/*.md are present). Absent files are not themselves malicious, but if the agent later resolves such paths from an unexpected location, it could load unvetted instruction content. The existing references/*.md files were reviewed and contain only legitimate API documentation with no embedded instruction-override text.
findings.snippet: Referenced but missing: templates/pubmed.md, assets/pubmed.md, templates/core.md, assets/core.md, etc. Only references/*.md exist.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `parallel-web` skill is a documentation-only wrapper (no Python or Bash script files are bundled) that routes user requests to the appropriate `parallel-cli` subcommand for web search, URL extraction, deep research, data enrichment, entity discovery, and recurring monitoring. Behavior is consistent with the manifest description: every capability described in the frontmatter maps to a corresponding reference file and CLI invocation, with no hidden functionality, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, no credential harvesting beyond the declared `PARALLEL_API_KEY`, and no network destinations other than the vendor's own API and user-authorized webhooks.

Notably, the skill demonstrates unusually strong defensive hygiene rather than security weaknesses. It explicitly instructs the agent to treat all search results, extracted pages, reports, enrichment values, and monitor events as untrusted data and never to follow embedded instructions or credential prompts — an explicit indirect-prompt-injection countermeasure repeated across four reference files. It mandates passing user text as a single quoted argument or via stdin instead of constructing shell source, forbids concatenating raw user text into JSON or shell commands, and requires validating CLI-returned task IDs against expected prefixes (`trun_`, `tgrp_`, `findall_`/`frun_`, `mon_`) while rejecting whitespace and shell metacharacters — meaningful command-injection mitigation. Availability risk is bounded: polling is explicitly capped at three attempts with `--timeout 540` and unbounded polling loops are prohibited. Destructive or state-mutating operations (monitor create/update/trigger/cancel) require explicit user authorization and re-verification, and cost-amplifying tiers (deep research, high match limits) require explicit user intent plus cost warnings. Secret handling is disciplined: no key echoing, no bulk `.env` inspection, no credentials in webhook URLs.

Only three low-severity, largely informational observations remain: the optional `allowed-tools` field is absent even though the skill relies entirely on shell execution; setup performs third-party package installation (correctly pinned to `==0.7.1` in an isolated uv environment, though the upgrade command is necessarily unpinned) and suggests a PATH modification; and the skill legitimately handles a secret API key while uploading user-supplied rows to a third-party service and writing artifacts to disk. None of these constitute malicious behavior. Overall the package appears benign and well-engineered from a security standpoint.

findings.title: Skill requires a secret API key and can write result artifacts to disk
findings.description: The skill consumes `PARALLEL_API_KEY`, may perform interactive/device login, sends user-supplied query text and user-supplied CSV/JSON rows to Parallel's third-party API, and can write result files (`-o research-report`, `--target enriched.csv`). It can also register outbound webhooks to arbitrary HTTPS endpoints. All of this is inherent to the stated purpose and is accompanied by strong guardrails: no key printing/logging, no `.env` enumeration beyond checking for the key name, webhook must be user-authorized and credential-free, previews must avoid sensitive input fields, and artifacts should go to a user-specified or temp path rather than the repo root. No hardcoded secrets and no exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure were found; this is noted for data-flow awareness only.
findings.snippet:
Do not print, log, or include `PARALLEL_API_KEY` in command arguments or output.
Do not inspect an entire `.env` file; ... never display its value.
--webhook "https://example.com/parallel-events" ... Send events only to a user-authorized HTTPS endpoint. Do not place credentials in the webhook URL.
findings.remediation: No change required for safety, but confirm with the user before uploading local CSV/JSON files or registering webhooks, and continue to source the key from the environment/credential store only.

The initial install is correctly pinned to an exact version and installed in an isolated uv tool environment, which is good practice; residual supply-chain risk stems only from trusting the upstream package/registry and from the unpinned upgrade command. No integrity hash or repository provenance is provided.
findings.snippet:
uv tool install "parallel-web-tools[cli]==0.7.1"
uv tool upgrade parallel-web-tools
If `parallel-cli` is not found after install, add `~/.local/bin` to PATH.
findings.remediation: Keep the exact version pin, document the expected publisher/repository for `parallel-web-tools`, and require explicit user confirmation before running install/upgrade commands or modifying PATH.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `pathml` skill is a well-documented, defensively engineered research-support skill for computational pathology workflows. All four bundled Python CLIs (`plan_pipeline.py`, `plan_inference.py`, `image_qc.py`, `slide_manifest.py`, plus shared `_common.py`) are network-free, dependency-light, and implement strong input hardening: URL rejection, symlink-component rejection, root-confinement (`relative_to` checks), regular-file/size caps, strict JSON parsing with duplicate-key and NaN/Infinity rejection, bounded row/node/edge/pixel counts, allowlisted file suffixes, atomic writes with 0o600 permissions and no-clobber-by-default behavior. No `eval`, `exec`, `os.system`, `subprocess`, `pickle`, `requests`/`urllib`, or credential-path access appears anywhere in the code. The only `os.environ`-adjacent usage is `os.sys.stderr` for error printing — there is no environment-variable harvesting and no outbound network capability, so the static pre-scan flags for "env var exfiltration" and "cross-file exfiltration chain" are false positives (they appear to be triggered by the presence of `os` imports plus documentation strings containing HTTPS URLs of upstream PathML/Hugging Face endpoints).

The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language. To the contrary, it repeatedly reinforces safe behavior: a no-network default with an explicit user-consent gate before any download-capable PathML class is instantiated, warnings that PathML's `.pt`/pickle/h5path loaders execute code and must never be pointed at untrusted artifacts, explicit prohibition of Python dynamic evaluation, module-shadowing warnings, PHI/de-identification handling rules, and a clear non-clinical-use disclaimer. Declared `allowed-tools` (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob) are consistent with actual behavior (local file reads, bounded local writes, CLI invocation). Installation guidance uses a pinned version (`pathml==3.0.5`) via `uv`, discourages `pathml[all]`, and documents platform prerequisites — good supply-chain hygiene. External HTTPS references are citations/primary sources for human review, not instructions to fetch and execute remote content, so they do not constitute transitive-trust delegation.

Minor, non-security observations: the skill declares `.py` files that use a bare `from _common import ...` (requires execution from the scripts directory), and several referenced doc paths listed by the scanner (`assets/*.md`, `templates/*.md`, `pathml.py`) do not exist — the `pathml.py` "reference" is actually a warning in SKILL.md about not naming local files after modules, not a bundled file. Neither is a security threat. No findings warranting a severity rating were identified.

The `pathway-enrichment` skill is a legitimate bioinformatics helper for over-representation and GSEA analyses using gseapy/g:Profiler. Review of the SKILL.md body, the single Python script (`scripts/run_enrichment.py`), and the three bundled reference files found no prompt injection, no instruction-override or concealment language, no credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, env harvesting), no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. Network activity is limited to well-known, documented public bioinformatics services (Enrichr, MSigDB, g:Profiler, Biomart) and is disclosed in the instructions and script docstring — it is intrinsic to the stated purpose, not exfiltration. File I/O is scoped to user-specified input files and an explicit --outdir. The static analyzer hint 'MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC' appears to be a false positive: no `eval()`, `exec()`, `os.system`, `subprocess`, or shell interpolation exists in any code block or script; the only dynamic constructs are pandas/gseapy API calls and argparse handling. Description and declared capabilities match actual behavior, and the keyword-rich description is domain-appropriate rather than keyword baiting. Only minor hygiene issues were identified (unpinned dependencies, absent optional manifest metadata). Overall the package appears safe to use.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
This is the vendored Anthropic "pdf" skill and it appears benign. All five bundled Python scripts perform purely local PDF/form/image operations using pypdf, pdfplumber, pdf2image and PIL: extracting form field metadata, validating bounding boxes, drawing validation overlays, filling fillable fields or adding FreeText annotations, converting pages to PNG, and extracting form structure. File paths are taken from explicit argv arguments, output is written only to user-specified paths, and there is NO network activity (no requests/urllib/socket/curl), NO environment-variable or credential access (no os.environ, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh), NO subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, NO base64 or other obfuscation, and no hardcoded secrets.

The pre-scan static findings (BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION, BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN, BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION) are assessed as FALSE POSITIVES: no script in the package reads environment variables or performs any outbound network call. The only cross-file linkage is the legitimate local import `from extract_form_field_info import get_field_info` in fill_fillable_fields.py, plus documented internal references to reference.md / forms.md, which are bundled skill files (normal, expected behavior). The "Referenced Files not found" entries (pypdf.py, reportlab.py, pdf2image.py, etc.) are library import names misparsed as file references, not missing local dependencies.

The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, no instruction override, no concealment directives, no role redefinition, and no instructions to fetch or execute content from external URLs. There is one monkeypatch of a pypdf internal method (DictionaryObject.get_inherited) in fill_fillable_fields.py; this is a narrowly scoped in-process workaround for radio/choice option parsing, not tool shadowing or sabotage. Residual observations are minor hygiene items only: an unconstrained manifest and unpinned pip install guidance. No CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM threats identified.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The peer-review skill appears benign and unusually well-scoped. All seven bundled Python scripts (`_common.py`, `validate_review_intake.py`, `select_reporting_guidelines.py`, `validate_claim_evidence.py`, `audit_statistics_reproducibility.py`, `audit_citations.py`, `generate_review_scaffold.py`, `lint_review.py`) use only the Python standard library and contain no network calls (no requests/urllib/socket/http), no subprocess or os.system invocation, no eval/exec/compile, no pickle/marshal, no environment-variable or credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, .env), no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. Data flow is strictly local: bounded JSON/CSV/Markdown inputs are read from explicitly supplied paths and reports are written to stdout or an explicitly named local file. The shared helper module implements defensive controls that reduce rather than create risk: 4 MiB input cap, 5,000-row CSV cap, 12,000-char cell cap, list-size caps, UTF-8-only decoding with NUL rejection, duplicate JSON key and duplicate CSV header rejection, symlink rejection for both inputs and outputs, refusal to overwrite existing outputs without --force, and atomic writes with 0o600 permissions. These bounds also mitigate resource-exhaustion/DoS concerns. Report minimization is intentional and consistently implemented — outputs emit IDs, counts, rule codes, and line numbers rather than manuscript, claim, or reference prose, which limits confidential-content leakage into logs or downstream contexts. No prompt injection, jailbreak, role redefinition, concealment directive ('do not tell the user'), or system-prompt-extraction language was found in SKILL.md or any reference file, in English or any other language. The instruction body is safety-additive: it establishes an explicit authorization gate before unpublished material is read, forbids sending confidential content to external services, forbids reading .env files/API keys/credentials, forbids network/LLM/image calls from bundled tools, forbids impersonating reviewers or editors, forbids fabricating findings or announcing editorial decisions, and requires human accountability. The `lint_review.py` regexes actively detect impersonation, editorial-decision, and false-execution claims. The only external URLs in the package are informational citations in `assets/source_ledger.csv`, `assets/reporting_guidelines.json`, and reference markdown; no script fetches them, and no instruction tells the agent to retrieve and follow remote content, so there is no indirect-prompt-injection or transitive-trust path. The description is specific to peer review and matches actual behavior, with no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, activation-priority manipulation, or capability inflation. All file reads are of internal, bundled assets (normal, expected behavior) or user-supplied local paths passed as explicit CLI arguments. Findings are limited to three LOW-severity hygiene items: missing optional `allowed-tools` metadata, a handful of documented-but-absent asset paths, and a self-attested security-validation document whose claims cannot be independently verified from the package (though the shipped code is consistent with them). No CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM issues were identified.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `pennylane` skill is a documentation/reference package for the legitimate PennyLane quantum computing framework. The SKILL.md body and all six reference markdown files consist solely of standard quantum-computing tutorial content (circuits, VQE/QAOA, optimizers, device backends, ML integration), which is fully consistent with the declared name, description, and `allowed-tools: Read, Bash, Python`. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `phylogenetics` skill is a legitimate, domain-appropriate bioinformatics workflow package. Compute cost from bootstrap replicates and thread counts is user-controlled and bounded by defaults (1000 bootstraps, 4 threads), consistent with normal phylogenetics practice rather than resource-abuse. This skill is a documentation/reference package for the "Pi" terminal coding agent. It contains 13 markdown files and no executable scripts (no .py, .sh, or other runnable code). The SKILL.md body is a routing table that maps user intents to internal reference files bundled with the package — reading these internal files is normal, expected skill behavior.

No prompt injection, jailbreak, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language was found in any file (checked language-agnostically). There is no data exfiltration, no credential harvesting, no hardcoded secrets, and no network calls performed by the skill itself. Provider environment-variable names and auth file paths (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ~/.pi/agent/auth.json) appear only as legitimate configuration documentation, with placeholder values such as "sk-ant-..." — not real keys or read-and-send patterns.

The pre-scan flag "MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC" appears to be a false positive: the fenced code blocks in these files are TypeScript/JSON/bash documentation samples (e.g. `execute(toolCallId, params)` tool-handler signatures, `pi.exec(command, args)` API descriptions, `eval "$(grep '^alias ' ~/.zshrc)"` in a documented shell-alias setting). None of it is skill-executed Python eval/exec, and none constructs commands from untrusted input within the skill.

Cross-component consistency is good: the manifest description matches the bundled content, and the skill explicitly includes a "Safety Defaults" section warning that Pi is not sandboxed, that extensions/packages/skills run with full process permissions, that secrets should not be stored in project files, and that untrusted repos should be isolated via container/VM. That is security-positive framing rather than a threat.

Residual concerns are minor and informational: an unusually broad activation description, a large number of unresolved assets/ and templates/ references, and documented (not executed) unpinned install commands. Overall this package appears benign.

findings.title: Very broad skill description increases activation surface
findings.description: The skill description is unusually long and enumerates many keywords (installing, configuring, providers, models, SDK, RPC, MCP, web search, subagents, video understanding, etc.). This is legitimate for a documentation-reference skill covering an entire product, but it broadens discovery/activation triggers considerably. No deceptive claims were found: the described purpose (Pi documentation reference) matches the actual bundled content, which is purely markdown documentation.
findings.snippet: description: Build with and use Pi, the minimal terminal coding harness. Use for installing Pi, configuring providers/models/settings/environment variables, creating Pi skills/extensions/packages/themes/prompt templates, embedding Pi through the SDK, integrating over RPC or JSON event streams, parsing sessions, running local models through the llama.cpp router, ... pi-web-access (web search, fetching, video understanding).
findings.remediation: Optionally narrow the description to the core intent ("reference documentation for the Pi terminal coding agent") to reduce unnecessary activation, and keep the detailed capability list in the instruction body.

findings.title: Documented install/package commands pull unpinned remote code (informational)

These are the vendor's own documented commands and are quoted as documentation rather than executed by the skill, but an agent following them would install unpinned third-party code with full user permissions. The documentation does include mitigations (`--ignore-scripts`, explicit warnings that packages run with full system access, and a security/containerization section).
