scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The polars-bio skill is a documentation-only skill that teaches usage of the legitimate open-source polars-bio Python library for genomic interval operations and bioinformatics file I/O. No executable scripts are included (no .py or .sh payloads shipped), and all provided content — SKILL.md plus references/interval_operations.md, references/file_io.md, references/sql_processing.md, references/pileup_operations.md — consists of accurate API documentation, parameter tables, and code examples consistent with the stated purpose.

Security review results:
- Manifest: name and description match observed behavior; no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, or over-broad capability claims. allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) is consistent with a skill that installs a package and reads/writes genomic files; nothing in the content exceeds these declarations.
- Instructions: no prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment ("do not tell the user"), no role redefinition, no safety-bypass language, in English or any other language.
- Scripts: none present. The pre-scan hint "BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS: eval/exec combined with subprocess" could not be corroborated anywhere in the delivered content — there are no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess calls, no shell pipelines, no base64/hex blobs, and no obfuscation. The only shell command documented is a version-pinned `uv pip install "polars-bio==0.31.0"`. This appears to be a false positive (likely triggered by SQL/DataFusion "execute query" wording or generic keyword matching in unresolved referenced filenames such as polars.py / polars_bio.py, which are absent).
- Data flow: no network exfiltration, no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, .env files, no environment-variable harvesting, no telemetry endpoints, no hardcoded secrets or API keys. Cloud credential use is only the standard, disclosed SDK behavior triggered by user-supplied s3://, gs://, or az:// paths.
- Behavioral/autonomy: no unbounded loops, no "retry until success", no cross-session memory bridging, no over-collection (no home-directory walks), no read→send tool chaining, and no instruction to follow content fetched from external URLs.

Residual concerns are minor and non-exploitable: an external (though pinned) PyPI dependency, standard ambient cloud credential usage, and several documentation references pointing to files that are not shipped. No CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM findings. The skill is assessed as benign and safe to use, with the caveat that the missing reference files should be shipped or removed to preserve package integrity.

findings.title: Cloud credential usage via environment variables for s3://, gs://, az:// paths
findings.description: Documentation describes that cloud URIs cause reads using ambient cloud SDK credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, Azure defaults). This is standard library behavior, is explicitly disclosed in the manifest `compatibility` field and reference docs, and there is no code in the package that reads, collects, logs, or transmits credentials. Only the destination bucket the user specifies receives requests. Informational only.
findings.snippet: "Cloud paths (s3://, gs://, az://) trigger reads through Apache OpenDAL using your environment's cloud SDK credentials. Credentials are read only when a cloud URI is accessed — not from broad .env scanning."
findings.remediation: Ensure users only pass trusted cloud URIs; prefer scoped, read-only credentials or allow_anonymous=True for public datasets. No package change needed.

findings.title: Documented dependency installation is version-pinned (informational)
findings.description: The skill instructs installing the third-party package polars-bio via `uv pip install "polars-bio==0.31.0"`. The version is explicitly pinned, which is good practice, but the skill does introduce an external PyPI dependency and its transitive native dependencies (DataFusion/Arrow bindings) into the user's environment. No install-time hooks, custom indexes, or GitHub-direct installs are used.
findings.snippet: uv pip install "polars-bio==0.31.0"
findings.remediation: No action strictly required. Optionally verify package integrity (hashes / trusted index) before installation and confirm the package name matches the official PyPI project to avoid typosquats.

findings.title: Multiple referenced files are missing from the package
findings.description: The instruction body and analyzer output reference several files that do not exist in the package (polars.py, polars_bio.py, configuration.md, bioframe_migration.md, and various assets/*, templates/* paths surfaced by the reference extractor). Missing references are a documentation-integrity issue: if such files are later added or resolved from outside the package directory, their content would be loaded as authoritative guidance. No malicious content is present today.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: polars.py (not found); Referenced File: polars_bio.py (not found); references/configuration.md and references/bioframe_migration.md described in Resources but not provided
findings.remediation: Ship all referenced reference files inside the package or remove the references. Never resolve documentation references from paths outside the skill directory or from network locations.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is the official Anthropic `pptx` skill (vendored from github.com/anthropics/skills), providing PPTX/POTX creation, editing, reading, validation, and rendering. Analysis of SKILL.md and all bundled scripts found no prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment directives, no credential access, no network exfiltration, no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated payloads. Behavior matches the manifest description: all file operations are scoped to user-supplied decks, temp directories, and the skill's own scripts. Security posture is notably good in several places: XML parsing uses defusedxml, ZIP extraction uses a safe_extract() helper that rejects symlinks and path-traversal entries, and the soffice wrapper deliberately builds a minimal allowlisted environment specifically so caller API keys/tokens are NOT forwarded to the converter subprocess. Findings are limited to low-severity hardening items: an aggressive (but functionally accurate) activation description, unpinned fallback npm installs, and the runtime-compiled LD_PRELOAD socket shim written to a predictable /tmp path. No evidence of malicious intent.

unanalyzable_file_list.reason: File exists but content is empty or unreadable

findings.title: Broad keyword-baiting activation description
findings.description: The skill description is written to maximize activation, listing many trigger keywords ("deck", "slides", "presentation", .pptx/.potx) and instructing the agent to trigger "any time" and "regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward". While reasonable for a file-format handler skill and consistent with the skill's actual functionality, this pattern is aggressive activation scoping. No malicious behavior accompanies it.
findings.snippet: "Trigger whenever the user mentions \"deck,\" \"slides,\" \"presentation,\" or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward."
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to the skill's core capability (PPTX creation/editing/reading) rather than instructing unconditional activation. Informational only — no action strictly required.

findings.title: Fallback unpinned package installation instructions
findings.description: SKILL.md instructs the agent to run `npm install pptxgenjs` and `npm install react-icons react react-dom sharp` if the corresponding requires fail. These installs are unpinned (no version constraints), which introduces a minor supply-chain risk if a malicious version is published. The instructions do gate the installs behind a require failure and the packages are legitimate, well-known npm packages, so risk is low.
findings.snippet: Only if that require fails: `npm install pptxgenjs` ... (`react-icons`, `react`, `react-dom`, and `sharp` are preinstalled — `npm install react-icons react react-dom sharp` only if a require fails).
findings.remediation: Pin versions for any fallback install (e.g. `npm install pptxgenjs@4.0.1`) or remove the install fallback and fail with a clear message instead.

findings.title: Runtime C source compilation and LD_PRELOAD injection into soffice subprocess
findings.description: scripts/office/soffice.py writes a C source file to the system temp directory, compiles it with gcc, and injects the resulting shared object into the LibreOffice subprocess via LD_PRELOAD to work around blocked AF_UNIX sockets in sandboxes. The C source is a static, inspectable literal that only shims socket/listen/accept/close — it performs no network, filesystem, or exfiltration activity, and the behavior is documented in SKILL.md. However, writing to a predictable, world-writable temp path (/tmp/lo_socket_shim.c / .so) and reusing an existing .so without integrity checking is a local TOCTOU/preload-hijack weakness: a local attacker who pre-creates /tmp/lo_socket_shim.so could get their code loaded into the soffice process.
findings.snippet:
_SHIM_SO = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "lo_socket_shim.so"
...
if _SHIM_SO.exists():
    return _SHIM_SO
src = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "lo_socket_shim.c"
src.write_text(_SHIM_SOURCE)
subprocess.run(["gcc", "-shared", "-fPIC", "-o", str(_SHIM_SO), str(src), "-ldl"], check=True, capture_output=True)
...
env["LD_PRELOAD"] = str(shim)
findings.remediation: Build the shim inside a per-run private directory created with tempfile.mkdtemp() (0700) instead of a fixed predictable path, or verify a hash of the existing .so before reuse. Prefer shipping the workaround as a vendored, checksummed artifact rather than compiling at runtime.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The pptx-posters skill is a well-engineered, defensively written local document-generation and auditing toolkit and appears benign. Review of all seven CLIs plus the two shared modules found no prompt injection, jailbreak language, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass instructions in SKILL.md or the reference markdown; the instruction body is a fail-closed procedural workflow that repeatedly demands human author approval and refuses to fabricate content. No network activity exists anywhere in the code: there are no imports of requests, urllib, socket, or http, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec/pickle/marshal usage, no environment-variable or credential harvesting (no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.netrc, os.environ reads), and no hardcoded secrets or obfuscated/base64 payloads. File access is tightly scoped: resolve_local_asset() rejects absolute paths, URI schemes, backslashes, and '..' segments and enforces containment under the manifest's own directory via resolve()+relative_to(); checked_input_file() rejects symlinks and non-regular files with size caps; checked_output_file()/commit_temp_file() refuse to overwrite existing destinations and create mode-0600 temp files in the destination directory. XML parsing rejects DTD/ENTITY declarations before parse (XXE/billion-laughs mitigation), ZIP handling never calls extract/extractall and pre-bounds the central directory, and the package inspector explicitly rejects macros, ActiveX, OLE, embedded parts, and all External-TargetMode relationships. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep, Python) are consistent with observed behavior (local file reads/writes plus a documented uv pip install of exactly pinned dependencies python-pptx==1.0.2, Pillow==12.3.0, lxml==6.1.1 — pinned, from PyPI, no direct GitHub installs, no typosquat indicators). The description is narrowly scoped with no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, activation-priority manipulation, or capability inflation, and it matches actual behavior. Only two LOW informational findings remain: documented-but-bounded compute consumption limits, and a set of reference paths in SKILL.md that do not resolve to bundled files.
llm_primary_threats: Bounded local resource consumption (accepted, documented caps)
Minor documentation/reference-path inconsistencies

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools, license, and compatibility metadata
findings.description: The manifest does not declare `allowed-tools`, `license`, or `compatibility`. These fields are optional, so this is informational only; however, absence of a declared tool scope means the skill's Python file-read behavior is not constrained by a manifest policy.
findings.snippet:

- compatibility: Not specified
- allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Python]`, a license, and compatibility information to make the skill's capability surface explicit.

findings.title: Repeated full-CSV loads of a ~4M-edge dataset can exhaust memory/CPU
findings.description: Every public function calls `_load_kg()`, which reads the entire multi-million-row knowledge graph CSV into a pandas DataFrame with no caching, chunking, or column selection. `get_disease_context` triggers at least two full loads, and repeated agent calls could exhaust memory or stall the host. This appears to be a performance design weakness rather than a deliberate DoS.
findings.remediation: Cache the loaded DataFrame (e.g., functools.lru_cache or module-level singleton), read only required columns, use chunked reads or a real database/graph backend, and enforce result-size limits.

findings.title: Hardcoded absolute path exposing developer's local filesystem/username
findings.description: The skill hardcodes a developer-specific data path (`/mnt/c/Users/eamon/Documents/Data/PrimeKG/kg.csv`) in both SKILL.md and query_primekg.py. This leaks the original author's username/directory layout and makes the skill non-portable. It is not an exfiltration vector by itself, but it is an information-disclosure and configuration hygiene issue.
findings.snippet: DATA_PATH = "/mnt/c/Users/eamon/Documents/Data/PrimeKG/kg.csv"
findings.remediation: Make the data path configurable via an environment variable or function argument with a sane relative default, and remove user-specific absolute paths from documentation.

findings.title: Unescaped user input used as a regex in pandas str.contains
findings.description: `search_nodes` passes `name_query` directly to `Series.str.contains` without `regex=False` or escaping. Malicious or malformed input (e.g., a catastrophic-backtracking pattern or invalid regex) can raise errors or cause excessive CPU use during matching. There is no code execution risk — no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess is used anywhere in the skill.
findings.snippet: mask = nodes['name'].str.contains(name_query, case=False, na=False)
findings.remediation: Pass `regex=False` (or `re.escape(name_query)`) and validate/limit query length before matching.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The protocolsio-integration skill is a defensively engineered, read-oriented API client for protocols.io. Across all five Python modules the security posture is unusually strong and consistent with the manifest claims:

- Network: only HTTPS GET requests, hard host allowlist (protocols.io, www.protocols.io, and a strict `<subdomain>.protocols.io` regex), port restricted to 443, no URL credentials, redirects explicitly rejected via a custom NoRedirectHandler, and ambient proxies disabled (ProxyHandler({})). Network activity requires an explicit `--execute` flag; default mode only prints a plan. There are no external/attacker-controlled domains anywhere.
- Credentials: only one named environment variable (PROTOCOLS_IO_ACCESS_TOKEN) is read; there is no full-environment enumeration, no .env loading, no ~/.aws or ~/.ssh access, and no hardcoded secrets. Tokens are never echoed — validate_auth_config.py returns presence booleans only, and plan output substitutes a placeholder for the Authorization header. Sensitive-key redaction is applied to both payloads and remote responses.
- Execution safety: no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess, no shell invocation, no dynamic imports, no deserialization of pickles, and no obfuscation or encoded blobs. Only the Python standard library is used, matching the compatibility statement; there is no pip/npm installation or supply-chain fetch.
- Filesystem: all input/output paths are constrained to the CWD with parent-traversal and symlink rejection, output files must not already exist, and PDF bytes are written with 0600 permissions via O_EXCL. Local file reads are size-capped.
- Resource bounds: page/item/byte/depth/timeout caps everywhere, retries limited to 0–2 for idempotent GETs only, Retry-After capped at 30s, and the linked-step traversal uses a visited-set guard so no unbounded loop exists.
- Mutation handling: plan_write_request.py has no network or execution path at all; it validates payload shapes strictly against documented field allowlists, redacts credential-like fields, and requires a confirmation phrase that still does not execute.
- Prompt-injection posture: the instructions and reference docs repeatedly and explicitly instruct the agent to treat protocol text, comments, filenames, links, signed upload fields, and error messages as untrusted data and never obey embedded instructions. This is defensive guidance, not injection. No instruction-override, concealment, role-redefinition, or safety-bypass language appears in any language.
- Manifest consistency: declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Python) match observed behavior — the scripts read local JSON, write a PDF output file, and run as Python; no Bash execution occurs. The description accurately narrows activation to protocols.io tasks and does not use keyword baiting or over-broad capability claims.

Only a trivial documentation-consistency observation was noted. No malicious behavior, data exfiltration, injection, obfuscation, or capability inflation was found.

All files explicitly linked from SKILL.md (references/*.md, assets/protocol-snapshot.schema.json) are present, so this is informational only — the missing template/asset variants are artifacts of path probing, not broken instructions. No security impact identified.

findings.remediation: Keep the referenced-file list consistent with the shipped package contents; no functional change required.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a well-constructed, defense-oriented documentation and tooling skill for PufferLib. All seven bundled Python CLIs are standard-library only, offline, deterministic, and bounded: no network libraries, no subprocess/shell execution, no eval/exec/dynamic imports, no pickle or torch.load, no os.environ reads, and no credential file access. Security controls are unusually strong and appear genuine: resolve_local_path() enforces root containment and rejects symlinks and traversal; inspect_checkpoint.py opens files with O_NOFOLLOW, requires a regular file, and hashes/classifies bytes without deserialization; _common.py implements strict JSON parsing (duplicate-key and non-finite rejection), bounded integer validation, slug-only identifiers that explicitly reject dotted import paths, and secret_key_paths() that rejects credential-bearing config keys. Resource use is capped everywhere (steps, envs, workers, repeats, file sizes) and multiprocessing deliberately excludes 'fork'. SKILL.md instructions contain no prompt injection, no concealment directives, no instruction overrides, and no safety-bypass language; the guidance consistently pushes toward pinned versions, verified digests, sandboxed builds, and explicit opt-in for external logging. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Bash, Grep, Python) are consistent with observed behavior — scripts only read local files under an explicit root and write to stdout. Referenced external URLs are legitimate upstream sources (PyPI, GitHub PufferAI, official docs, arXiv/OpenReview) cited as documentation, not fetched or executed by any script. Several referenced-file paths reported as 'not found' (templates/*, assets/*, pufferlib.py) are inventory artifacts of link scanning, not real dangling dependencies of the instructions. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This pydicom skill appears benign and unusually security-conscious. The pre-scan flag BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS could not be substantiated — no eval(), exec(), os.system(), or subprocess usage exists anywhere in the provided code; it appears to be a false positive (likely triggered by identifiers such as 'inspect', 'importlib.metadata', or 'process_file'). scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `pytorch-lightning` skill is a legitimate, well-scoped documentation-and-boilerplate skill for the PyTorch Lightning deep learning framework. It behaves consistently with its manifest: the name, description, and compatibility notes all match the actual content, which consists of three inert Python template scripts (LightningModule, LightningDataModule, Trainer configuration examples) and seven reference markdown documents.

Analysis of all components found no malicious behavior:
- **SKILL.md instructions**: No prompt injection, instruction override, role redefinition, concealment directives ("do not tell the user"), or safety-bypass language in any language. Instructions are purely descriptive/technical.
- **Scripts**: No network calls, no `eval`/`exec`/`os.system`/`subprocess`, no file I/O outside standard training artifacts, no credential or environment-variable reads, no obfuscation, encoding, or hidden payloads. Placeholder data is synthetic (`torch.randn`).
- **allowed-tools consistency**: Declares `Read, Write, Edit, Bash`. Bash usage is limited to documented `uv pip install lightning` / `tensorboard`; Write/Edit are consistent with a code-scaffolding skill. No violations observed.
- **Data flow**: No read→send or collect→post chains. No home-directory traversal or over-collection.
- **Supply chain**: `uv pip install lightning` and optional logger installs are unpinned, but these are the canonical upstream PyPI packages for this framework with no typosquatting indicators; the risk is negligible in context.

**The static pre-scan findings are false positives.** The reported `BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION` and `BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_*_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN` signals are triggered by benign, expected ML-framework patterns in the documentation: `os.environ[\"NCCL_TIMEOUT\"] = \"3600\"` (a local write, not a read, for distributed-training timeouts in references/distributed_training.md), the `tracking_uri=\"http://localhost:5000\"` MLflow example (a loopback address), and standard cloud experiment-tracker logger instantiations (W&B, MLflow, Comet). No code path reads sensitive environment variables or credentials and transmits them to an external endpoint. There is no cross-file chain that connects a data-collection sink to a network sink.

Only two minor, non-exploitable issues were identified: a hardcoded API-key placeholder in a documentation example (insecure-pattern modeling, no real secret) and a set of dangling `templates/`/`assets/` file references. Overall the skill is assessed as SAFE for use.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The qiskit skill is a well-structured, documentation-heavy technical reference for building and executing quantum circuits with Qiskit 2.x and IBM Quantum Runtime. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directives, role redefinition, or safety-bypass instructions were found in SKILL.md or any bundled reference file. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `qutip` skill is a well-engineered, defensive scientific-computing skill for quantum dynamics simulation with QuTiP 5.3.0. No security threats were identified.

Analysis details:
- **Manifest**: Name, description, and compatibility notes accurately reflect behavior (local simulation/planning CLIs, no network use). `allowed-tools` is not specified, which is optional per spec and only informational here; the skill's actual behavior (local Python execution and local file read/write of JSON) is consistent with its stated purpose.
- **SKILL.md body**: Contains only technical physics/numerics guidance. No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, safety-bypass language, or instructions to fetch/execute external content. It explicitly warns *against* risky patterns: "Do not create coefficient source strings from user input", "This skill never uses Python dynamic-code execution", and "Do not load untrusted QuTiP object/result files because object serialization can execute code."
- **Scripts**: All five CLIs plus `_common.py` use `argparse` with constrained `choices`, strict bounds validation (`finite_float`, `bounded_int`, `bounded_dimensions`), and raise `CliError` on violations. There is no `eval`, `exec`, `compile`, `pickle`, `subprocess`, `os.system`, or any network/socket/HTTP usage. JSON parsing is hardened: `parse_constant` rejects NaN/Infinity, `object_pairs_hook` rejects duplicate keys, unknown keys are rejected via `validate_keys`, and output serialization uses `allow_nan=False` with a size cap.
- **File I/O safety**: `checked_input_file`/`checked_output_file` reject `://` URLs, reject symlinks, require regular files, enforce a 1 MiB input cap and 8 MiB report cap, restrict suffixes to `.json`, require an explicit `--force` to overwrite, and write atomically via `mkstemp` + `os.chmod(0o600)` + `os.replace`. No home-directory traversal, no credential paths (`~/.aws`, `~/.ssh`), no environment-variable harvesting, no hardcoded secrets.
- **Resource limits**: Explicit caps on Hilbert dimension (64), subsystems (8), model objects (32), time points (5001), trajectories (2000), sweep runs (6), and total sweep trajectories (4000) mitigate compute-exhaustion risk. No unbounded loops or retry logic.
- **Dependencies**: Documented installs are exactly pinned (`qutip==5.3.0`, `qutip-qip==0.4.2`, etc.), `load_qutip()` verifies the installed version matches the pin, and the skill explicitly advises against installing the unreleased `qutip-cupy` from Git. No typosquatting indicators; all packages are the official QuTiP-organization distributions.
- **Referenced files**: The five `references/*.md` files that were provided are internal to the package and contain only legitimate technical documentation with no embedded instructions to the agent and no hidden payloads. The scanner-listed `assets/*`, `templates/*`, and `qutip.py` paths are false positives from substring matching of reference filenames; the SKILL.md only references `references/*.md`. Missing files are a documentation-hygiene non-issue, not a security concern.
- **Cross-component consistency**: Every documented script exists, and each script's behavior matches its described purpose. No hidden capabilities, no tool chaining toward exfiltration (read→send), no cross-context bridging, and no over-collection.

Recommendation: No remediation required. Optionally, the author could declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash, Python]` for explicitness and add the missing `references/` files if any links are stale.

The `rdkit` skill is a legitimate cheminformatics documentation-and-example package. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; it is purely technical guidance on RDKit APIs. All three bundled Python scripts (molecular_properties.py, similarity_search.py, substructure_filter.py) are self-contained, use only RDKit/argparse/csv/pathlib, and perform exactly what the description claims: parse molecules, compute descriptors, compute fingerprint similarity, and filter by SMARTS. There is no network activity, no environment-variable or credential access (no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, no os.environ), no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no base64/obfuscated payloads, and no filesystem traversal beyond user-specified input/output paths. Declared `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash` is consistent with the scripts' behavior (reading molecule files, writing CSV/SDF/SMILES outputs, running CLI scripts); no violation detected. These are placeholder patterns rather than real hardcoded credentials, but they encourage a practice that can lead to credential leakage into logs or source control. The environment-variable approach (ROWAN_API_KEY) is also documented and preferred. No exfiltration of the key to any third-party endpoint occurs.

...

print(f"Your webhook secret: {secret.secret}")

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `scanpy` skill is a legitimate, well-structured bioinformatics toolkit for single-cell RNA-seq analysis. Its manifest description matches the actual behavior of all bundled scripts and reference documents: every script is a thin, argparse-driven CLI wrapper around standard `scanpy`/`anndata` API calls that reads a local input file and writes local .h5ad/CSV/figure outputs.

No malicious behavior was found. Specifically: (1) no prompt injection, jailbreak, role-redefinition, or concealment language anywhere in SKILL.md or the reference markdown — instructions are purely technical guidance in a single language; (2) no network exfiltration — the only URLs are documentation links and official CRAN/Bioconductor/PyPI repositories, and no script performs HTTP requests or socket operations; (3) no credential or secret access — no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.netrc, no environment-variable harvesting, no hardcoded keys; (4) no dynamic code execution — no eval, exec, pickle.loads, subprocess, or os.system anywhere in the Python scripts; (5) file access is proportionate and scoped to user-supplied input paths and explicitly named output prefixes, with no directory walking of $HOME or over-collection; (6) all file reads are of internal bundled resources (assets/*.json, references/*.md) or explicit user-provided data files, which is expected for a self-contained skill; (7) no unbounded loops, retries, or autonomy directives — the pipeline is deterministic and single-pass.

Residual issues are low-severity hygiene items: unpinned runtime package installs plus one `install_github` and `sudo`-based system package installation in the R interop runbook (supply-chain/privilege surface), an undeclared `allowed-tools` field despite the skill needing Bash/Python/Write, a documentation bug where a `die()` helper is used without being imported in qc_analysis.py, and a number of documented resource paths that do not exist in the package. None of these indicate malicious intent; they warrant cleanup rather than blocking.

Privileged system package installation via sudo in R interop runbook
Undeclared tool permissions for a skill that executes scripts and writes files

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The scholar-evaluation skill is a defensively engineered, standard-library-only local data-validation toolkit and is assessed as SAFE. All seven Python scripts (calculate_scores.py, weight_sensitivity.py, summarize_agreement.py, generate_report_scaffold.py, check_process.py, validate_rubric.py, _common.py) perform deterministic JSON/CSV schema validation and arithmetic. There is no network activity, no credential or environment access (no os.environ, no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, no dotenv), no hardcoded secrets, no subprocess/os.system, no eval/exec/compile, no pickle/marshal deserialization, no dynamic imports, and no obfuscation or encoded payloads. The shared _common.py implements strong input hardening: extension allowlisting, symlink rejection, regular-file checks, 2 MiB size caps, JSON duplicate-key rejection, depth (20) / node (25,000) / list (1,000) / object-field (100) / string-length (4,000) bounds, non-finite-number rejection, unknown-field rejection, and an explicit denylist of private-PII field names (ssn, cv_text, email, applicant_name, etc.). Output writing is constrained to .json suffixes with symlink rejection, no-overwrite-by-default, and a 2 MiB cap; error reports emit only stable codes and JSON paths, never supplied values, avoiding data leakage through diagnostics. Loops are bounded (MAX_CSV_ROWS=20,000, MAX_CRITERIA=50, MAX_EVALUATIONS=50, delta in (0,0.5]); weight_sensitivity's scenario count is O(criteria × evaluations) with hard caps, so no DoS/compute-exhaustion risk. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, safety-bypass language, or system-prompt extraction attempts; its imperative language consists entirely of self-restricting safety guardrails (prohibiting use for hiring, promotion, tenure, admissions, funding, awards, discipline, and person ranking) that narrow rather than expand agent capability. Description and behavior are consistent: no capability inflation, keyword baiting, or brand impersonation; the ScholarEval reference is explicitly bounded as an unvalidated arXiv preprint with no code, model, or network dependency on it. Bundled assets are benign synthetic templates with pseudonymous identifiers and intentionally fail-closed defaults (content_validity_status: not_established, all process-checklist booleans false). Reading these internal bundled files is normal self-contained skill behavior. Only two LOW informational observations were recorded: a slightly broad Bash declaration that is textually constrained to fixed python3 invocations and confirmed unused by any script, and unresolved alternate-directory path candidates that correspond to no documented path and carry no fallback or fetch logic.

Analysis resolution attempted several alternate directories (e.g., `templates/...`, `assets/source_ledger.md`, `references/rubric_template.json`) that do not exist. All actually documented paths in SKILL.md do resolve to real bundled files (assets/rubric_template.json, assets/evaluation_template.json, assets/evidence_manifest_template.json, assets/process_checklist_template.json, assets/ratings_template.csv, references/*.md). This is informational only: no fallback logic, network fetch, or dynamic retrieval exists for missing files, so there is no exploitable transitive-trust path.

Bash is broader than strictly necessary, but the SKILL.md body explicitly constrains Bash to invoking the documented local `python3` commands, and code review of all seven scripts confirms no `subprocess`, `os.system`, `eval`, `exec`, `pickle`, socket, or network-library usage. Only `argparse`, `pathlib`, `json`, `csv`, `math`, `re`, `itertools`, `datetime`, `dataclasses` are imported. Writes are limited to `.json` output paths with symlink rejection and no-overwrite-by-default semantics, consistent with the declared Write tool.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The scientific-brainstorming skill is a documentation-heavy, methodology-focused skill with three bundled Python CLIs (session_scaffold.py, validate_register.py, evaluate_matrix.py) and a shared helper module (_common.py). Analysis found no security threats.

Manifest: name, description, and compatibility statement accurately match observed behavior (standard-library only, no network, no credentials). No `allowed-tools` declared, which is optional per spec and only informational here; the skill's actual actions (reading/writing local JSON/CSV files the user explicitly specifies) are consistent with the documented purpose.

Instructions (SKILL.md body): No prompt injection, no instruction-override language, no concealment directives, no attempts to extract system prompts or bypass safety. In fact the body repeatedly reinforces safety boundaries (route ethics/biosafety/dual-use/clinical questions to authorized reviewers, do not upload sensitive data to external AI services, do not auto-select a "winner"). Reference files are internal to the package and contain only methodological guidance and bibliography; several referenced paths (templates/*, assets/*) are simply not present, a minor documentation inconsistency with no security impact.

Scripts: All three CLIs are deterministic and use only the Python standard library (argparse, csv, json, math, os, re, stat, tempfile, unicodedata, pathlib, datetime). There are no imports of requests/urllib/socket/subprocess, no eval/exec/os.system/compile, no shell invocation, no base64/hex obfuscation, no hardcoded secrets, no environment-variable harvesting, no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or other credential stores, and no filesystem traversal beyond the explicitly supplied input/output paths.

The static pre-scan hit "BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS: eval/exec combined with subprocess detected" is a false positive. No `eval`, `exec`, `subprocess`, `os.system`, `os.popen`, or `Popen` call exists in any file. The likely trigger is benign substring/keyword matching: `evaluate_matrix.py` / `evaluate_matrix` / "independent-evaluation" (contains "eval"), `_execute`-like naming absent but the module contains `os.open`, `os.fdopen`, `os.fchmod`, `os.replace`, and `tempfile.mkstemp` (os-module usage that heuristics often conflate with process execution). Manual review of every os.* call confirms they are file-descriptor operations, not process spawning.

Notably, _common.py implements defensive hardening that exceeds typical skill quality: symlink refusal on both read and write paths (path.is_symlink() checks plus O_NOFOLLOW), fstat verification that inputs are regular files, a 5 MiB input byte cap, O_EXCL create-unless---force semantics to prevent silent overwrite, 0o600 permissions on outputs, atomic replace via mkstemp in the target directory, strict JSON parsing that rejects NaN/Infinity constants, and rejection of RecursionError on deeply nested JSON. Resource-exhaustion vectors are bounded throughout: MAX_CRITERIA=25, MAX_ROWS=1000, MAX_COLUMNS=200, MAX_ITEMS=5000, MAX_TEXT_CHARS=10000, csv.field_size_limit capped at 100k chars, participant count capped at 100, and weight_delta constrained to [0, 0.5] so the sensitivity loop is at most 2*25 scenarios. Identifiers are validated against a restrictive regex (^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$), which also blocks path-traversal-style values in ID fields. Output paths must resolve to an existing parent directory and end in .json.

Cross-component consistency is strong: the description promises ideation facilitation with decision logs, and the scripts produce exactly that (a scaffold register, a structural validator, and a disclosed weighted matrix that leaves `decision` null with an explicit notice that no conclusion was drawn). No hidden capabilities, no tool chaining toward exfiltration, no cross-context bridging, no over-collection, no unbounded autonomy, no dependency installation or unpinned packages, and no external URL fetching at runtime (URLs appear only as citations in reference markdown).

Recommendation: safe to use. The only non-security observation is the set of missing referenced files under templates/ and assets/, which could be cleaned up for documentation hygiene.

The scientific-critical-thinking skill is a documentation/guidance package: SKILL.md plus six substantive reference markdown files covering scientific method, biases, statistical pitfalls, evidence hierarchy, logical fallacies, and experimental design. No script files are bundled with this skill, and all reviewed content is legitimate, high-quality methodological guidance with no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, credential access, obfuscation, or data-collection instructions. The declared purpose matches the actual content and the description appropriately scopes activation (and even defers to a `peer-review` skill), so there is no evidence of capability inflation or keyword baiting. The static analyzer's env-var/network exfiltration signals are explained by the documented, opt-in, user-requested figure-generation path that delegates to the separate `scientific-schematics` skill using OPENROUTER_API_KEY; this transmission is transparently disclosed in SKILL.md with a caution about sensitive content, so it is a low-severity third-party data-flow consideration rather than covert exfiltration. Minor issues are a manifest/instruction inconsistency (declared allowed-tools Read/Write/Edit while a bash command is shown for the companion skill) and multiple non-existent templates/assets references. Overall risk: LOW; the skill appears safe to use.

No malicious behavior was found: there is no prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directive, obfuscation, eval/exec, shell interpolation of user input, credential harvesting (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), or exfiltration to an attacker-controlled host. Remaining issues are hygiene-level: .env auto-loading from the current working directory, unpinned pip dependencies, several referenced documentation files that do not exist, and documented helper functions (run_quality_checks, detect_overlaps, etc.) that are not implemented. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The scientific-slides skill is a legitimate, well-documented presentation-authoring toolkit. Its behavior matches its manifest and description: it plans slide decks, calls an AI image-generation model via OpenRouter, assembles images into PDFs, converts PDFs to images, and validates slide decks. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directives, or role-redefinition attempts were found in SKILL.md or any reference file. No hardcoded secrets, no obfuscated/encoded payloads, no eval/exec of dynamic content, and no reads of credential stores (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, browser data, keychains) were present.

The static pre-scan flags (ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION, EVAL_SUBPROCESS, CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN) are false positives on review: the 'env var + network' pattern is the intended OPENROUTER_API_KEY being sent as the Bearer token to the documented OpenRouter endpoint; the 'eval/subprocess' pattern is sys.executable subprocess.run() with a fixed argv list (no shell=True, no string interpolation into a shell, no eval/exec of attacker data); and the 'cross-file chain' is simply the wrapper -> AI-script -> requests call path. Notably, the wrapper scripts implement a defensive allowlist (FORWARDED_ENV_VARS) so the child process receives only the API key plus benign networking/locale variables instead of the full parent environment — a security-positive design. The LaTeX compile path uses -no-shell-escape, blocking shell-escape code execution from untrusted .tex files.

Residual concerns are minor and inherent to the stated purpose: local image files supplied via --attach are base64-uploaded to a third-party service, SKILL.md encourages the agent to auto-discover and attach figures from the working directory, .env is auto-loaded from the current working directory, and dependencies are recommended unpinned. Overall risk: LOW.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The scientific-visualization skill is a well-engineered, benign publication-figure toolkit. All bundled Python scripts (export_plan.py, palette_audit.py, image_metadata.py, style_preview.py, figure_export.py, style_presets.py, assets/color_palettes.py, scripts/_common.py) perform only local, deterministic figure styling, export, and metadata inspection. There is no network access (no requests/urllib/socket/subprocess), no credential or environment-variable harvesting, no eval/exec of dynamic content, no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. The only dynamic module loading is importlib.util.spec_from_file_location pointed at the skill's own bundled assets/color_palettes.py (a static data file), which is normal for self-contained skill packages. The shared helper module _common.py actively implements defensive controls: symlink rejection for inputs and outputs, byte-size caps, refusal to overwrite without --force, atomic writes with 0600 permissions, and bounded report sizes. image_metadata.py additionally guards against decompression bombs (pixel limits), XML entity/DTD expansion (XXE/billion-laughs) in SVG, bounded element counts, and avoids executing PostScript. SKILL.md contains no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; instead it emphasizes scientific integrity and explicitly disclaims compliance certification. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep) match observed behavior (reading assets, writing figure/report files, running bundled CLIs). Dependencies documented in SKILL.md are exactly version-pinned (matplotlib==3.11.1, seaborn==0.13.2, plotly==6.9.0, kaleido==1.3.0, pillow==12.3.0, pypdf==6.14.2) and installed via isolated `uv run --isolated --no-project`, with the transitive-lock limitation explicitly disclosed. The static pre-scan flags (env-var exfiltration, eval/subprocess, cross-file exfiltration chains) are FALSE POSITIVES: `os` usage is limited to os.fdopen/os.fsync/os.chmod/os.replace/os.close and os.PathLike type hints in _common.py and figure_export.py; there is no os.environ/getenv read, no eval/exec/subprocess, and no outbound transmission primitive anywhere in the package, so no data-flow sink exists to complete an exfiltration chain. Several files listed as "referenced" are not found (e.g., references/sources.md variants under templates/), but these are documentation path-permutation artifacts of the scanner and represent at most minor documentation hygiene, not a security threat. No findings warrant reporting.

The scientific-writing skill is a well-engineered, defensive-by-design documentation and validation toolkit. All eight bundled Python scripts use only the standard library, make no network calls, read no environment variables or credential paths, perform no eval/exec/subprocess/pickle operations, and contain no hardcoded secrets or obfuscated payloads. The shared helper module (_common.py) enforces conservative safety bounds: file-size caps (5 MB), record/node/depth limits for JSON, CSV field-size limits, rejection of symbolic-link inputs, extension allow-lists, duplicate-JSON-key rejection, non-finite number rejection, and fail-closed write semantics (write_new_text refuses to overwrite existing paths or symlinks; scaffold_manuscript refuses to create into an existing directory and creates with mode 0o700). Input identifiers are validated against strict regexes before use, so no path traversal or injection vector is present. The SKILL.md instruction body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; on the contrary, it repeatedly requires human accountability, prohibits fabrication, and mandates explicit authorization plus policy review before any external transfer of unpublished, sensitive, PHI, or proprietary material. Data flow is strictly local: read local file -> validate -> print JSON issue codes/line numbers, with deliberate avoidance of echoing manuscript or source text (reducing sensitive-data leakage into agent logs). Manifest description matches actual behavior; no capability inflation or keyword baiting was detected, and the description is appropriately scoped to manuscript drafting/auditing. allowed-tools is not declared, which is optional per spec and only informational here (the skill legitimately needs Bash/Python/Read/Write for its documented CLIs, and behavior is consistent with the documented workflow). Referenced files: many listed paths under templates/ and duplicated assets/ or references/ variants were not found, but every file actually cited in SKILL.md (assets/*, references/*) resolves and contains benign, policy-oriented guidance; the "not found" entries appear to be scanner path-permutation artifacts rather than missing dependencies, and no external URL is fetched or executed - the source ledger lists URLs only as human-readable citations. No security findings warranting a report were identified.

The visible skill content (SKILL.md and references/api_reference.md) is high-quality, accurate scikit-bio documentation: sequence analysis, alignment, phylogenetics, diversity, ordination, statistics, and file I/O. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The scikit-survival skill is a well-engineered, defensively written statistics/ML tooling package and appears benign. All five bundled Python CLIs operate purely on local files with strict validation: `_common.py` centralizes input hardening (rejects URLs containing '://', rejects symlinks, requires regular files, enforces size/row/feature/time-point bounds, validates output suffixes, refuses to overwrite without --force, writes atomically with 0o600 temp files) and explicitly disables pickle (`np.load(..., allow_pickle=False)`, `np.save(..., allow_pickle=False)`, object-dtype rejection in `atomic_save_npz`). There is no network I/O anywhere: no requests/urllib/httpx/socket imports, no subprocess, no os.system, no eval/exec, no base64 or other obfuscation, and no credential or filesystem-wide traversal. No hardcoded secrets. The only environment-adjacent call is `importlib.metadata.version()` used to record package versions in a JSON report — this reads package metadata, not environment variables or secrets. Consequently the pre-scan's BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION, BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN, and BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION signals are assessed as FALSE POSITIVES: the 'exfiltration chain' corresponds to the intended, documented local pipeline (train_survival_model.py writes a bounded .npz that evaluate_survival_metrics.py reads, and model_report.py renders local JSON to local Markdown), with no external sink whatsoever. `model_report.py` additionally sanitizes rendered values (finite-float check, 160-char string cap, backtick stripping, aggregate-scalars-only) to prevent row-level data or markdown injection leaking into reports. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with observed behavior (reading local CSV/NPZ/JSON, writing JSON/NPY/NPZ/MD, running CLIs via Bash); no violation. Referenced files that resolve (references/*.md) contain only legitimate statistical documentation with links to official scikit-survival docs and academic DOIs; no instructions to fetch or execute remote content. The 'not found' assets/ and templates/ paths, plus sklearn.py/sksurv.py, are artifacts of the reference extractor matching prose examples and alternate directory conventions, not real missing dependencies — the skill body only references references/*.md, all of which are present. Repeated ethical guardrails ('not clinical advice', 'use only de-identified authorized local data', 'no PHI in reports') are appropriate rather than manipulative. No prompt injection, no jailbreak language, no concealment directives, no capability inflation (description is narrow and matches behavior). Only two low-severity hygiene observations are recorded.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The "shap" skill is a legitimate, well-documented machine-learning explainability guide. The SKILL.md body contains only technical guidance for using the SHAP library (explainer/masker selection, additivity validation, plotting), with no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language. The bundled script (scripts/tabular_report.py) is self-contained: it loads scikit-learn's built-in breast cancer dataset, trains a deterministic RandomForest, computes SHAP values, validates additivity, and writes CSV/JSON/PNG artifacts to a user-specified output directory. There are no network calls, no credential or environment-variable access, no eval/exec/os.system usage, no deserialization of untrusted artifacts, no obfuscation, and no hardcoded secrets. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Bash) are consistent with the documented behavior (reading bundled reference files and running the script via uv); the script writes only to the explicitly provided --output-dir, which is expected for a report generator invoked through Bash. Dependencies are pinned (shap[plots]==0.52.0) and installed into an isolated uv environment, which is good supply-chain hygiene. The reference documents notably reinforce safe practice, explicitly warning against deserializing untrusted pickle/joblib model artifacts, against printing environment variables or credentials in bug reports, and against embedding sensitive identifiers in exported plots. Several referenced filenames reported as "not found" (assets/*, templates/*, shap.py, sklearn.py) are artifacts of link/name extraction — shap.py and sklearn.py appear in troubleshooting text as examples of module-shadowing names to avoid, not as files to load. No security threats identified.

The "simpy" skill is a legitimate, well-engineered educational/tooling package for building bounded discrete-event simulations with SimPy. No security threats were identified.

Manifest: name and description accurately match behavior. `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob` is consistent with the scripts' actions (reading local JSON/CSV/JSONL inputs, writing local JSON/CSV/JSONL reports, invoking CLIs via Bash). No violation of declared restrictions.

Instructions (SKILL.md body): Contains only simulation-methodology guidance. No prompt injection, no instruction override, no concealment directives, no role redefinition, no attempts to bypass safety policies, and no requests to fetch or trust external content. References point to internal `references/*.md` files bundled with the package; the extra `templates/*` and `assets/*` paths reported as "not found" are artifacts of file-name matching against the reference filenames and are not fetched from external sources.

Scripts: All five Python files use only the standard library plus SimPy. There is no network activity (no requests/urllib/socket), no subprocess/os.system, no eval/exec/pickle/importlib dynamic loading, no environment-variable or credential access (no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, tokens), and no hardcoded secrets. The only "secret-like" constants are deterministic RNG seeds (DEFAULT_SEED = 20260723), which is benign.

Security-positive engineering was observed: strict JSON allowlists that reject unknown keys, duplicate keys, and NaN/Infinity constants; input path validation that rejects URLs and symlinks, requires regular files, and enforces size caps; output path validation that refuses symlinks and refuses overwrite without --force; atomic writes via mkstemp with chmod 0600; and explicit bounds on horizon, events, entities, replications, queue capacity, and trace records (mitigating resource exhaustion / infinite-loop risks). The BoundedEnvironment subclass enforces a hard event budget, and Student-t quantile inversion uses fixed iteration counts with explicit convergence failure, so no unbounded loops exist.

Minor, non-security notes only: `resource_monitor.py` and `EventTraceRecorder` monkey-patch SimPy instance methods and read the private `env._queue` attribute. This is documented in the skill's own references as an implementation-detail dependency requiring a pinned SimPy version; it is a maintainability/robustness concern within the user's own process, not a security threat (no privilege escalation, no external data flow). Documentation dates are set in 2026 and cite a SimPy 4.1.2 release that may not correspond to reality, but the install command is properly version-pinned (`simpy==4.1.2`) from the official PyPI index with no untrusted GitHub/direct-URL installs, so there is no supply-chain injection vector.

Data flow is entirely local: local file in → computation → stdout or local file out. No collection of data beyond the explicitly supplied configuration/artifact files, no directory traversal, no cross-context or cross-session behavior, and no autonomous escalation.

The stable-baselines3 skill is a documentation/template package for reinforcement learning with Stable Baselines3. Manifest metadata (name, description, compatibility, allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash) is consistent with the actual content: three template Python scripts that create Gymnasium environments, train PPO/SAC/DQN agents, save models/logs locally, and evaluate/record videos. No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language appears in the markdown body or reference files. No network exfiltration, credential/environment-variable access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, os.environ harvesting), hardcoded secrets, obfuscation/base64 stagers, or reverse shells were found. The static pre-scan flag \"BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS (eval/exec combined with subprocess)\" appears to be a false positive: the only matches are benign RL-domain terms — `evaluate_policy`/`evaluate_agent`/`eval_callback`/`eval_env` (substring \"eval\") and SubprocVecEnv/multiprocessing usage inherent to SB3's parallel environment feature. There is no Python `eval()`/`exec()` call, no `os.system`, and no `subprocess` invocation with user-controlled input anywhere in the package. File writes are limited to local ./logs, ./models, and ./videos directories, consistent with the declared Write/Edit permissions and stated purpose. Residual concerns are minor hygiene issues only: unpinned dependency version ranges in install instructions and several documentation references to files not present in the package. Model loading via PPO.load() on user-supplied paths involves pickle deserialization of untrusted checkpoints, which is an inherent SB3 behavior rather than a skill-introduced flaw, but users should only load trusted model files. Overall the skill appears benign and appropriate for its stated purpose.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The statistical-analysis skill is a legitimate, well-scoped research-methods helper. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; its "Statistical Integrity" section actually encourages transparency. The single bundled script (scripts/assumption_checks.py) performs only local, in-memory statistical computation using numpy/pandas/scipy/statsmodels/matplotlib: normality (Shapiro-Wilk), Levene's test, outlier detection, linearity, and OLS regression diagnostics. There are no network calls, no file system writes or traversal, no environment variable or credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, and no hardcoded secrets. Data flow is confined to a caller-supplied DataFrame, so there is no read→send or collect→upload tool-chaining pattern. The description is broad in activation scope (many statistical trigger phrases) but this proportionally matches the skill's genuine functionality and is not deceptive keyword baiting. The bundled reference markdown files contain only statistical documentation and code examples consistent with the stated purpose, with no embedded instructions to the agent and no external URLs used as instruction sources (only benign documentation links such as python.arviz.org). Remaining observations are hygiene issues: unpinned dependency install commands, absent optional manifest metadata, and several referenced files that are not present in the package. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate, well-documented statistics skill for power/sample-size analysis. All content is domain-appropriate and internally consistent: the YAML description, instruction body, reference markdown files, and both Python scripts all concern closed-form and Monte Carlo power calculations. No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language appears in SKILL.md or any reference file. The two Python scripts (power.py, simulate_power.py) use only numpy, scipy, statsmodels, pandas, and matplotlib for numerical computation; there are no network calls (no requests/urllib/socket/curl), no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no filesystem traversal, no reading of credential paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), no environment-variable access, and no hardcoded secrets or base64/obfuscated payloads. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with observed behavior — Bash is used only for optional dependency installation, and the only write operation is saving a matplotlib power-curve PNG to a user-supplied path (power_curve(save=...)), which matches the documented purpose. Referenced files resolve to internal, bundled markdown under references/; the \"not found\" entries for templates/ and assets/ variants are static-scanner path-guessing artifacts, not missing external fetches, and no external URLs are fetched or trusted. The pre-scan heuristics BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION, BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN, and BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION are assessed as FALSE POSITIVES: manual review of both scripts found no os.environ/getenv usage and no outbound network primitives whatsoever, so no read-then-send chain exists. Loops are bounded (n_sims counters, bisection capped at 200 iterations, explicit 1e6 guards in _reg_sample_size and find_sample_size), so no DoS/compute-exhaustion concern beyond the inherently CPU-intensive but user-parameterized nature of Monte Carlo simulation. The only observation worth noting is minor supply-chain hygiene from unpinned minimum-version dependency ranges. Overall risk: LOW — the skill appears safe to use.

The skill itself acknowledges this ("Pin versions in production; unpinned is fine for exploration"), and all packages are well-known mainstream scientific libraries from PyPI with no typosquatting indicators or direct GitHub/VCS installs.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The "statsmodels" skill is a legitimate documentation/reference skill for statistical modeling in Python. It contains no script files, no network calls, no credential access, and no obfuscated content. The SKILL.md body consists entirely of statistical modeling guidance, workflows, and best practices with no prompt-injection, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language. Referenced files that exist (references/*.md) contain only standard statsmodels code examples (OLS, GLM, ARIMA, diagnostics) that operate on user-supplied in-memory data; nothing reads sensitive paths or transmits data externally. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with documentation search (`rg`) and dependency installation guidance; the single install command (`uv pip install statsmodels==0.14.6`) is version-pinned, which is good supply-chain practice. Description accurately reflects behavior, and it even directs users to an alternative skill rather than over-claiming capability, so there is no capability inflation or keyword baiting. Several referenced paths (assets/*.md, templates/*.md) do not exist, but these appear to be scanner path-resolution artifacts rather than genuine references in the instruction body, and missing internal documentation files pose no security risk. External URLs are limited to official statsmodels.org documentation links presented for human reference, not for automated content ingestion, so there is no transitive-trust/indirect-injection vector. No security findings.

This is a legitimate documentation-only skill providing guidance on using the SymPy symbolic mathematics library. The YAML manifest (name, description, license, compatibility, allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash) is consistent with the content: a math-documentation skill that may write/run example code. No script files are actually present in the package; all content is benign markdown reference documentation containing standard SymPy API examples.

No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, role redefinition, or activation-priority manipulation was found. The description is narrowly scoped (symbolic math) and does not exhibit keyword baiting or capability inflation. There is no data exfiltration: no network calls, no HTTP libraries, no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, credential stores, or environment variables. No hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, no tool-chaining (read→send) patterns, no over-collection or directory traversal, and no unbounded autonomy directives.

The static pre-scan flags (env var exfiltration, eval+subprocess, cross-file exfiltration chain) are assessed as FALSE POSITIVES: they are triggered by benign documentation snippets discussing SymPy's code-generation/compilation features (codegen, autowrap/ufuncify, lambdify), pickle serialization examples, and explicit security warnings about parse_expr's internal use of eval. Notably, the skill proactively warns users NOT to call parse_expr on unsanitized input and shows input-validation patterns — the opposite of malicious intent.

Remaining issues are minor documentation/hygiene concerns: unpinned pip installs and broken/missing referenced file paths (assets/*, templates/*, sympy.py, matplotlib.py, scipy.py). Overall risk: LOW — the skill appears safe for use.

However, the documentation explicitly warns that `parse_expr()` uses eval internally, must never be used on unsanitized input, and provides validation guidance and restricted transformations. No skill-provided script performs eval/exec on untrusted input; the static pre-scan flags for eval+subprocess and env-var exfiltration appear to be false positives triggered by documentation snippets (codegen/autowrap, pickle, lambdify) rather than actual executable exfiltration logic. No network calls, credential access, or environment-variable harvesting exist anywhere in the package.

metadata.aisubtech_name: Safety Harms and Toxicity: Scams and Deception

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate vendor documentation skill for the Tamarind Bio computational-biology cloud platform. It contains no script files; all code is illustrative Python in markdown showing `requests` calls against the documented https://app.tamarind.bio/api endpoints and an MCP server at mcp.tamarind.bio. No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives ("do not tell the user"), safety-bypass language, obfuscation, base64/hex payload staging, eval/exec, subprocess execution, or reads of sensitive credential stores (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, browser data, shell history) were found in any provided content. The pre-scan's ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION and CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN signals are explained by the benign, documented pattern of reading TAMARIND_API_KEY from the environment and sending it as the `x-api-key` header to the skill's own declared vendor domain — repeated across four markdown files (SKILL.md, examples.md, api_reference.md, workflows.md), which is what produced the "cross-file chain" heuristic. The EVAL_SUBPROCESS signal is not corroborated by anything in the supplied text (no eval/exec/subprocess appears); it likely stems from unreviewed .py files in the inventory (7 python files reported but "No script files found" was passed for review) — those should be inspected separately before final clearance. The manifest description accurately matches the documented behavior, security hygiene is explicitly encouraged ("Never hardcode the key", "never commit keys"), and the skill even warns against a typosquat-adjacent risk ("the PyPI package named `tamarind` is an unrelated Neo4j tool. Do not `pip install tamarind`"), with no package installs or unpinned dependencies requested. Residual concerns are minor and design-inherent: runtime fetching of remote llms.txt/openapi.yaml as authoritative guidance, unbounded `while True` polling loops, inline-file-content upload semantics that could transmit unintended local files, a broad trigger-keyword list, and an undeclared `allowed-tools` field. Assessed as low risk overall.
llm_primary_threats: Third-party API credential handling (env var transmitted to external SaaS)
Transitive trust in runtime-fetched remote documentation/LLM index files
Unbounded polling loops (minor availability/resource concern)
Local file upload / inline-content disclosure to external platform
Broad trigger-keyword activation surface
Unverified static signal (eval/subprocess) in Python files not supplied for review

findings.title: API key read from environment and sent to external service (expected but noteworthy)
findings.description: The skill reads TAMARIND_API_KEY from the environment and transmits it as the `x-api-key` header to https://app.tamarind.bio/api and https://mcp.tamarind.bio/mcp. This is the documented, legitimate authentication mechanism for the declared vendor platform, and the skill explicitly instructs never to hardcode or commit keys. Static analyzers flagged this as "env var + network call" exfiltration, but the destination matches the declared purpose and vendor domain. Risk is limited to the credential being scoped to a single third-party SaaS provider.
findings.snippet:
HEADERS = {"x-api-key": os.environ["TAMARIND_API_KEY"]}
requests.get(f"{BASE}/tools", headers=HEADERS)
findings.remediation: No action strictly required. Ensure the key is scoped/rotatable, restrict egress to app.tamarind.bio / mcp.tamarind.bio, and avoid logging headers.

findings.title: Local file upload and inline-content semantics can lead to unintended data disclosure
findings.description: File-typed parameters treat a plain string value as INLINE FILE CONTENT that is uploaded to the vendor, and the skill documents `uploadFileContent(filename, content, encoding="base64")` for sending arbitrary local file bytes through the MCP channel. Combined with `PUT /upload/{filename}` reading local paths, an agent misresolving a filename or over-collecting could transmit unintended local files to a third party. This is inherent to the platform's design rather than a hidden backdoor, and the skill does warn about the inline-content foot-gun.
findings.snippet: "for a file-typed parameter, a plain string value is treated as inline file content" ... uploadFileContent(filename, content, encoding="base64")
findings.remediation: Require explicit user confirmation of the exact local path(s) before any upload, and never pass agent-generated or user-quoted strings into file params without confirming they are intended file references.

findings.title: Runtime fetching of remote schemas/instruction indexes (llms.txt, openapi.yaml) is treated as authoritative
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to prefer fetching live remote content (`https://app.tamarind.bio/llms.txt`, `https://app.tamarind.bio/openapi.yaml`, `https://docs.tamarind.bio/llms.txt`, and `.md` doc pages) over bundled copies, describing them as the "source of truth". `llms.txt` files are LLM-directed content, so a compromise or MITM of the vendor domain could inject instructions the agent would follow. This is a common and generally acceptable pattern for vendor API skills, but it does delegate trust to external network-sourced content.
findings.snippet: "Tamarind publishes live, machine-readable sources. Prefer fetching them at runtime over trusting any hardcoded list" — `https://app.tamarind.bio/llms.txt` — LLM index
findings.remediation: Treat fetched remote documents as data, not instructions; require HTTPS/cert validation, and do not execute or obey directives found in fetched llms.txt/docs content.

findings.title: Unbounded polling loops in example code
findings.description: Several examples use `while True:` polling loops with `time.sleep(15..30)` and no maximum attempt/timeout ceiling. The skill mitigates the most obvious hang by explicitly telling the agent to break on all terminal statuses (including `Deleted`), but a job stuck in `Running`, or an API returning an unexpected/missing status key, could cause indefinite looping and continuous network requests. Additionally, `parent.get("batchStatus")` returning None loops forever.
findings.remediation: Add a maximum wait/attempt bound and exponential backoff to polling examples, and handle missing/unknown status values by exiting the loop with an error.

findings.title: Large trigger-keyword list in metadata broadens activation surface
findings.description: The manifest includes a `trigger-keywords` field with ~30 comma-separated terms (AlphaFold, Boltz, ESMFold, docking, x-api-key, adme, enzyme, peptide, protein language models, molecular design, ...). The keywords are all genuinely in-domain for the described functionality, so this is not deceptive capability inflation, but the breadth (e.g. generic terms like "molecular design", "enzyme", "peptide", "x-api-key") could cause the skill to activate for local/offline cheminformatics requests. The skill does partially mitigate this by stating that purely local work should use RDKit/BioPython.
findings.snippet: 'trigger-keywords': 'protein structure prediction, AlphaFold, Boltz, Chai, ESMFold, ... x-api-key, developability, adme, enzyme, peptide, protein language models, molecular design'
findings.remediation: Trim generic keywords to those uniquely tied to Tamarind/cloud execution to reduce unintended activation.

findings.title: `allowed-tools` not declared while skill requires network, filesystem writes, and code execution
findings.description: The manifest omits the optional `allowed-tools` field even though the documented workflows require outbound HTTP, Python execution, and local file writes (writing result zips, `pending_jobs.json`, reading arbitrary local PDB/SDF files for upload). Missing `allowed-tools` is informational per spec, but declaring it would make the network/write footprint explicit and reviewable. No restriction violation is present since none is declared.

- allowed-tools: Not specified
... open("my-alphafold-run.zip", "wb").write(requests.get(url).content)
findings.remediation: Declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash, Python]` (or the minimal needed set) to make the capability footprint explicit.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill is a legitimate, documentation-style reference for TileDB-VCF genomic variant storage. The description accurately matches the instruction body, and there are no script files bundled with the package. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, role redefinition, or system-prompt extraction attempts were found in any language. No data exfiltration, credential harvesting, obfuscated/encoded payloads, reverse shells, or command-injection patterns are present — all code blocks are illustrative Python/CLI examples using the official tiledbvcf API, and all network endpoints are legitimate TileDB/vendor domains (cloud.tiledb.com, github.com/TileDB-Inc). The static pre-scan hit for 'eval/exec combined with subprocess' appears to be a false positive: no eval, exec, os.system, or subprocess constructs appear in the supplied content (likely triggered by benign strings such as 'executed in a distributed fashion' or example shell blocks). Residual concerns are minor and hygiene-related: unpinned conda/pip/docker installation commands with auto-confirm flags, documentation-level guidance to export an API token to an environment variable, missing optional allowed-tools/compatibility metadata, and a notable vendor upsell section promoting TileDB-Cloud. Overall risk: LOW.
llm_primary_threats: Unpinned dependency/supply-chain installation guidance
Credential handling guidance via environment variables (informational)
Missing optional manifest metadata (no declared allowed-tools)
Vendor promotional/upsell content embedded in instructions

findings.title: Guidance to store API token in environment variable / cloud credential usage
findings.description: The skill documents exporting a TileDB Cloud REST token to an environment variable (TILEDB_REST_TOKEN) and referencing cloud credential names (acn="my-s3-credentials"). No hardcoded secrets exist and no code reads or transmits secrets; this is standard vendor documentation. Noted only as informational since the agent would be handling authentication tokens in shell context (risk of token leakage into shell history/logs).
findings.snippet: export TILEDB_REST_TOKEN="your_api_token"
findings.remediation: Recommend using a credentials file or secret manager instead of exporting tokens inline, and warn users not to paste real tokens into chat/shell history.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools and compatibility metadata; promotional vendor content
findings.description: The manifest omits the optional 'allowed-tools' and 'compatibility' fields, so no tool restrictions are declared even though the instructions direct the agent to run Bash installs and Python code. The instructions also include a substantial marketing/upsell section for TileDB-Cloud (pricing, sales@tiledb.com contact, signup links). This is commercial promotion rather than a security exploit, and it is consistent with the stated genomics purpose, but it slightly broadens the skill beyond pure technical reference.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified; compatibility: Not specified; 'Contact: sales@tiledb.com for enterprise needs'
findings.remediation: Declare allowed-tools explicitly (e.g., [Read, Bash, Python]) and clearly separate vendor promotional content from technical guidance.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions (conda/pip/docker)
findings.description: The skill instructs installation of packages via mamba/conda/pip and pulling Docker images without version pinning or checksum verification (e.g., 'pip install tiledb-cloud', 'mamba install -y -c conda-forge -c bioconda -c tiledb tiledb-py tiledbvcf-py ...', 'docker pull tiledb/tiledbvcf-py'). Channels and images used are the legitimate upstream TileDB/bioconda sources, so risk is low, but unpinned installs with '-y' auto-confirm could pull unexpected/compromised versions.
findings.snippet:
mamba install -y -c conda-forge -c bioconda -c tiledb tiledb-py tiledbvcf-py pandas pyarrow numpy
pip install tiledb-cloud[life-sciences]
docker pull tiledb/tiledbvcf-py
findings.remediation: Pin package versions (e.g., tiledbvcf-py==0.x.y) and Docker image digests/tags, and avoid '-y' auto-approval so the user can review what is installed.

findings.title: Referenced helper files (tiledbvcf.py, tiledb.py) do not exist in package
findings.description: The instructions reference file names tiledbvcf.py and tiledb.py (these are actually Python import module names, not bundled scripts) which the scanner resolved as missing referenced files. No executable scripts ship with the skill, so there is no code to audit; the risk is only that an agent may attempt to read or create non-existent local files. Note: the pre-scan 'eval/exec + subprocess' heuristic is not corroborated by any content in the provided SKILL.md, which contains no eval, exec, os.system, or subprocess usage.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: tiledbvcf.py (not found); Referenced File: tiledb.py (not found)
findings.remediation: Clarify that these are PyPI/conda module imports rather than bundled scripts, or bundle the referenced example scripts so their contents can be reviewed.
