scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The timesfm-forecasting skill appears benign and well-engineered. Its stated purpose (zero-shot univariate time-series forecasting with Google's TimesFM, plus a resource preflight checker) matches the actual code behavior across all scripts. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directives, or role-redefinition text was found in SKILL.md or the reference documents; the instruction body is purely technical documentation. No credential access (no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, keyring, or browser profile reads), no environment-variable harvesting beyond a benign HF_HOME lookup for disk-space checking, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation/base64/hex payloads, no eval/exec/os.system with interpolated input, and no outbound network transmission of local data. Subprocess usage is limited to fixed-argument, read-only system introspection (`sysctl -n hw.memsize`, `vm_stat`) with no shell=True and no user-controlled arguments. File operations are scoped: reads are of user-specified CSVs and skill-internal example data; writes go only to user-specified output paths or the skill's own examples/*/output directories. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the observed behavior of running Python/Bash scripts and writing forecast outputs. Data flow is local-only (CSV in → forecast CSV/JSON/PNG/GIF/HTML out); the only network egress is pulling official model weights from HuggingFace and a Chart.js CDN reference embedded in generated HTML — neither is used as an instruction source for the agent. Referenced documentation files that exist (references/*.md) are legitimate technical content with no embedded directives; several listed \"missing\" references (assets/*, templates/*, torch.py, timesfm.py, statsmodels.py) are false-positive extractions from prose/module names rather than real missing dependencies, though references/system_requirements.md, api_reference.md, and data_preparation.md are cited in SKILL.md and do resolve. Remaining findings are low-severity supply-chain hygiene (unpinned pip installs, unpinned HF revision, CDN script without SRI) and an availability consideration (a --skip-check flag that can bypass the otherwise well-implemented OOM-prevention preflight). No malicious behavior identified; safe to use with normal dependency-pinning hygiene.
llm_primary_threats: Unpinned dependency and remote artifact retrieval (supply-chain hygiene)
Bypassable resource preflight enabling potential memory exhaustion

findings.title: Remote model weights and CDN script fetched at runtime
findings.description: Scripts download TimesFM weights from HuggingFace (`from_pretrained("google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch")`) without revision pinning or checksum verification, and the generated HTML embeds a remote CDN script tag (`https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js`) without SRI. This is expected behavior for a foundation-model skill and the sources are official/well-known, but unpinned remote artifacts are a mild supply-chain consideration. No model or web content is treated as instructions for the agent, so this is not indirect prompt injection.
findings.snippet:
model = timesfm.TimesFM_2p5_200M_torch.from_pretrained("google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch")
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js"></script>
findings.remediation: Pin the HF `revision` for reproducibility and add a subresource-integrity hash (or vendor the JS locally) for the Chart.js include.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions
findings.description: SKILL.md instructs the agent/user to install packages (`uv pip install timesfm[torch]`, `pip install torch>=2.0.0`, `pip install timesfm[xreg]`) without pinned versions. This is a minor supply-chain hygiene issue: an unpinned install could pull a newer or compromised release. All packages referenced are legitimate, well-known upstream projects (timesfm from Google Research, torch, jax/flax), and no third-party GitHub or unknown index is used besides the official PyTorch wheel index.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install timesfm[torch]
pip install torch>=2.0.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121
findings.remediation: Pin versions (e.g., timesfm==1.x.y, torch==2.4.1) and prefer a lockfile so the agent installs reproducible, verified dependencies.

findings.title: Resource-intensive model loading with bypassable safety preflight
findings.description: The skill loads a 200M-parameter model (~800MB download, ~1.5GB RAM) and forecast_csv.py exposes a `--skip-check` flag that bypasses the mandatory RAM/disk/GPU preflight, which could lead to memory exhaustion or unresponsive systems on constrained machines. Notably, the skill is designed defensively: check_system.py blocks on insufficient RAM/disk and forecast_csv.py exits non-zero when preflight fails by default. Batch sizes are bounded and derived from detected hardware. Risk is informational rather than malicious.
findings.snippet: parser.add_argument("--skip-check", action="store_true", help="Skip system preflight check (not recommended)")
findings.remediation: Require explicit user confirmation for `--skip-check`, and cap `per_core_batch_size` / `max_context` when the check is skipped to avoid OOM on low-resource hosts.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
This is a legitimate technical documentation skill for PyTorch Geometric (PyG) authored by K-Dense Inc. It contains no executable scripts of its own — all code is illustrative Python inside markdown fenced blocks demonstrating standard PyG APIs (Data/HeteroData construction, GCN/GAT/SAGE/GIN layers, MessagePassing subclassing, NeighborLoader sampling, GAE/VGAE link prediction, GNNExplainer, custom dataset classes, and DDP training).

No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, role redefinition, or safety-bypass language was found in the SKILL.md body or any reference file, in English or any other language. There are no eval/exec/os.system calls on untrusted input, no reverse shells, no obfuscated or base64-encoded payloads, no hardcoded credentials or API keys, no reads of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, or credential stores, no filesystem traversal, and no read-then-send tool chains.

The pre-scan's ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION and CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN signals are assessed as false positives: the only os.environ writes are MASTER_ADDR='localhost' and MASTER_PORT='12345' for torch.distributed process-group initialization, and the only network endpoints are official project domains (pytorch.org, data.pyg.org, github.com/pyg-team, captum.ai) plus a placeholder 'https://example.com/data.csv' in a download_url() docs sample that the file itself annotates with a trusted-source/checksum caution.

Description-to-behavior consistency is strong and appropriately scoped (it even explicitly narrows activation: "Use when working with torch_geometric, not for general NetworkX analytics or non-graph PyTorch models"), so there is no capability inflation or keyword baiting. Remaining observations are minor hygiene issues: missing optional allowed-tools, unpinned pip installs from the official PyG wheel index, and several dangling referenced file paths (largely import-heuristic artifacts). Overall risk: LOW — safe to use.

findings.title: Static analyzer env-var/network flags are benign DDP setup code, not exfiltration
findings.description: Pre-scan flagged 'environment variable access with network calls' and a cross-file exfiltration chain. Manual review of the referenced files shows the only environment variable usage is standard PyTorch distributed setup (os.environ['MASTER_ADDR'] = 'localhost', os.environ['MASTER_PORT'] = '12345') inside documentation code blocks for multi-GPU DDP training, plus dist.init_process_group('nccl'). No environment variables are read and transmitted anywhere. Network references are limited to legitimate, well-known domains (pytorch.org, data.pyg.org, github.com/pyg-team, captum.ai) and an illustrative 'https://example.com/data.csv' in a download_url() docs example that is explicitly accompanied by a caution to use trusted sources and verify checksums. This finding is informational only — the static signal appears to be a false positive.
findings.snippet:
os.environ['MASTER_ADDR'] = 'localhost'
os.environ['MASTER_PORT'] = '12345'
dist.init_process_group('nccl', rank=rank, world_size=world_size)

download_url('https://example.com/data.csv', self.raw_dir)  # "Use trusted sources only; verify checksums"
findings.remediation: No action required. Optionally note in docs that download_url() fetches remote data and should only target trusted, checksum-verified sources (already stated).

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation from external wheel index
findings.description: Installation instructions use unpinned package installs (`uv pip install torch`, `uv pip install torch_geometric`) and install optional extension wheels from an external index (`-f https://data.pyg.org/whl/torch-2.8.0+cu128.html`). While data.pyg.org is the official PyG wheel host and the packages are legitimate upstream projects, unpinned versions mean the resolved artifact can change over time, which is a mild supply-chain consideration. No typosquatting, no GitHub installs from unknown repos, and no post-install hooks were observed.
findings.snippet:

uv pip install torch_geometric
uv pip install pyg-lib torch-scatter torch-sparse torch-cluster \
  -f https://data.pyg.org/whl/torch-2.8.0+cu128.html
findings.remediation: Pin exact versions (e.g., torch_geometric==2.7.0) consistent with the stated compatibility matrix, and reference hash/index-verified installs where possible.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `torchdrug` skill is a legitimate, well-scoped documentation/reference package for building TorchDrug 0.2.1 machine-learning workflows. No script files are present; all content is markdown guidance describing standard TorchDrug APIs (datasets, models, tasks, core.Engine). No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, or role redefinition was found in SKILL.md or the reference files. There is no network exfiltration, credential access, environment-variable harvesting, obfuscation, eval/exec, or hidden data collection. Bash snippets are limited to benign version checks (`python --version`, printing torch/torchdrug versions) and installation commands that use pinned versions (torch==2.0.0, torch-scatter==2.1.1, torch-cluster==1.6.1, torchdrug==0.2.1) sourced from the official PyG/PyTorch wheel index, which is good supply-chain hygiene rather than a risk. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the described activity of generating/debugging code and running installation/version commands. External links point only to official TorchDrug docs and the upstream GitHub release page and are cited as documentation, not as instruction sources to be blindly executed, so no transitive-trust/indirect-injection issue arises. The description is specific and matches content, so no capability inflation or keyword baiting. Several referenced paths listed by the scanner (assets/*.md, templates/*.md, torch.py, torchdrug.py) are not present; these appear to be false-positive extractions from code snippets and prose (e.g., `import torchdrug`, `protein.pdb`) rather than real missing dependencies, and the genuinely referenced references/*.md files that were provided are benign. Overall, the skill appears safe.

The `transformers` skill is a documentation-only reference package for the Hugging Face Transformers library. SKILL.md and the five bundled references/*.md files contain no prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment directives, no obfuscated payloads, and no hardcoded secrets. All code examples are standard, publicly documented Transformers/Hub API usage (pipelines, AutoModel loading, generate(), Trainer, tokenizers). Network activity is limited to huggingface.co model download/upload, which matches the declared description and compatibility notes. The static pre-scan's ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION and CROSS-FILE EXFILTRATION CHAIN alerts are false positives: they stem from documented HF_TOKEN/HF_HOME environment usage co-located with legitimate Hub download and push_to_hub examples, and the skill's own security guidance explicitly warns against hardcoding tokens, recommends secret managers, minimal token scope, and HF_HUB_DISABLE_IMPLICIT_TOKEN=1. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with installing packages and writing training scripts; dependencies are version-pinned to exact releases, which is good supply-chain hygiene. The only residual notes are informational: trust_remote_code=True is mentioned (with an appropriate reviewed-code caveat), push_to_hub transmits local artifacts externally, and a few scanner-inferred referenced files are absent from the package. No malicious behavior identified; the skill is assessed as benign.

findings.title: Documented environment variable (HF_TOKEN) usage combined with Hub network calls
findings.description: Static pre-scan flagged environment variable access combined with network calls (HF_TOKEN / HF_HOME plus Hugging Face Hub downloads and push_to_hub uploads). Review of SKILL.md and reference documentation shows this is legitimate, expected behavior for the Hugging Face Transformers library: the token is used to authenticate to huggingface.co for gated/private model downloads and optional model/tokenizer uploads. The documentation explicitly discourages hardcoding tokens, recommends `hf auth login`, secret managers, narrowest token scope (`read` vs `write`), and `HF_HUB_DISABLE_IMPLICIT_TOKEN=1`. No exfiltration to third-party or attacker-controlled endpoints is present. Residual (informational) risk: workflows such as `trainer.push_to_hub()` / `model.push_to_hub()` / `tokenizer.push_to_hub()` transmit locally trained artifacts to an external service using an env-supplied credential, so users should confirm before uploading.
findings.snippet:
export HF_TOKEN="..."  # Read token from a secret manager, not source code
trainer.push_to_hub("username/my-finetuned-model")
model.push_to_hub("username/model-name")
findings.remediation: No action strictly required. Optionally note that push_to_hub uploads local data to huggingface.co and should be run only with explicit user confirmation, and keep the existing guidance to use read-scoped tokens for download-only workflows.

findings.title: Documentation mentions trust_remote_code=True (arbitrary code execution risk from Hub models)
findings.description: The SKILL.md body instructs use of `trust_remote_code=True` for gated or custom architectures. This flag causes arbitrary Python code hosted in the model repository to execute locally, which is a genuine supply-chain/code-execution vector when applied to untrusted Hub repos. The skill does mitigate this by scoping it to cases where the model card requires custom code "you have reviewed", so the guidance is responsible rather than malicious.
findings.snippet: **Gated or custom architectures:** accept the model license on the Hub, then load with `trust_remote_code=True` only when the model card requires custom code you have reviewed.
findings.remediation: Keep and strengthen the existing caveat: recommend pinning a specific `revision=` commit hash when using trust_remote_code, and prefer safetensors-only models without remote code where possible.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `treatment-plans` skill is a defensively engineered, documentation-only clinical formatting/validation toolkit and shows no evidence of malicious behavior. All six bundled Python scripts operate purely on local JSON files using the standard library: there is no network I/O, no environment-variable or credential access, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no pickle, no base64 or obfuscated payloads, and no hardcoded secrets. Security posture is notably strong: `_common.py` implements strict path hardening (rejects URL-like paths, UNC/network shares, NUL bytes, and symlinks), fail-closed output handling (no implicit overwrite, atomic writes with 0o600/0o700 permissions), and robust JSON parsing controls (duplicate-key rejection, non-finite number rejection, size/depth/node/list/string bounds) that mitigate resource-exhaustion and JSON-parser confusion attacks. Reports are deliberately minimized to rule codes, counts, and field paths so clinician-authored content and PHI are not echoed. The markdown body contains no prompt injection, jailbreak, concealment, role-redefinition, or system-prompt-extraction language; instead it establishes explicit refusal boundaries, an emergency-routing escalation rule, a privacy data gate prohibiting transmission to any external model/API/telemetry service, and a fail-closed release gate requiring human clinician sign-off. The description accurately matches implemented behavior (no capability inflation or keyword baiting), file reads are limited to the skill's own `assets/` templates and user-specified local package directories, and there are no third-party dependencies or installation steps, so supply-chain exposure is nil. Only two LOW/informational issues were identified: the optional `allowed-tools` field is absent despite documented Bash/Python usage, and a number of referenced documentation paths do not resolve in the analyzed package. Neither issue enables data exfiltration, code execution, or clinical decision-making. Note also the bundled references/security_validation.md, which self-documents a prior remediation removing network calls, API keys, and environment access — the current code is consistent with that claim.

findings.title: Missing optional allowed-tools declaration
findings.description: The YAML frontmatter does not declare `allowed-tools`, although the skill instructs the agent to execute several bash/python commands (script invocation, unittest discovery, ast parsing). This is informational only: the field is optional per the Agent Skills spec, and the documented behavior (local standard-library JSON processing, local file writes) matches the actual script implementations. No network, subprocess, environment-variable, or credential access appears in any bundled script.
findings.snippet: - allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Optionally declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash]` to make the required tool surface explicit and auditable.

findings.title: Several referenced documentation files are missing from the package
findings.description: SKILL.md and references/README.md point to reference files that are not present in the analyzed package (e.g. references/shared_decision_handoff.md is present but numerous scanner-derived path variants such as templates/*.md and assets/*.md are absent). Missing referenced files can cause incomplete guidance for the safety boundaries the skill relies on, but no malicious or external content is fetched — all reads target internal, bundled paths only.
findings.snippet: Referenced but not found: assets/README.md, assets/safety_scope.md, assets/privacy_governance.md, templates/*.md, references/*_template.json
findings.remediation: Ensure every path named in SKILL.md exists in the package, or remove stale references so the documented safety and privacy guidance is always resolvable.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The SKILL.md body itself is a clean, technically accurate documentation-style skill for UMAP dimensionality reduction. It contains no prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment directives, no credential access, no network exfiltration, and no autonomy or over-collection patterns; all code samples are ordinary scikit-learn/UMAP/HDBSCAN usage, dependencies are version-pinned, and it even includes defensive advice about module shadowing. Discovery metadata is narrowly scoped to UMAP workflows with no keyword baiting or capability inflation.\n\nThe significant concern is a manifest-to-package mismatch: the submission states 'No script files found' and SKILL.md documents no bundled scripts, yet the file inventory reports 2 Python files, and static analyzers flagged environment-variable-plus-network exfiltration chains across those files as well as eval/exec combined with subprocess. Those file bodies were not provided for review, so the findings cannot be confirmed and are rated MEDIUM rather than CRITICAL. Manual inspection of the two undisclosed Python files is required before this skill should be trusted. Additionally, the documentation pins umap-learn==0.5.12 and describes it as an April 2026 release, which appears to be a fabricated version claim and should be corrected.

findings.description: Static analysis reported BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS (dynamic evaluation via eval/exec together with subprocess invocation) in the package's Python files. A documentation-only UMAP reference skill has no legitimate need for dynamic code evaluation or shell/process spawning. If present, this enables arbitrary code execution on the user's machine. Content of the flagged files was not supplied, so severity is capped at MEDIUM pending verification.

findings.remediation: Review the Python files and eliminate eval/exec and subprocess usage, or replace with explicit, non-dynamic library calls. If execution is required, validate inputs against an allowlist and require user confirmation.

findings.description: The manifest does not declare `allowed-tools` or `compatibility`, yet the instructions direct the agent to run shell installs (`uv pip install ...`) and execute Python code. Missing allowed-tools is optional per spec (informational), but combined with the reported presence of undisclosed executable Python files, the absence of tool scoping removes a useful guardrail.

findings.remediation: Declare an explicit minimal `allowed-tools` list (e.g., Read, Python) and add compatibility notes. If package installation is required, state it explicitly so users can consent.

findings.title: Static analyzers report env-var exfiltration and eval/subprocess chains in undisclosed Python files
findings.description: The pre-scan file inventory lists 2 Python files in the package, but the skill submission shows 'No script files found' and SKILL.md never documents any bundled executable scripts. Static analyzers flagged BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION (environment variable access combined with network calls), BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN across 2 files, and BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION. If accurate, the package contains undisclosed code that harvests environment variables (potential API keys/credentials) and sends them over the network — behavior wholly unrelated to the stated dimensionality-reduction purpose. Because the file bodies were not provided for review, this cannot be confirmed and is rated MEDIUM pending manual inspection of the two Python files.
findings.snippet: Pre-scan: BEHAVIOR_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION; BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_EXFILTRATION_CHAIN: 2 files; BEHAVIOR_CROSSFILE_ENV_VAR_EXFILTRATION: 1 files — while SKILL.md declares no scripts.
findings.remediation: Manually inspect and disclose all .py files in the package. Remove any os.environ harvesting combined with outbound HTTP requests, or document and justify the network destinations. Publish the script list in SKILL.md so declared capability matches shipped code.

findings.title: Reference-file resolution artifact: import names mistaken for bundled scripts
findings.description: The reference extraction lists umap.py, sklearn.py, hdbscan.py, matplotlib.py, and tensorflow.py as referenced-but-missing files. These names appear in SKILL.md only inside a defensive 'Common Issues' note warning users not to create local modules that shadow installed packages. findings.snippet: Do not keep project files named `umap.py`, `sklearn.py`, `hdbscan.py`, or `tensorflow.py` beside notebooks or scripts.
findings.remediation: Escape or rephrase module names so they are not parsed as file references, and explicitly enumerate the actual bundled files (e.g., references/api_reference.md) in the skill documentation.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The "uncertainty-and-units" skill is a legitimate, well-engineered scientific metrology toolkit. All six bundled CLIs are self-contained, standard-library-first Python programs that perform unit conversion, GUM uncertainty propagation, Monte Carlo sampling, result formatting, static code auditing, and physical plausibility checks. No security threats were identified.

Specific checks performed:
- SKILL.md body: purely technical metrology guidance. No prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment directives, no role redefinition, no safety-bypass language in any language.
- Manifest consistency: description (unit tracking, uncertainty propagation, code auditing) matches script behavior exactly. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with local CLI execution and optional --output file writes; nothing exceeds them.
- Code execution safety: user-supplied measurement expressions are NOT passed to eval/exec/compile. `_common.parse_expression` parses with `ast.parse(mode="eval")`, whitelists node types, rejects underscore-prefixed names, restricts calls to a fixed function whitelist, forbids keyword args, and bounds character count, node count, nesting depth, and literal exponents. `reduce_expression` performs an explicit interpreter walk over only + - * / ** and named handlers. This is a notably conservative design.
- audit_units.py parses target files with `ast.parse` and explicitly never imports or executes them.
- File I/O safety: `checked_input_file`/`checked_output_file` reject `://` URLs, reject symlinks, require regular files, enforce suffix allowlists, bound input size (4 MiB), require existing non-symlink parent directories, and refuse to overwrite without --force. Writes are atomic via same-directory mkstemp with 0o600 permissions.
- Network/credentials: zero network calls (no requests/urllib/socket/subprocess). No access to ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, environment variables, or any credential store. No hardcoded secrets or tokens.
- Obfuscation: no base64/hex blobs, no dynamic imports of attacker-controlled names, no hidden payloads. Imports are limited to stdlib plus pint/uncertainties/numpy/scipy.
- Resource limits: MAX_TRIALS, a 40M sample-budget guard, MAX_VARIABLES, MAX_COMPONENTS, MAX_ENTRIES, MAX_FILES, and report size caps bound compute and memory. No unbounded loops or retries.
- Supply chain: dependencies are fully version-pinned (pint==0.25.3, uncertainties==3.2.3, numpy==2.5.1, scipy==1.18.0) and installed only via a documented command the user runs explicitly; no automatic installs, no GitHub/direct-URL installs, no typosquat-looking names.
- Referenced files: reference markdown files are internal to the package; four exist and contain benign technical documentation with no embedded instructions to the agent. Several listed paths (assets/*, templates/*, scipy.py) are artifacts of the reference-extraction heuristic rather than real declared dependencies; their absence is a documentation-completeness nit, not a security issue.
- External URLs in SKILL.md point to authoritative standards bodies (BIPM, NIST, PyPI, ReadTheDocs) and are cited as reading material only; the agent is not instructed to fetch and follow their contents.
- Data flow: no read-then-send chains, no over-collection, no directory traversal, no cross-session/context bridging.

Provenance is declared (version 1.0, skill-author K-Dense Inc., MIT license). Overall the skill demonstrates defensive-programming practices well above typical, and is assessed as safe.

The `usfiscaldata` skill is a documentation-oriented reference package for querying the public U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data REST API. All content reviewed (SKILL.md plus six reference markdown files) is consistent with the stated purpose: it documents endpoints, query parameters, response formats, and provides read-only Python/R examples using `requests`/`pandas` against the single legitimate domain `api.fiscaldata.treasury.gov` (a genuine .gov endpoint requiring no authentication). No prompt injection, instruction overrides, concealment directives, role redefinition, or safety-bypass language was found in any human language. No credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, env harvesting), no exfiltration sinks, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscation/base64 stagers, and no external-URL instruction fetching were observed. Notably, the pre-scan flag 'BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS: eval/exec combined with subprocess' appears to be a FALSE POSITIVE: no `eval()`, `exec()`, `os.system`, or `subprocess` calls exist in the reviewed content. The only bash-like content is a documentation `uv pip install requests pandas` snippet, and the only dynamic-looking constructs are benign f-string URL/filter composition and `pd.to_numeric`/`pd.to_datetime` conversions. Pagination helpers are explicitly bounded (`max_pages=50`, `max_records=500_000`, capped `page[size]`, exponential backoff on HTTP 429), which mitigates rather than creates resource-exhaustion risk. Remaining observations are hygiene-level: unpinned dependency versions, an over-broad `allowed-tools` declaration (Write/Edit/Bash for a read-only reference skill), and several unresolved assets/templates reference paths. Overall the skill appears benign and low risk.
llm_primary_threats: Unpinned dependency installation (minor supply-chain hygiene)
Over-broad declared allowed-tools (over-permissioning)

findings.title: Declared allowed-tools broader than needed (Write/Edit/Bash for a read-only API reference skill)
findings.description: The manifest declares `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash` while the skill is purely a documentation/reference skill for issuing HTTP GET requests to a public Treasury API. No script performs file writes or modifications, so Write/Edit permissions are unnecessary and broaden the blast radius if the skill content were later modified. This is an over-permissioning hygiene concern, not an observed exploit.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash
findings.remediation: Reduce allowed-tools to the minimum required (e.g., Read, Bash) for executing example queries.

findings.remediation: Pin dependency versions (e.g., `requests==2.32.3 pandas==2.2.3`) or defer installation to the user/environment manager.

findings.remediation: Ensure all referenced paths resolve within the package; remove stale references.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The 'vaex' skill is a documentation-only skill that teaches use of the legitimate open-source Vaex library for out-of-core DataFrame analytics. No executable scripts are shipped (no .py or .sh payloads present in the package as delivered). The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment directives, and no role redefinition; instructions are consistent with the declared description and with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) — Bash is legitimately used for pip installs and Write/Edit for exporting data files. All substantive referenced content is internal to the package (references/*.md) and contains only standard, accurate Vaex API examples: opening HDF5/Arrow/Parquet/CSV files, aggregations, plotting, ML transformers, and I/O. The static analyzer's 'env var exfiltration' and 'cross-file exfiltration chain' signals appear to be false positives triggered by ordinary cloud-storage documentation (~/.aws/credentials, s3fs/gcsfs keys, s3://gs:// export calls, SQLAlchemy connection strings) rather than any autonomous read-then-send behavior; there are no hardcoded real secrets, no attacker-controlled domains, no eval/exec/os.system, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, no home-directory traversal, and no over-collection. Residual issues are minor hygiene concerns: unpinned dependency installs and a set of dangling file references (including a non-existent vaex.py). Overall risk: LOW — the skill appears benign.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions
findings.description: SKILL.md instructs installing packages via `uv pip install vaex` and `uv pip install vaex-core vaex-viz vaex-hdf5 vaex-ml`, plus `uv pip install s3fs gcsfs adlfs`, without pinned versions. These are well-known legitimate PyPI packages (no typosquatting indicators), but unpinned installs allow supply-chain drift and unexpected version behavior.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install vaex
uv pip install vaex-core vaex-viz vaex-hdf5 vaex-ml
uv pip install s3fs gcsfs adlfs
findings.remediation: Pin versions (e.g., `vaex==4.19.0`) or reference a lockfile/requirements file with hashes to ensure reproducible, verifiable installs.

findings.title: Documentation demonstrates cloud credential usage and remote/cloud data transfer patterns
findings.description: Reference documentation includes examples that read cloud credentials (~/.aws/credentials, environment variables, gcsfs token files) and export DataFrames to remote destinations (s3://, gs://, ws:// Vaex server), as well as SQL connection strings with inline credentials. These are legitimate, standard Vaex library usage patterns and are documented as user-driven operations, not automated collection or exfiltration to attacker-controlled endpoints. This likely accounts for the static analyzer's 'env var exfiltration' and 'cross-file exfiltration chain' heuristics (credential/env references co-located with network I/O examples in docs). Informational only.
findings.snippet:
df = vaex.open('s3://bucket-name/data.parquet')  # default credentials (~/.aws/credentials or env vars)
fs = s3fs.S3FileSystem(key='access_key', secret='secret_key')
engine = create_engine('postgresql://user:password@host:port/database')
df.export_parquet('s3://bucket-name/output.parquet')
findings.remediation: No action strictly required. Optionally add a note advising users to avoid hardcoding access keys/secrets in code and to prefer environment-based or role-based credential providers, and to confirm destination buckets before exporting data.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The venue-templates skill is a benign academic writing/formatting helper. Its three Python scripts perform only local, well-scoped operations: enumerating bundled LaTeX scaffolds from a hardcoded in-file dictionary, copying a bundled template to a user-specified output path with placeholder substitution, and invoking Poppler's pdfinfo/pdffonts on a user-supplied PDF via subprocess.run with a fixed argument list (no shell=True, no user-controlled command name). There are no network calls, no imports of requests/urllib/socket, no environment-variable or credential access, no eval/exec, no base64 or other obfuscation, no dependency installation, and no filesystem traversal beyond the skill's own assets directory and explicit user-provided paths. The pre-scan's flags for 'environment variable exfiltration', 'eval/exec combined with subprocess', and 'cross-file exfiltration chain' are FALSE POSITIVES: no os.environ/getenv, no eval/exec, and no outbound transmission exist anywhere in the package; the only subprocess use is a hardcoded pdfinfo/pdffonts invocation. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; on the contrary it repeatedly instructs verification against official sources and discourages presenting scaffolds as official templates. The description accurately matches implemented behavior and is appropriately scoped (no keyword baiting or activation-priority manipulation). Bundled .tex assets and reference markdown contain only ordinary LaTeX boilerplate and writing guidance with legitimate publisher/agency URLs (nature.com, plos.org, nsf.gov, nih.gov, neurips.cc, etc.) presented as documentation for human/agent verification rather than as content to be fetched and obeyed. Only minor hygiene issues were identified: unescaped user text inserted via re.sub (regex backreference/LaTeX escaping robustness), an undeclared optional allowed-tools field, and several documented file paths that do not exist in the package.

findings.title: Unescaped user input written into LaTeX output via regex substitution
findings.description: customize_template.py inserts user-supplied --title/--authors/--affiliations/--email values into a .tex file using re.sub without escaping. Regex backreference sequences (e.g. \1, \g<0>) or LaTeX control sequences in user input can corrupt output or, if the resulting .tex is later compiled with shell-escape enabled, could contribute to command execution. Impact is limited: the script writes only to a user-specified output path and performs no compilation itself. SKILL.md already warns 'User-provided text may need LaTeX escaping.'
findings.snippet: content = re.sub(pattern, replacement, content, count=1)
findings.remediation: Use re.sub with a lambda replacement (or re.escape on replacement backslashes) to avoid backreference interpretation, and sanitize LaTeX special characters (\, {, }, $, %, &, #, _, ~, ^) in user-provided values.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The visible content of what-if-oracle is benign: SKILL.md and references/scenario-templates.md contain only a structured scenario-planning prompt framework with no prompt injection, no concealment directives, no role redefinition, no safety-bypass language, and no external URL fetching (the only links are DOI citations and a GitHub upstream reference, which are not instructed to be retrieved and executed). The description accurately matches the documented behavior, and reading its own bundled references file is normal, expected self-contained behavior.\n\nThe significant concern is a content/inventory discrepancy: the package reportedly contains 2 Python files and 1 Bash script whose contents were not provided and which are never mentioned in SKILL.md, and static analyzers flagged environment-variable access combined with outbound network calls forming a cross-file exfiltration chain across those files. For a documentation-only reasoning skill, there is no legitimate justification for env-var harvesting plus network egress. Because the actual code was not supplied for review, this is rated MEDIUM (unverified but plausible credential exfiltration) rather than CRITICAL; manual inspection of the hidden scripts is required before trusting this package. Secondary issues are the missing allowed-tools/compatibility declarations and two dangling references to non-existent template files.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is the Anthropic-authored `xlsx` skill (vendored by K-Dense Inc.) for creating, editing, and validating Excel/OOXML files. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, jailbreak, concealment, or instruction-override language — it is entirely domain guidance about openpyxl, formula compatibility, and financial-model formatting conventions. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) are consistent with the scripts' behavior (local file I/O plus invoking `soffice`, `gcc`, `git diff`, and `timeout`). No network calls, no credential/environment harvesting (soffice.py in fact deliberately allowlists environment variables so agent secrets are NOT forwarded to the converter subprocess), no hardcoded secrets, no base64/obfuscated payloads, no eval/exec of dynamic input. Security-positive practices are present: defusedxml for XML parsing, a safe_extract() zip-slip/symlink guard, atomic rezip, and a refusal path that protects external-link cached values. The only notable risk is the AF_UNIX socket workaround in scripts/office/soffice.py, which compiles an embedded C shim with gcc at runtime and injects it via LD_PRELOAD into soffice; the code is transparent and its purpose is documented, but the fixed, predictable /tmp artifact path is reused with only an existence check, creating a local shim-hijacking opportunity. The static pre-scan's \"eval/exec + subprocess\" hit corresponds to lxml/defusedxml parsing and subprocess.run calls, not dynamic code evaluation. Overall: benign, well-engineered document-tooling skill with one hardening gap.
llm_primary_threats: Runtime C compilation and LD_PRELOAD library injection with predictable /tmp artifact path (local hijack risk)
Unpinned pip install fallback (minor supply-chain exposure)

findings.title: Unpinned pip install fallback instruction
findings.description: SKILL.md instructs the agent to run `pip install` for openpyxl, pandas, or markitdown if an import fails or the markitdown command is missing. No version pinning or index restriction is specified, so a fallback install could pull an unexpected or compromised version. Risk is low because the package names are well-known and the install is only a fallback.
findings.snippet: Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.
findings.remediation: Pin versions (e.g. openpyxl==3.1.5) and prefer a curated/internal index when the agent must install dependencies.

findings.title: Runtime C code compilation and LD_PRELOAD injection into soffice subprocess
findings.description: scripts/office/soffice.py writes an embedded C source file to the system temp directory, compiles it with gcc at runtime, and injects the resulting shared object into LibreOffice via LD_PRELOAD. The shim hooks socket/listen/accept/close/read libc calls and can call _exit(0) on the process. While the stated purpose (working around blocked AF_UNIX sockets in sandboxes) is plausible and the source is fully visible (not obfuscated), this is a legitimate-but-high-risk pattern: it performs local code generation + compilation + library injection, and the artifact path (/tmp/lo_socket_shim.so) is a predictable, world-writable location. A pre-existing or attacker-planted file at that path would be reused without integrity checking (it only checks existence), allowing local privilege/code-execution hijacking of every subsequent soffice invocation.
findings.snippet:
_SHIM_SO = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "lo_socket_shim.so"
...
def _ensure_shim() -> Path:
    if _SHIM_SO.exists():
        return _SHIM_SO
    src = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "lo_socket_shim.c"
    src.write_text(_SHIM_SOURCE)
    subprocess.run(["gcc", "-shared", "-fPIC", "-o", str(_SHIM_SO), str(src), "-ldl"], check=True, capture_output=True)
...
env["LD_PRELOAD"] = str(shim)
findings.remediation: Create the shim in a private, non-predictable directory (tempfile.mkdtemp with 0700 permissions) rather than a fixed /tmp path, or verify a hash of the compiled artifact before reuse. Document the LD_PRELOAD behavior in SKILL.md and make it opt-in only when AF_UNIX is actually blocked.

findings.remediation: Remove eval/exec or use safer alternatives

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill is a documentation-only reference guide for the Zarr-Python 3 library. All supplied content (SKILL.md plus five bundled reference markdown files) consists of legitimate technical documentation: array creation, chunking/compression, storage backends, Dask/Xarray integration, performance patterns, and v2-to-v3 migration notes. No prompt injection, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language was detected in any language. No executable scripts were included; the referenced 'zarr.py' and all 'assets/'/'templates/' paths are absent, which is a documentation hygiene issue rather than a security threat. Notably, the credential guidance is defensive rather than exploitative — it explicitly advises using IAM roles/workload identity, never printing or logging credential values, and not inspecting broad .env files. Installation commands use pinned versions ('zarr==3.2.1', 's3fs==2026.4.0') and advise lockfiles, showing good supply-chain hygiene; no unpinned or typosquatted packages, no GitHub installs from unknown repos. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with a docs skill that shows shell install commands, and no behavior exceeds them. All external URLs point to official zarr/xarray/dask documentation and are cited as reading material only — the skill does not instruct the agent to fetch and execute remote content. The pre-scan EVAL_SUBPROCESS signal could not be corroborated against any provided file and appears to be a false positive from generic code-fence pattern matching. Overall risk: LOW; the package appears benign.

findings.title: Static analyzer flag (BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS) not reproducible in provided content
findings.description: The pre-scan reported 'eval/exec combined with subprocess' and the file inventory lists one Python file, but no script files were provided for review and the referenced 'zarr.py' resolves as not found. All provided content is documentation-only markdown containing illustrative zarr/numpy/dask/xarray API snippets with no eval, exec, os.system, subprocess, network exfiltration, or credential access. This finding is informational: the flagged Python file could not be inspected, so its behavior is unverified.
findings.remediation: Provide the missing Python file for review or remove the dangling 'zarr.py' reference. Verify no eval/exec/subprocess usage exists in any bundled script before distribution.

findings.title: Third-party skill referencing upstream project name (minor provenance concern)

The SKILL.md does explicitly disclose that it is a community guide and not an official zarr-developers package, which mitigates most impersonation concern. Noted only as informational provenance context; no deceptive behavior, keyword stuffing, or activation-priority manipulation was found, and the description accurately matches the documentation content.

"This skill is a **community guide** maintained by K-Dense Inc., not an official zarr-developers package."
